items.title: WeaveVLA: 3D Relational Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Models
items.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage pretrained vision-language representations for instruction-conditioned robot control, yet their understanding of task-relevant 3D relations and how these relations evolve during manipulation remains largely implicit. To address this challenge, we introduce WeaveVLA, a framework that enhances VLA action generation by explicitly modeling task-relevant relative 3D relations…
items.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage pretrained vision-language representations for instruction-conditioned robot control, yet their understanding of task-relevant 3D relations and how these relations evolve during manipulation remains largely implicit. To address this challenge, we introduce WeaveVLA, a framework that enhances VLA action generation by explicitly modeling task-relevant relative 3D relations and maintaining relational context across observations. WeaveVLA employs a task-conditioned sparse graph neural network to encode relative 3D relations among objects, the gripper, and nearby references. Pair-specific recurrent edge states integrate geometric evidence across observations to maintain evolving spatial context. A learned-query readout summarizes the updated graph representations into compact relational tokens, which condition the action expert alongside the original vision-language context. An auxiliary geometry reconstruction objective further encourages spatial structure preservation. We instantiate WeaveVLA on StarVLA-GR00T and π_{0.5}, achieving over 98\% average success on LIBERO with both backbones. On LIBERO-Plus, WeaveVLA improves success from 74.9\% to 82.0\% and from 85.7\% to 87.8\%, respectively, with additional improvements on CALVIN DrightarrowD. On three real-world tasks, the StarVLA-GR00T-based variant improves average success from 55.6\% to 70.0\% under standard conditions and from 33.3\% to 53.3\% under OOD perturbations, surpassing the π_{0.5} baseline in both settings.

items.title: MORSE: Optimizing Streaming Memory Design via Open-World Auto-Research
items.summary: A streaming video system must decide in a single pass what evidence to retain under bounded frame storage, before it knows which details a future question will require. Recent recursive self-improvement methods automate the design of the harness that stores and retrieves this evidence. They revise the harness in response to failures, but the editor must still devise each repair from its prior knowledge and a…
items.abstract: A streaming video system must decide in a single pass what evidence to retain under bounded frame storage, before it knows which details a future question will require. Recent recursive self-improvement methods automate the design of the harness that stores and retrieves this evidence. They revise the harness in response to failures, but the editor must still devise each repair from its prior knowledge and a predefined set of tools. A failure that recurs across videos, however, may point to a problem that prior work has already addressed. We introduce MORSE (Memory Optimization with Recursive Self-Evolvement), an open-world auto-research framework that uses recurring failures to guide an online search for solutions. Its editor groups failures in training traces by cause, then searches papers, model cards, and code for methods it can adapt or pretrained perception models it can use. When the editor introduces a new perceptual capability, it can also revise how the harness stores and retrieves the resulting evidence for a frozen video-language model. On held-out validation streams, MORSE first selects revisions that improve answer quality, then seeks faster revisions that preserve those gains within a specified tolerance. Across three streaming video benchmarks, MORSE consistently achieves the highest answer accuracy within each frozen-backbone comparison. On OVO-Bench, our Qwen3-VL-8B harness answers queries in 0.30 seconds on average while achieving 75.1% accuracy, 3.1 percentage points ahead of the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen backbone.

items.title: From Rewarding What Models Say to How They Think: Attention Process Reward Model for LLM Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important component in large language models (LLMs). However, existing RL approaches focus on final outputs or textual solution trajectories, leading to coarse-grained rewards and unreliable reasoning. Such paradigms focus mainly on what the model outputs while overlooking how the model internally reasons. Therefore, can we reward how a model thinks internally rather than…
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important component in large language models (LLMs). However, existing RL approaches focus on final outputs or textual solution trajectories, leading to coarse-grained rewards and unreliable reasoning. Such paradigms focus mainly on what the model outputs while overlooking how the model internally reasons. Therefore, can we reward how a model thinks internally rather than merely what it says? We first reveal the problem of textual reward aliasing in existing reward modeling approaches. Motivated by this, we propose the Attention Process Reward Model (APRM), which assigns internal rewards based on hidden states and attention maps to capture high-quality reasoning patterns. With only approximately 46M parameters, APRM is trained using ranking and counterfactual objectives, and its reward guides RL optimization while being periodically updated to handle distribution shifts. Integrated with representative RL methods, APRM achieved an average pass@8 gain of 2.88\%. Our results demonstrate the promise of incorporating internal reasoning signals into RL for LLMs.

items.title: ViDiHand2: Unifying Video Diffusion Priors and Hand Geometry for 3D Hand Motion Reconstruction in the Wild
items.summary: Learning robot manipulation from egocentric human videos requires accurate metric 3D hand motion. Recent methods leverage pretrained video diffusion model (VDM) priors to recover occluded hands directly from full-frame videos, but their appearance-based depth regression generalizes poorly to unseen cameras. In this work, we propose ViDiHand2, a geometry-driven framework that reformulates VDM-based hand depth…
items.abstract: Learning robot manipulation from egocentric human videos requires accurate metric 3D hand motion. Recent methods leverage pretrained video diffusion model (VDM) priors to recover occluded hands directly from full-frame videos, but their appearance-based depth regression generalizes poorly to unseen cameras. In this work, we propose ViDiHand2, a geometry-driven framework that reformulates VDM-based hand depth estimation from direct regression into fine-grained geometric constraint solving. Specifically, we introduce Fine-Grained Geometric Lifting and Clip-Level Ray Fitting, which recover metric depth by enforcing geometric consistency between pixel-aligned 2D joints and the metric structure of MANO hands, while leveraging temporal observations across the clip. Since the lifting relies on these 2D joints, to improve robustness under occlusion and image truncation, we further develop Confidence-Gated Fusion to adaptively combine geometrically lifted joints with MANO predictions according to localization confidence. Finally, we enhance the VDM backbone to better capture spatial-temporal representations and produce the per-frame 2D joint and MANO predictions that both steps rely on. Extensive experiments on seven public datasets demonstrate that ViDiHand2 consistently outperforms 18 baselines, reducing in-the-wild absolute joint error by 42% and detection failures by 8.82x compared with the best baseline on each metric, while running at 57 FPS. The code is available at https://github.com/NTUYWANG103/ViDiHand.

items.title: MMMem: Self-Improving Agents with Task-Aware Multimodal Experience Consolidation
items.summary: AI agents accumulate conversations, images, and documents through long-term interactions with users. Answering later questions often requires connecting evidence across these records, yet the resulting understanding is rarely retained, allowing mistakes to recur on related questions. Existing multimodal memory methods largely focus on storing and retrieving records, with limited mechanisms for learning from…
items.abstract: AI agents accumulate conversations, images, and documents through long-term interactions with users. Answering later questions often requires connecting evidence across these records, yet the resulting understanding is rarely retained, allowing mistakes to recur on related questions. Existing multimodal memory methods largely focus on storing and retrieving records, with limited mechanisms for learning from completed tasks and consolidating task-specific experience. We therefore propose MMMem, a task-aware multimodal memory framework that extracts and consolidates experience from completed tasks through four complementary strategies. First, source-linked multi-view memory organizes original text, images, and rendered pages alongside generated scene images that combine clues across records for retrieval. Second, source-generated tasks support knowledge alignment at two levels: warm-up consolidates source knowledge into task-relevant experiences in external memory, while self-training adapts the model's parametric knowledge to task demands. Third, the same vision-language model distills completed tasks into experiences that record the task context, conclusion, and support links. Finally, task-aware retrieval recalls source views and relevant experiences for answering and verification, while source-supported reuse guides long-term retention. Across three memory benchmarks and two vision-language readers, MMMem outperforms eight baselines. With Qwen3.5-9B, MMMem achieves relative gains of 36.9%, 17.6%, and 15.2% over the best-performing baselines on LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2, respectively. Ablations show consistent gains from training and memory warm-up, while case studies illustrate how individual components work in practice.

items.title: UUBench: Understanding the Unspoken toward Full-Duplex Multimodal Interaction
items.summary: Effective real-time, full-duplex multimodal interaction requires systems to understand not only what users say, but also the communicative needs conveyed through prosody, facial expressions, gestures, and context, and to generate audiovisual responses that appropriately address those needs. Existing evaluations offer limited insight into whether systems translate an understanding of such unspoken needs into…
items.abstract: Effective real-time, full-duplex multimodal interaction requires systems to understand not only what users say, but also the communicative needs conveyed through prosody, facial expressions, gestures, and context, and to generate audiovisual responses that appropriately address those needs. Existing evaluations offer limited insight into whether systems translate an understanding of such unspoken needs into effective responses. We introduce UUBench, a benchmark for assessing how well multimodal interactive systems Understand the Unspoken intent and address users' implicit communicative needs. The inherent subjectivity of implicit intent inference poses a key challenge for evaluation. To address this, we introduce Process-Oriented Scoring, which grounds the assessment of intent fulfillment in observable auditory and visual cues, such as prosody and gestures. Rather than relying solely on a single overall score, it evaluates how well a response addresses the communicative needs conveyed by each applicable primitive dimension. We aggregate the dimension-level scores according to each dimension's relevance to the annotated evidence. Beyond intent fulfillment, Outcome-Oriented Scoring evaluates the naturalness, appropriateness, and human-likeness of the reply itself under audio-only, visual-only, and audiovisual conditions. To make these judgments traceable to observable evidence, we propose a Fact-Grounded Scoring JEV module, which uses structured, timestamped audiovisual observations of the user and the digital human's reply to assess one dimension or criterion at a time. UUBench provides a foundation for assessing whether multimodal interactive systems respond effectively to meaning beyond literal wording, supporting progress toward context-aware, real-time, full-duplex interaction.

items.title: WeMM-Ecom: Advancing Multimodal Content Understanding for WeChat E-Commerce
items.summary: We present WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models that deliver frontier e-commerce capabilities while achieving state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales. The family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. Our training pipeline begins with two-stage continued pre-training that progressively raises the…
items.abstract: We present WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models that deliver frontier e-commerce capabilities while achieving state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales. The family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. Our training pipeline begins with two-stage continued pre-training that progressively raises the proportion of e-commerce data within a diverse multimodal data mixture, followed by hybrid-thinking post-training that combines on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning to support both non-thinking and thinking modes. For evaluation, we construct a comprehensive suite of 28 e-commerce benchmarks (23 in-house and five open-source) covering eight business scenarios and complement it with 64 public general-purpose benchmarks. On the e-commerce suite, WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B surpasses substantially larger open-source flagship models, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, HY4, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. On the general-purpose suite, every WeMM-Ecom model surpasses its similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterpart, with the lightweight variants (e.g., WeMM-Ecom-2B) showing clear advantages over leading lightweight models such as Qwen3.5-2B, MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B, and LFM3-VL-2B. Beyond benchmarks, WeMM-Ecom now powers hundreds of production use cases in WeChat, including catalog management, multimodal product search, and livestream commerce, serving billion-scale requests per day. We publicly release all model weights and detail our data curation, training recipe, and benchmark construction to facilitate future work on domain-specialized multimodal models. We have released the model weights and code to facilitate future research at https://github.com/Tencent/WeMM-Ecom.

items.title: Embo-Harness: Towards Understanding Frontier-Model-as-Policy Harness
items.summary: Frontier multimodal models exhibit extraordinary generalization in generating robot actions from observations and instructions, enabling a new paradigm in which they serve directly as policies within closed-loop robotic harnesses. However, the design principles of such harnesses, and the capabilities underlying their strong performance, remain unclear. We present Embo-Harness, a framework for systematically studying…
items.abstract: Frontier multimodal models exhibit extraordinary generalization in generating robot actions from observations and instructions, enabling a new paradigm in which they serve directly as policies within closed-loop robotic harnesses. However, the design principles of such harnesses, and the capabilities underlying their strong performance, remain unclear. We present Embo-Harness, a framework for systematically studying frontier-model-as-policy harnesses. We investigate four components of the robotic agentic loop, namely, prompting, planning, action execution, and tool use, and distill six empirical findings into a practical recipe. This recipe prioritizes interfaces that exploit the model's native visual reasoning and tool-use capabilities over handcrafted plans, skills, or action priors, and identifies effective choices for action representation, chunking, reasoning effort, visual observations, short multi-action sequences, and policy refinement. On RoboLab-120, Embo-Harness achieves an 83.3\% success rate, outperforming the strongest reported baseline by 26.2 percentage points. It also succeeds in 15 of 20 zero-shot trials across four real-world manipulation tasks. Beyond performance, controlled interventions indicate that the studied model depends more strongly on accurate spatial target estimation than on explicit low-level joint or trajectory generation. These results provide both a practical recipe for building strong frontier-model-as-policy harnesses and a clearer account of the capabilities that drive their performance.

items.title: What Makes Good Data for Training Coding Agents? A Systematic Study on SWE-Gym
items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains coding agents on software tasks whose hidden tests decide the reward, yet task collections check these tests only against the reference fix. We ask what makes a task good training data, focusing on the correctness of its reward labels. We audit SWE-Gym with two LLM families, and a suspected error counts only if execution reproduces it. items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains coding agents on software tasks whose hidden tests decide the reward, yet task collections check these tests only against the reference fix. We ask what makes a task good training data, focusing on the correctness of its reward labels. We audit SWE-Gym with two LLM families, and a suspected error counts only if execution reproduces it. We find that unsolved often means mislabelled: 74% of the tasks that a 9B base model never solves have a test that rejects correct fixes (a false negative), versus 20% of those it sometimes solves. We repair or remove such tasks, and the audited tasks that remain train better policies. At equal size and matched difficulty, models trained on them score 2.4 and 2.7 points higher on held-out tasks from SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro than models trained on the original tasks, whereas simply dropping the never-solved tasks shows no such gain. We further find that wrong patches that pass (false positives) make up about a quarter of all passing patches, and that new tests that catch a quarter of them do not change held-out scores detectably. A pass rate shows whether a task yields reward, not whether that reward is right, so the reward labels themselves must be checked. To this end, we release SWE-Gym-Verified with its 1,087 audited tasks, every verdict with its executed evidence, our training sets, and the full audit pipeline.

items.title: HIVE-Bench: Evaluating Patch-Level Visual Representations for Egocentric Robot Manipulation
items.summary: Pretrained vision is a common start for robot learning, but most comparisons still score one pooled vector from a third-person image. Bimanual policies instead read dense patch tokens from cameras on the robot. We introduce HIVE-Bench: one shared flow-matching policy reads 20 encoders from seven families on 24 egocentric bimanual tasks, across adaptation, task sharing, and sweeps of data, model size, and layer.…
items.abstract: Pretrained vision is a common start for robot learning, but most comparisons still score one pooled vector from a third-person image. Bimanual policies instead read dense patch tokens from cameras on the robot. We introduce HIVE-Bench: one shared flow-matching policy reads 20 encoders from seven families on 24 egocentric bimanual tasks, across adaptation, task sharing, and sweeps of data, model size, and layer. Keeping the patches matters. Averaging each view to one token removes most of the success, adaptation helps every pair we test, and one shared policy keeps most of the success of separate policies at a fraction of the updates. The same tokens are then scored with statistics, state and object readouts, published vision scores, and an inverse-dynamics readout. That readout of the commanded motion is one of the strongest measurements available before a policy is trained. Recognition, depth, and correspondence do not transfer reliably. Fine-tuning can improve the action readout even when other measurements move the other way, and no statistic is stable enough to replace a rollout before any deployment.

items.title: RUIBench: What Makes a Good Robot-Use Interface?
items.summary: Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging. We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI), which determines how agents express and execute physical actions. To systematically study its impact, we introduce RUIBench, comprising 30 manipulation tasks across five suites spanning world…
items.abstract: Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging. We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI), which determines how agents express and execute physical actions. To systematically study its impact, we introduce RUIBench, comprising 30 manipulation tasks across five suites spanning world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation. We further develop RUIKit, a unified framework that crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms, yielding 13 interfaces under shared perception and control. In simulation, changing only the RUI shifts a frontier agent's success rate from 45% to 81%, and that of a fine-tuned 4B model from 13% to 47%. Our analysis reveals that effective interfaces reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback, with their benefits shaped by agent behavior and physical uncertainty. We further uncover a verification gap, where agents frequently declare success despite observable failures, revealing the need for task-level verification beyond individual actions. Together, these findings establish RUI design as a critical factor in embodied agent reliability.

items.title: WorldLeague: Benchmarking Physical Agency
items.summary: AI systems can now operate Blender, follow instructions in complex video games, and manipulate objects with robot arms. What range of physical goals can today's AI systems achieve autonomously? Answering this question requires testing systems on tasks that demand different combinations of perception, memory, planning, and action. We introduce WorldLeague, a benchmark that compares AI systems on a common set of 60…
items.abstract: AI systems can now operate Blender, follow instructions in complex video games, and manipulate objects with robot arms. What range of physical goals can today's AI systems achieve autonomously? Answering this question requires testing systems on tasks that demand different combinations of perception, memory, planning, and action. We introduce WorldLeague, a benchmark that compares AI systems on a common set of 60 simulated robot tasks by measuring progress toward each task's physical goal from the robot's trajectory. Robots explore scenes to gather evidence in WorldSeek, rearrange objects in WorldShape, and adapt to changes in WorldShift. Tying these goals to a single control interface limits which AI systems can be compared. In WorldLeague, vision-language models (VLMs) choose targets and motions, while vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs) use their native controls. For each of six capability dimensions, we measure how much progress a system makes toward its goals (Interactive Score) and how often it achieves them (physical success rate). Together, these measures form the system's Physical Agency Profile. Among 13 representative AI systems, Claude Fable 5.2 achieves 13 of the 60 goals and earns the highest mean Interactive Score (28.58/100). Fable leads in four dimensions, while GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra tie for first on rule-following tasks. Even when VLMs answer every final question correctly, they receive an Interactive Score of zero in 71.8\% of those episodes. WorldLeague gives Embodied AI, Physical AI, and Agentic AI a shared basis for comparing what AI systems achieve autonomously, from partial progress toward a physical goal to full goal completion. Project Webpage: https://xyangzhou.github.io/WorldLeague

items.title: Write, Evolve, Read: Streaming Cameras into a Persistent World State for 4D Occupancy Forecasting
items.summary: 4D occupancy forecasting predicts the 3D semantic occupancy of a driving scene seconds ahead. Over a few seconds, the scene changes little while the vehicle moves, so most of the space ahead has already been seen. Sorting the future into unchanged, changed, and unseen space, we find that current camera-based world models fall short on the unchanged part: they fail to hold on to what they have already seen, rather…
items.abstract: 4D occupancy forecasting predicts the 3D semantic occupancy of a driving scene seconds ahead. Over a few seconds, the scene changes little while the vehicle moves, so most of the space ahead has already been seen. Sorting the future into unchanged, changed, and unseen space, we find that current camera-based world models fall short on the unchanged part: they fail to hold on to what they have already seen, rather than to forecast what will change. We therefore make what the model has seen its state. PersistWorld streams camera frames into a persistent 3D world state anchored in the scene, writing each frame once instead of rebuilding the state from past frames. The state is learned end to end with the forecast, and an evolver predicts it at any queried time along the ego trajectory. On Occ3D-nuScenes, PersistWorld raises the IoU of the best camera-based world model by 19 points at 1-3 s and by 18 to 24 points up to 8 s, while running more than twice as fast. Code and models: https://github.com/wangzian828/PersistWorld. Project page: https://wangzian828.github.io/PersistWorld

items.title: Distill the Correction, Not the Rewrite: Hindsight Twins for Self-Improving Text-to-Image Models
items.summary: Text-to-image models can learn from their own mistakes by distilling a self-teacher conditioned on a vision-language critic's revised prompt. However, such self-teachers barely improve alignment, and both they and their hindsight-contrast variants absorb the critic's unintended additions to the scene, such as lighting or scenery. We attribute this to two factors: (1) the prompt already specifies the desired fix, so…
items.abstract: Text-to-image models can learn from their own mistakes by distilling a self-teacher conditioned on a vision-language critic's revised prompt. However, such self-teachers barely improve alignment, and both they and their hindsight-contrast variants absorb the critic's unintended additions to the scene, such as lighting or scenery. We attribute this to two factors: (1) the prompt already specifies the desired fix, so a useful revision must go beyond the failed span, often rewriting the entire scene and adding details that overshadow the fix; (2) although the critic localizes the error to a single span, self-teachers condition on the rewrite, entangling the intended fix with unintended additions. Motivated by these insights, we propose Hindsight Twins (HinT), which fills the critic's revision template once with the intended fix and once with the observed error and distills only their velocity difference, anchored at the user's prompt. Because text encoders spread the edit of a single slot to all other tokens, HinT further aligns the twins' token states outside the slot. Across Qwen-Image-2512, SD3.5-M, and FLUX.2-klein, HinT keeps the rate of critic-induced bias at the base-model level while matching or exceeding the alignment gains of prior self-distillation, and it keeps improving over twelve rounds of self-training where contrastive baselines decay.

items.title: GameDojo: Benchmarking Real-Time Interactive Agents in Video Games
items.summary: Interactive intelligence requires agents to act on observations and adapt to the consequences of actions. Studying these abilities calls for diverse, challenging tasks under controlled conditions. We introduce GameDojo, a controllable interactive gameplay benchmark of 120 boss encounters across 20 games for evaluating model capabilities, learning algorithms, and agent harnesses. Coding agents reconstruct the…
items.abstract: Interactive intelligence requires agents to act on observations and adapt to the consequences of actions. Studying these abilities calls for diverse, challenging tasks under controlled conditions. We introduce GameDojo, a controllable interactive gameplay benchmark of 120 boss encounters across 20 games for evaluating model capabilities, learning algorithms, and agent harnesses. Coding agents reconstruct the environments and write gameplay scripts, producing GameDojo-Data with 600 hours of gameplay trajectories. Experiments reveal substantial challenges for frontier models, especially in real-time interaction. Training on GameDojo-Data brings GameDojo-4B to frontier performance, with the strongest real-time performance. We also find joint training improves individual tasks, and learned policies transfer across bosses. Together, these findings establish GameDojo as a challenging and valuable interactive gameplay benchmark for the community. Our project page is at https://gamedojo-benchmark.github.io/ , and our code is at https://github.com/THUSI-Lab/GameDojo .

items.title: Typhoon OCR 2: From Thai Document Transcription to Multilingual, Multi-Task OCR
items.summary: Typhoon OCR 1.5 focused on reading Thai documents. However, in real-world workflows, users often need to extract specific information or preserve the structure of an entire page for further processing. Typhoon OCR 2 handles both tasks in a single model, with prompt-driven extraction and structured full-page parsing. Full-page parsing covers Thai, English, and Chinese. We release compact 2B and 0.8B models adapted…
items.abstract: Typhoon OCR 1.5 focused on reading Thai documents. However, in real-world workflows, users often need to extract specific information or preserve the structure of an entire page for further processing. Typhoon OCR 2 handles both tasks in a single model, with prompt-driven extraction and structured full-page parsing. Full-page parsing covers Thai, English, and Chinese. We release compact 2B and 0.8B models adapted from open document parsers through supervised fine-tuning on curated Thai and public multilingual data, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with task rewards and a rule penalizing unfinished responses. Among evaluated open models, Typhoon OCR 2 2B scores highest on Thai MDPBench (80.7 versus 68.9 for Typhoon OCR 1.5) and on ThaiOCRBench (59.91 versus 40.45), which covers recognition, extraction, and document understanding. The 2B model remains close to its base on English olmOCR-bench (84.7 versus 84.4) and on OmniDocBench, which evaluates English and Chinese together (90.97 versus 91.03). On MDPBench, GRPO reduces the mean share of pages with repetition loops for the 2B model from 3.2% to 0.7%, with a smaller and statistically uncertain score gain for the 0.8B model. We release the model weights, Python package, and evaluation suite.

items.abstract: Depth-recurrent (Looped) models raise effective depth by applying a shared stack of blocks several times. Scaling them usually requires pipeline parallelism, but commonly used interleaved 1F1B is drawn for an acyclic stage graph in which each micro-batch enters each stage once. Once that stack is split across stages, the same stage is visited several times on one micro-batch and later stages feed earlier ones: native 1F1B has no slot for the extra visit, cannot rank a first iteration against a second, and its neighbour-only send/receive order has no back edge to the first stage, so the arrangement stalls or fires out of order. We present Loop-PP, which rebuilds both the timetable and the communication for this cyclic layout. It schedules different iterations of the same stage separately, specializes a 1F1B skeleton into a globally consistent order over those visits, and emits a static instruction stream per rank that separates posting from waiting so communication overlaps local compute. Loop-PP is bit-identical to a single-stage reference. On 8B-60B MoE models, it lowers peak memory by as much as 32.8\%, and with compute budget fixed, the best observed throughput rises by 12.7\%.

items.title: SWEEP-Bench: Do Embodied Policies Act on the Speed They See?
items.summary: Robot policies must adapt to the speed of moving objects, yet existing benchmarks rarely measure this ability across diverse tasks and speeds. We introduce SWEEP-Bench, a simulation benchmark with 80 conveyor-belt manipulation tasks spanning 16 skill categories, each evaluated at 13 belt speeds (0.10-0.40 m/s). items.abstract: Robot policies must adapt to the speed of moving objects, yet existing benchmarks rarely measure this ability across diverse tasks and speeds. We introduce SWEEP-Bench, a simulation benchmark with 80 conveyor-belt manipulation tasks spanning 16 skill categories, each evaluated at 13 belt speeds (0.10-0.40 m/s). Objects are transported through physical contact with a visibly moving belt. Each task has a static counterpart, and each evaluation episode uses the same randomized scene at all 13 speeds. We fine-tune eight vision-language-action and world-action models on demonstrations spanning the full speed range, comparing observations from the current frame alone with those including two past frames. For six models, the success rate peaks at intermediate speeds, and their failures indicate that they tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed rather than to the actual one. Past frames raise the success rate by 10-40 percentage points for three models, and linear probes show that the belt speed is also most linearly decodable from these three. Adding ground-truth speed input to four of the models improves all of them, and a speed estimated from the images keeps most of this gain. These results show that SWEEP-Bench exposes speed-dependent failures and suggest that past frames help only policies from which the speed is most decodable, such as those pretrained on multiple frames. Project page: https://damin3927.github.io/SWEEP-Bench

items.title: Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation
items.summary: Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a…
items.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.

items.title: 3AGameFactory-Motion: Agentic Rigging and Reliable Complex Motion Generation for Diverse 3D Assets
items.summary: Animating arbitrary 3D assets from instructions requires both structural inference and motion control, yet existing motion benchmarks mostly cover conventional human or animal skeletons with simple instructions. We introduce DivDynBench, which evaluates rigging and motion generation across six morphology categories, with instructions requiring multi-phase part coordination and explicit timing, angle, repetition, and…
items.abstract: Animating arbitrary 3D assets from instructions requires both structural inference and motion control, yet existing motion benchmarks mostly cover conventional human or animal skeletons with simple instructions. We introduce DivDynBench, which evaluates rigging and motion generation across six morphology categories, with instructions requiring multi-phase part coordination and explicit timing, angle, repetition, and trajectory constraints. With large language models, we systematically compare three common paradigms: specialized motion generation, video generation followed by motion recovery, and direct agent-driven generation. We analyze their control capabilities, cross-morphology adaptability, and generation costs. Guided by this comparison, we propose an Agentic Motion Framework in which an agent writes compact parametric skeleton and motion programs, and a deterministic executor performs rigging, kinematic solving, and geometric correction. Compact parameter control reduces generation overhead and improves rigging reliability and motion-control accuracy, providing practical guidance for deploying complex 3D motion generation.

items.summary: Long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation is essential for interactive animation and humanoid robotics, where an agent must respond to changing instructions and spatial goals while moving. Existing autoregressive diffusion methods generate motion incrementally, but bounded attention caches limit access to distant history, while repeated denoising introduces substantial inference overhead. items.abstract: Long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation is essential for interactive animation and humanoid robotics, where an agent must respond to changing instructions and spatial goals while moving. Existing autoregressive diffusion methods generate motion incrementally, but bounded attention caches limit access to distant history, while repeated denoising introduces substantial inference overhead. We present Motion Mamba 2.0, a Mamba-based root-body diffusion architecture that integrates local attention, resumable recurrent states, and persistent content memory (PCM) for long-horizon controllable motion generation. PCM transforms compressed motion history from Mamba recurrent states, together with state changes and text-conditioned features, into dynamically updated content slots accessible to local attention. To enable efficient inference, we further develop an execution scheme tailored to this architecture, combining CUDA Graph replay, fused kernels, and execution-flow simplification while preserving the canonical history update. Evaluations on retargeted HiPHI demonstrate accurate terminal control over rollouts of up to 39.52 s, while short-horizon comparisons on BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D show that the model also retains strong spatial control and text-motion matching. On an RTX 4090, the optimized execution reduces median complete-window latency from 1685.35 to 276.14 ms, achieving a median paired speedup of 6.138times while preserving identical outputs and committed states in the tested rollouts. Moreover, we conduct extensive real-world evaluation on the Unitree G1, demonstrating sequential text-guided action composition, expressive motion, and interactive locomotion through keyboard and mouse control.

items.abstract: Motivation: In spite of the much improved protein structure prediction methods, the success rate remains low for antibody-antigen complexes. While this can be improved by computationally demanding massive sampling, results are still much poorer than for most other types of protein-protein interactions. In principle, improvement can be achieved by using templates that are close enough to the native structure of the complex, but these are generally not available for antibody-antigen complexes. Results: We explore the use of templates, generated by the computationally inexpensive rigid body docking program PIPER. Applied to a leakage-free antibody-antigen benchmark set, standard AlphaFold 3 with 1000 random seeds yields acceptable or better models as the top predictions for 56.2% of complexes. Adding the PIPER generated templates in the unmasked version of AlphaFold 3 either increases the success rate to 63.4%, or reaches the same 56.2% success rate in about 200 runs. The template-based approach similarly improves antibody-antigen prediction by Boltz-2. This result demonstrates that the space explored by the ML based approach can be expanded by adding templates prepared by traditional docking, compensating for the lack of evolutionary relationship and the limited availability of training data. Availability and Implementation: The ClusPro server (https://cluspro.bu.edu/login.php) containing the PIPER program is free for non-commercial applications and the program is available by request (https://www.vajdalab.org/). All other study data are included in the article and/or supporting information.

items.abstract: Laminins are large, heterotrimeric glycoproteins that are a major structural component of basement membranes and the extracellular matrix. Although they are difficult to produce recombinantly because of their large size, a smaller fragment of the laminin heterotrimer that supports cell adhesion and cell migration, termed E8, can be recombinantly expressed. Here, we use AlphaFold to optimize laminin E8 fragments and design a panel of interchangeable laminin α, β, and γ chains that can be combined to produce all isoforms recombinantly. These recombinant E8 fragments support adhesion of cells bearing their cognate integrins, and will be useful tools for stem-cell, organoid, and laminin-binding integrin biology research.

items.abstract: Monoclonal antibodies are central to modern targeted cancer therapy and immunotherapy. However, clonal heterogeneity and dynamic changes in the tumor microenvironment can enable solid tumors to evade single-target therapies. Multispecific antibodies offer a strategy to address these limitations by integrating distinct binding specificities within a single molecule. Yet neither increasing the number of targets nor increasing binding affinity alone guarantees clinical benefit. A central challenge is to coordinate immune-cell redirection, conditional activation, and Boolean logic gating with precise spatial and temporal control. These capabilities must be achieved while ensuring molecular developability, meeting chemistry, manufacturing, and controls requirements, and maintaining an adequate therapeutic window. Using intended biological function as the organizing principle, this Review examines how molecular architecture, affinity engineering, Fc-region engineering, and logic-gated design shape pharmacological profiles and clinical safety. We also discuss the implications of internalization kinetics for bispecific antibody-drug conjugates. We then examine mechanisms of therapeutic resistance and immune-niche remodeling within the tumor microenvironment and assess progress in clinical translation. Particular attention is given to the fidelity of preclinical models, biomarker limitations, strategies to widen the therapeutic window, and combination and sequential treatment regimens. Finally, we discuss emerging directions, including logic-gated activation, in situ immune priming with oncolytic viruses or vaccines, and artificial intelligence-guided antibody design. Together, these perspectives provide a framework for aligning molecular design with biological context and translational requirements to guide the development of next-generation multispecific cancer therapeutics.

items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence applied to panoramic radiographs has been proposed to triage which mandibular third molars require cone-beam computed tomography before extraction. We searched seven databases and registers to June 2026 for studies of any machine- or deep-learning model applied to panoramic radiographs against a three-dimensional reference standard, appraised them with QUADAS-3 and PROBAST+AI, and rated certainty with GRADE. Twenty-one studies were included. Across seven pooled studies, a Bayesian bivariate model gave a summary sensitivity of 0.81 (95% CrI 0.75–0.87) and specificity of 0.87 (95% CrI 0.70–0.95) for detecting mandibular third molar–inferior alveolar nerve contact, yet every study was at high risk of bias, only one was externally validated, and certainty was very low. In nine within-study comparisons no study reported readers as more accurate than the model, though each was internal and unblinded. No architecture was consistently superior and prognostic models for nerve injury remained preliminary. Registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251000827).

items.abstract: Abstract Dear Editor,l appreciate Karunya et al.'s comprehensive review of the epidemiology, global burden, and evolution of head and neck cancer radiotherapy (HNC)[1], and believe that artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to link all of these technological advances to earlier diagnosis, more personalised treatment and more equitable access to radiotherapy. First, AI can solve some real world challenges of high quality radiotherapy planning. The use of deep-learning systems for automatic segmentation of target volumes and organs at risk (OAR), the prediction of achievable dose distributions, supporting plan optimization, and quality assurance (QA) is of particular relevance in HNC, where target volumes are often irregularly shaped and closely contiguous to the salivary glands, pharyngeal constrictors, spinal cord, brainstem, and other radiosensitive organs. In some studies, AI-driven planning has shown to save time and improve the quality of plans, while in others, it has been found to be as efficient as traditional planning, but further clinical validation is required[2]. The potential impact of AI on ART could be even more pronounced during this multiple-week course of radiotherapy, as changes in the position of the tumour, weight loss, and tumour regression can affect target coverage or the dose to normal tissue. Cone beam computed tomography enhancement or generation, automatic re-contouring, dose recalculation and identification of patients likely to benefit from replanning are all aspects of the ART pathway that can be accelerated with the help of AI. There is promising performance for AI-based OAR segmentation, models to predict the need for adaptation, and it was noted that the evidence available to date is largely retrospective, and so human review should be integral, especially for tumour boundaries and small critical structures[3]. Last, the advantages of AI-assisted ART should be measured by clinically meaningful outcomes, not just geometric precision, such as xerostomia, dysphagia, and dependence on feeding tubes, among other toxicities. Second, AI can help to enhance early detection and risk-based referral in areas with high burden. Smartphone assisted oral examination is a potentially scalable option for delayed presentation in India, where tobacco use, areca-nut consumption, alcohol consumption and lack of specialists are involved in delayed presentation. Such models could be applied to aid prioritization of oral potentially malignant disorder cases for teleconsultation or biopsy or specialist referral in Indian community screening datasets, using deep-learning algorithms applied to oral photographs acquired by trained frontline health workers[4] They need to be used as a triage tool, however, not as a stand-alone diagnostic instrument. The performance of any algorithm must be assessed in a variety of populations, devices, lighting conditions, lesion locations, and levels of health worker training and training, or otherwise, the algorithm may actually exacerbate diagnostic disparities and inequities. Limited external validation, methodological inconsistencies, and a lack of prospective studies are also identified as significant challenges in the broader HNC AI literature[5].Third, AI offers a chance to shift away from anatomy-based treatment decision. Models that take into account HPV or p16 status, smoking history, tumour subsite, imaging, digital pathology, molecular markers and longitudinal treatment data could be used to estimate locoregional control, distant failure, survival and toxicity for each individual patient. These estimates could ultimately help inform treatment-intensity decisions, biomarker-directed treatment selection criteria, surveillance planning, and biomarker-directed trial eligibility[6]. Therefore, although evidence suggests that radiomic models have moderate diagnostic accuracy, at this time, there is not enough consistent evidence to replace the currently validated pathological HPV testing and treatment de-intensification should be reserved for appropriately designed clinical trials. More generally, models using clinical and radiomic data have yielded promising results for predicting tumour control and radiotherapy toxicity, but need larger, multi-institutional datasets and prospective validation[7]. A pathway to implementation that would be constructive would be the four following steps that would be pre-clinical “silent mode” evaluation of the software prior to use; software validation across institutions, imaging vendors, treatment platforms, and subgroups; deployment of the software with uncertainty alert systems and auditable overrides; and post-implementation monitoring for software toxicity, disease control, workflow efficiency, and subgroups performance. Resource limited centres should not be recipients of models developed in only a well-resourced centre, but should also be a co-design and validation centre. It will be critical that the software is lightweight, that it integrates easily with current CT and linear-accelerator equipment, that calibration can be completed locally, that the workforce can be trained to use it, and that its cost-effectiveness is easily understood. Federated or distributed learning can also enable collaborative model improvements, without the need to centralize sensitive patient information. The review by Karunya et al. serves as a useful framework in which to consider how responsibly validated AI may help enhance planning accuracy, the ability for adaptive treatment, improving early detection and biologically driven personalization. But “automation for the sake of automation” isn't the priority; the goal should be to deliver measurable and equitable improvements in patient outcomes.

items.abstract: Abstract Background and Objectives: To develop a region of interest (ROI)-free model for ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) identification and diagnosis in cervical MRI with interpretable feature representations. Methods A total of 4861 cervical MRI images of 1028 patients from 3 hospitals were enrolled and divided into the training, validation, and external test datasets. We evaluated the performance of the ROI-free and automated cervical OPLL (RACO) model based on the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, feature attention maps, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. In addition, we also evaluated the effectiveness of the RACO model in the different OPLL types. Results The AUC of the RACO model was 0.91 and 0.88 in the validation and external test datasets, respectively. In the validation dataset, the AUCs of ResNet-101, EfficientNet-S, and Shufflenet models were 0.52, 0.53 and 0.62, respectively. Grad-CAM showed that the RACO model generated accurate peak responses on the target area. In addition, the RACO model showed the highest accuracy in the continuous subgroup (97.08%) and the lowest accuracy in the localized subgroup (93.82%). Conclusion The RACO model showed excellent performance, and interpretable attention maps may support clinical decision-making and reduce radiation exposure for patients.

items.abstract: Background: Targeted therapy for patients with suspected respiratory infections traditionally requires bacterial culture followed by phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST), a process that can take up to 5 days. In acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), delays in identifying the causative pathogen and its resistance profile may be especially harmful because patients are critically ill and often receive broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics. The growing burden of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) further complicates clinical decision-making by reducing effective treatment options and increasing the risk of inadequate initial therapy. Culture-free, AI-driven computational metagenomic strategies have the potential to drastically shorten this window, enabling more rapid targeted therapy prescription. To show the feasibility of such approaches, we develop a proof-of-concept framework based on clinical metagenomics. Methods: We simulated respiratory metagenomes using real-world bacterial genomes with associated antimicrobial susceptibility phenotypes. Each simulated metagenome contained a fixed commensal background and one clinically important respiratory pathogen, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or Pseudomonas aeruginosa, at 5% or 10% bacterial read abundance. Realistic reads were simulated for Oxford Nanopore, PacBio, and Illumina sequencing platforms. Random Forest (RF) classifiers were trained and evaluated using five-fold, strain-grouped cross-validation with fold-specific χ 2 -ranked 13-mer features. ResFinder and KARGA were included as reference-based metagenomics benchmarks and evaluated using the same five held-out folds across the three sequencing platforms and two pathogen-abundance conditions. Results: RF performance varied substantially across species, antibiotics, and sequencing platforms. The strongest and most consistent results were observed for K. pneumoniae, with accuracy reaching approximately 0.96 for ceftazidime, 0.93 for amikacin, and 0.92 for ciprofloxacin. Performance for P. aeruginosa was more heterogeneous: long-read models performed well for amikacin, reaching 0.89 with PacBio and 0.88 with Nanopore, whereas Illumina performed substantially better for ciprofloxacin, ceftazidime, and levofloxacin, reaching accuracies of approximately 0.87, 0.77, and 0.70, respectively. Across most organism-antibiotic combinations, RF accuracy was numerically higher than the classification accuracies obtained with KARGA and ResFinder, which generally remained near 0.50. Increasing pathogen abundance from 5% to 10% and increasing the number of selected features from 2,500 to 5,000 generally produced modest improvements in classification accuracy, although the magnitude of improvement varied across organism-antibiotic combinations and sequencing platforms. Conclusions: Genome-wide k-mer machine learning can recover phenotype-associated antimicrobial resistance signals from simulated respiratory metagenomes, although performance depends strongly on the organism, antibiotic, and sequencing platform. These results represent a simulation-based proof of concept.

items.abstract: Background: Decisions about deploying large language model (LLM) agents in health care require the cost of completed work in production. Published evidence reports benchmark accuracy, benchmark-level cost, and time or financial outcomes for ambient documentation, and list prices alone do not determine the cost of completed work. To our knowledge, no deployed clinical agent fleet has published a measurement method that ties compute cost, latency, failures and retries to completed work. Objective: This study aims to estimate the compute cost of completed work by the orchestrated clinical agents of a deployed LLM agent fleet over a 12-week window of production telemetry, using estimators, data-quality gates and an analysis plan fixed before any window data are extracted for the study. Methods: The setting is a private outpatient clinic in London, United Kingdom, where wai, a multi-agent system supporting clinic operations, is deployed. The population is every run of the 20 orchestrated clinical documentation and decision-support agents starting between September 21 and December 13, 2026. The run store writes 2 records for every run, a non-terminal record before the model call and a terminal record after it, and has no attempt counter or parent-run link. Estimators defined on that structure cover cost per resolved execution and per completed intention, retry and failed-intention shares of compute, error and failure rates, latency, cost per draft offered for clinician review and a latency-cost frontier, by agent, task class and acceptance stratum. Cost is recorded in GBP pence, converted from provider-returned US dollar cost at a fixed rate and rounded per model call. The plan fixes weekly aggregation, small-cell suppression, bootstrap intervals over weeks, 2 prespecified comparisons, 5 sensitivity analyses and 4 data-quality gates whose failure converts an estimate into a bound or an unmeasured stratum. Two staff-level measures in an earlier version were dropped. Revenue, pricing, margin and staffing inference are excluded. Results: The measurement window opened on September 21, 2026, and closes on December 13, 2026, and telemetry is being recorded in routine operation. No window data had been extracted for this study at submission. Aggregate whole-table counts that include window records were extracted on November 19, 2026, for companion manuscripts and are disclosed. Extraction will begin no earlier than December 15, 2026, and the results are expected to be submitted for publication in 2027. Conclusions: The compute cost of completed clinical agent work can be specified as estimators over the run-level telemetry this deployment records, provided paired recording rows are separated from retries, missing terminal states are bounded and rounding of recorded cost is reported. This protocol fixes those estimators, and the reporting consequence of each known instrumentation defect, before extraction. Trial Registration: None. The analysis plan will be registered on Open Science Framework Registries before any window data are extracted for this study.

items.abstract: Background: Accurate identification of pregnancy episodes from electronic health records (EHRs) is essential for maternal and fetal health research. Existing approaches rely primarily on diagnosis and procedure codes, which may miss pregnancies documented outside the health system and are susceptible to coding errors. Clinical notes contain richer information but remain largely unexplored for this task. Objectives: To evaluate whether a large language model (LLM) can reconstruct complete pregnancy episodes directly from clinical notes. Methods: Chronologically concatenated notes and messages were provided to GPT-5, which identified episodes and extracted variables including assisted reproductive treatment, gestational age, outcome, and complications. Performance was benchmarked against manual chart review (gold standard) and a hierarchical ICD-code algorithm in 30 patients comprising 74 pregnancies (20 patients in a held-out test set). Results: The LLM identified 53 of 54 test-set pregnancies versus 40/54 for a hierarchical ICD-code algorithm, with fewer spurious episodes (3 vs 24), corresponding to an F1 score for pregnancy detection against chart review of 0.96 vs 0.68. Among pregnancies identified by both methods, median absolute error was 0 vs 25.5 days for start dates (p<0.001) and 0 vs 1 day for end dates (p=0.044), and outcome accuracy was numerically but not significantly higher (0.84 vs 0.74 for exact outcome types; 0.92 vs 0.84 with abortion subtypes grouped). It additionally recovered information unavailable in structured data, including reproductive-treatment type and fetus-level outcomes. Conclusions: An LLM applied to clinical narratives identified pregnancy episodes more completely and with more accurate dates than an ICD-code algorithm while capturing richer clinical detail. Because the two approaches used different input data, these gains reflect both the information in clinical notes and the LLM itself. LLM-based extraction from clinical notes is a promising complement to code-based pregnancy phenotyping that warrants evaluation in larger, multi-institutional cohorts.

items.abstract: Rationale: Wildfire smoke is an increasing public health threat, yet most epidemiologic studies estimate average smoke-health associations across broad spatial or temporal scales. Such approaches may obscure substantial heterogeneity across individual smoke waves, leaving an important evidence gap for dynamic public health preparedness, risk communication, and clinical practice. Objectives: To estimate event-specific excess respiratory acute care utilization during smoke waves and identify smoke wave features associated with higher excess utilization. Methods: We conducted a statewide study of 18,271,754 respiratory acute care encounters in California from 2006 to 2019. A smoke wave was defined as at least 2 consecutive days during which county-level wildfire smoke fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exceeded the 95th percentile over the study period. We applied a machine learning-integrated two-stage interrupted time-series design to estimate excess respiratory acute care utilization during each event. We then used meta-regressions to examine multiple spatiotemporally varying effect modifiers such as smoke wave duration, intensity, timing, and co-occurring climate and meteorological conditions. Measurements and Main Results: A total of 1,249 smoke waves were identified and examined in this study. Excess respiratory acute care utilization varied substantially across smoke waves. Higher excess utilization was associated with longer smoke wave duration, greater intensity, winter occurrence, short recovery period, overlap with holidays, drought conditions, or co-occurrence with precipitation or extreme heat events. Conclusions: This study proposes a novel analytical framework to systematically evaluate spatiotemporal drivers of heterogeneity in wildfire smoke respiratory health effects. The findings can inform dynamic preparedness and public health response to smoke events.

items.abstract: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a major cause of vision loss, with a significant impact on the elderly population worldwide. Machine learning and deep learning methods, combined with optical coherence tomography (OCT), are promising for the rapid diagnosis of AMD. However, most models focus only on one single OCT imaging modality or neglect clinical information. To improve this problem, we design a deep multimodal framework that integrates OCT images with clinical text data for the detection of AMD. Then, we evaluate the proposed model using metrics, such as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F-score, and the area under the curve (AUC), achieving excellent detection results at both the image level and patient level. Next, we conduct computational efficiency analysis and independent external validation to further demonstrate the efficiency and generalizability of the proposed model.In addition,we provide visualization results with explainable AI technique to further show the effectiveness of the proposed model. Our proposed model using multimodal strategy involving machine learning along with available clinical text and OCT imaging data accurately predicts individuals with AMD. Therefore, the use of machine learning and explainable AI in AMD detection may ultimately improve early diagnosis and offer more precise and personalized treatment strategies, improving the management ofAMD and preservingvision.

items.abstract: Objective: Guidance for large language model (LLM) drafting in clinical care relies on human review, yet review is rarely measured as a control. We aimed to define computable measures of review fidelity, establish which a deployed system can compute, and pre-specify their first analysis. Materials and Methods. For a multi-agent clinical system in routine use at one private London outpatient clinic, we defined acceptance coverage, attribution completeness, the unedited acceptance rate (UAR), a bounded normalized edit distance, availability latency and an unedited fast-approval rate (UFA). We checked each measure against the system's code and database structure at a fixed commit on four approval routes and pre-specified a prospective 12-week analysis. Results. The UAR equals the mass at zero of the edit-distance distribution, and availability latency bounds reading time from above only. Clinical documentation keeps draft and signed text with a recorded signer, so the core measures are computable there. Help-desk edit telemetry is written only when the agent's version has been stored. The WhatsApp agent route records no edit signal, and its approver need not be named. No route records when a draft is opened. Documentation accept events were not written before a change committed on November 16, 2026. Model-generated content, including live voice-agent speech, also reaches patients without approval. No measured values are reported. Discussion. Acceptance alone cannot separate accurate drafts from approval without reading, and three of four routes cannot yet support the family. Conclusion. Review fidelity can be specified as telemetry at the approval event. Validation against missed errors is required.

items.abstract: Background: In randomized trials, first-line immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based therapy has shown excess early mortality versus chemotherapy- or targeted therapy-containing regimens. ICI monotherapy is nonetheless often chosen for frail patients because it is perceived as less toxic, although these patients may be most vulnerable to this early mortality. Whether treatment benefit varies with baseline prognosis is unknown, as poor-prognosis patients are underrepresented in trials. Methods Using the US Flatiron Health electronic health record-derived database, we emulated target trials among 8,688 patients initiating first-line therapy during 2011-2023 across five comparisons: pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy versus pembrolizumab in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC; PD-L1 CPS ≥ 1 or unknown) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC; PD-L1 TPS ≥ 50%); carboplatin plus gemcitabine versus pembrolizumab in urothelial carcinoma; pembrolizumab versus chemotherapy in dMMR/MSI-H colorectal cancer; and ipilimumab plus nivolumab versus BRAF/MEK inhibition in BRAF-mutant melanoma. Baseline prognosis was estimated with machine learning models predicting 6-month survival. Overlap-weighted pseudo-observation regression evaluated whether differences in 2-year restricted mean survival time (RMST) varied with predicted survival. Results In HNSCC, adding chemotherapy to pembrolizumab did not clearly improve RMST overall (11.5 days; 95% CI, -18.4 to 41.1), but benefit was 102.4 days greater at the 10th versus 90th percentile of predicted survival (95% CI, 40.5 to 164.3; interaction P=.001). Similar gradients favored carboplatin plus gemcitabine over pembrolizumab in urothelial carcinoma (10th-90th percentile difference, 51.4 days; 95% CI, 4.8 to 98.1; P=.03) and, less certainly, adding chemotherapy to pembrolizumab in NSCLC (73.7 days; 95% CI, -3.7 to 151.2; P=.06). Higher-risk patients in these cohorts were more often trial-ineligible. ICI-based therapy improved overall RMST in colorectal cancer (difference, 79.7 days; 95% CI, 49.5 to 107.0) and melanoma (68.3 days; 95% CI, 33.9 to 101.9), without clear variation by predicted survival (interaction P=.32 and P=.91). Conclusions Among patients with poorer prognosis, chemotherapy-containing regimens were associated with greater benefit than ICI monotherapy in HNSCC and urothelial carcinoma, and possibly NSCLC. ICI-based therapy appeared beneficial across prognosis in dMMR/MSI-H colorectal cancer and BRAF-mutant melanoma. Baseline prognosis may complement tumor biomarkers when selecting first-line immunotherapy strategies.

items.abstract: AbstractBackground: The Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP) organises covarying symptoms and maladaptive traits into transdiagnostic dimensions to address limitations of categorical diagnosis. Naturalistic symptom descriptions may complement structured assessments. Objective: This protocol describes a reproducible mixed-methods workflow to derive symptom indicators from forum posts and examine their organisation relative to HiTOP. Methods and analysis: The target sample is 80,000 public Reddit posts. After local de-identification, a large language model (LLM) will extract symptom labels and supporting paraphrases. Two human experts will independently review outputs for up to 250 posts. Three embedding models will flag potentially equivalent symptom labels for local LLM assessment. Two experts will qualitatively review the most frequent canonical symptom labels (at least 1,000) and develop a codebook of symptom categories, continuing until a prespecified saturation criterion is met. An LLM will assign canonical symptom labels to these categories, producing binary post-level indicators. Multiverse-inspired structural analyses will compare network, component, factor, and clustering representations across discovery, internal tuning, and holdout partitions. Evaluation will assess interpretability, stability, and agreement with expert mapping to HiTOP. Supplementary analyses will include agent-assisted exploration, codebook application to DepressionEmo and the Reddit Mental Health Dataset, and pooled integrative analysis that may include additional comparable corpora. Discussion: The study will examine whether symptom co-expression within posts forms interpretable patterns corresponding to HiTOP.Ethics: The Ethics Committee of Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin approved the study (EA2/274/25). The study was preregistered on 8 May 2026 (German Clinical Trials Register, DRKS00040244). Keywords: Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology, natural language processing, large language models, Reddit, mixed methods, study protocol

items.abstract: Background: Resveratrol (RES) has been reported to attenuate allergic and virus-induced airway inflammation in preclinical models, but the evidence is fragmented across species, stimuli, doses and biological levels. We quantified it as a beneficial outcome pathway (BOP), the counterpart of an adverse outcome pathway. Methods: Three databases were searched (October 2026). Contrasts of pure RES against allergic or viral stimuli in cells, tissue and animals were extracted with the assistance of a locally run large language model, expressed as the fraction of stimulus-induced change reversed, fuzzy-encoded and used to parameterise a 15-node Bayesian network whose 23 key-event relationships (KERs) encode a priori causal hypotheses. Predictions were validated by leave-one-study-out cross-validation and compared qualitatively with six clinical trials. Results: 60 studies (1,204 contrasts, 1,012 encoded; 178 arms) were modelled; 88.9% of encoded contrasts favoured RES. KERs were concordant (NF-κB→cytokines: P(≥moderate reversal) 0.92 vs 0.22 with or without parent reversal). Expected reversal of airway hyper-responsiveness was 0.49–0.51 across timing and dose bands, whereas within studies higher doses gave larger reversal (0.28, 95% CI 0.15–0.39; 18 of 20 studies). Context-only prediction did not beat the node marginal (Brier 0.384 vs 0.376), whereas observed upstream events did (0.301 vs 0.361 when a parent was observed). Only 10 of 78 in vitro concentrations tested across studies were plasma-achievable (≤2.4 µM); SIRT1 was measured in 4 studies. Conclusions: RES effects are consistently observed together along the hypothesised pathway, but concordance does not establish causation, and the literature does not resolve dose, timing, physiological concentrations or SIRT1 involvement. The network is a transparent, updatable prior for confirmatory experiments.

items.abstract: Abstract Background: Colonoscopy artificial intelligence (AI) performance depends on the endoscopic view analysed by the model. Yet pipelines often specify only image dimensions, leaving the analysed region undefined. Optical corners, recorder interfaces and picture-in-picture displays vary across acquisition systems, so identical network dimensions can contain different visual evidence. We developed ColFOV, a semantic-guided field-of-view (FOV) method that derives stable, task-selectable FOV inputs from multiple frames. Methods: We combined four-class semantic predictions across multiple frames to delineate the endoscopic field and derive two stable input regions for downstream analysis. Full-FOV retains the complete endoscopic field, whereas inner-FOV focuses on tissue. A lightweight U-Net predicted masks for tissue, optical corners, recorder interfaces and picture-in-picture regions. Training and validation used 367 frames from 52 recordings spanning phantom, public clinical and hospital sources. We then evaluated field delineation on 267 external still frames from ten video-processor families unseen during development. To examine the consequences for downstream AI, we measured retained tool and fold-edge annotations and compared paired monocular depth estimates. Paired differences were summarised with sequence-level bootstrap confidence intervals and two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results: The four-class model achieved a mean intersection over union (IoU) of 0.973 in validation, and field sensitivity reached 0.99 on the external frames. The two inputs retained different visual evidence for downstream analysis. Across 1,560 public clinical frames, full-FOV retained every annotated tool and fold-edge pixel, whereas inner-FOV retained 79.1\% of tool pixels and largely excluded the dark periphery. On tissue visible in both inputs, inner-FOV reduced median-aligned absolute relative error from 0.174 to 0.110 (a 36.9\% reduction) with the same depth model. Error was lower in all 120 sequences. Conclusions: ColFOV makes the visual field presented to a colonoscopy AI model an explicit, reproducible choice. It derives stable full- and inner-FOV inputs and records their bounding boxes and resize transforms. External evaluation showed high field sensitivity. Annotation-retention and paired depth analyses further showed that the selected region changes both the content available to a model and its predictions within shared tissue. Field-of-view definition should therefore be tested and reported alongside the downstream model.

items.abstract: Abstract Introduction. Surveillance in Africa has transited from paper registers under the Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response strategy to electronic case reporting, mobile and community reporting, geospatial analysis and genomic pipelines. Methods. We therefore searched Scopus on 25 July 2026, screened 600 publications against stated criteria to 563 documents, and analysed them by bibliometric mapping and six-topic structural topic models, with prevalence estimated by publication year. Each document was coded for the African countries it studied, the diseases it addressed, and the technologies it used. The attention each country received was compared with the presence of authors’ affiliations. The research spanned three decades, dispersed across four disciplines that were not mapped. Results. Publication outputs grew at 14.9% annually with no detectable structural break, even during the pandemic periods (Ebola and COVID-19). Sources rose from 38 to 167, and countries increased from 20 to 46. About 26.5% were cited within the corpus, and four of the six most co-cited references were institutional documents rather than peer-reviewed research. Digital health innovation increased marginally annually, while clinical HIV data declined. Geospatial analysis and machine learning dominated the studies. Local authorship is prominent in the studies. Conclusion. This field of Digital Disease Surveillance has grown steadily in Africa, and it consists of short, unconnected studies citing policy instruments rather than addressing analytical methods or interoperability implementation reviews. Continuity in the subject matter is therefore recommended.

items.abstract: Abstract Purpose:: In metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC), therapeutic decisions are mainly based on radiological evaluations, while the dynamics of circulating biomarkers remain underused in clinical practice. This study aims to develop and validate a prognostic tool based on longitudinal measurements of key biomarkers to predict the short-term risk of progression or death in mCRC patients undergoing chemotherapy. Methods: : Using data from the PRODIGE 9 trial, we modeled biomarker kinetics by deriving specific variables such as gaps, slopes and curvature. To address the marked skewness of some covariates, Box-Cox transformations were applied. Multiple machine learning models were tested, each combined with a backward variable selection procedure guided by repeated cross-validation. Logistic regression was retained as the final model due to its accuracy and interpretability. The model was then calibrated and externally validated using the PRODIGE 20 and FFCD 1201 trials. As biomarker sampling was less frequent in these datasets, Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) based on conditional expectation was used to impute intermediate values and harmonize follow-up times. Results: : The model stratifies patients into two risk groups (Low Risk, At Risk), offering effective risk discrimination and potentially guiding the timing of radiological examinations. Conclusion: : This approach highlights that the early kinetics of circulating biomarkers can reliably predict short-term outcomes in mCRC patients. The developed tool could support clinical decision-making and help optimize the use of imaging examinations.
