items.abstract: Liquid biopsy offers repeated, minimally invasive molecular profiling of cancer, but its clinical value depends on the analyte, analytical platform, and intended use. In this Review, we evaluate current liquid-biopsy technologies for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment guidance, with a particular emphasize on tumor-derived extracellular vesicles (TDEVs) as a bridge between biomarker detection and therapeutic intervention. We examine genomic and epigenomic profiling, single-cell and single-vesicle analysis, and multi-omics integration as complementary approaches for assessing tumour burden, heterogeneity and treatment response. Circulating tumor DNA genotyping guides targeted therapy in selected advanced cancers, whereas many early-detection and vesicle-based applications require prospective validation. We highlight how the TDEV lipid bilayer protects diverse molecular cargo that reflects evolving tumour phenotypes and how TDEV-mediated communication contributes to metastasis, immune evasion and therapeutic resistance, creating opportunities to target pathogenic vesicle signalling. We also assess engineered vesicles from malignant and non-malignant cells as drug-delivery and cancer-vaccination platforms, while noting that tumour-derived carriers may retain oncogenic or immunosuppressive cargo. Most candidate vesicle biomarkers remain supported by retrospective studies, and therapeutic platforms are largely preclinical or in early clinical testing. We discuss the requirements for clinical translation, including reliable identification of tumour-derived vesicles, standardized workflows and prospective multicentre validation for diagnostics, and reproducible manufacturing, cargo characterization, potency testing and product-specific pharmacokinetic and safety evaluation for therapeutics. Finally, we consider how multimodal profiling and artificial intelligence might improve signal integration, and argue that clinical adoption will depend on demonstrating that vesicle-guided decisions and interventions improve patient outcomes.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming prostate cancer screening and early detection through the integration of clinical-risk calculators, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), digital pathology, genomics, biomarkers, and liquid biopsies. AI-enhanced risk models may improve biopsy decisions, while AI-assisted MRI interpretation can increase the detection of clinically significant disease and reduce false positives, unnecessary biopsies, and overdiagnosis. Digital pathology algorithms may support more reproducible tumor identification, Gleason grading, and prognostic stratification. Genomic risk scores, kallikrein-based tests, and emerging circulating biomarkers further enable precision screening by identifying men at elevated risk and refining the selection for imaging or biopsy. However, most available systems address isolated components of the diagnostic pathway, and evidence from prospective, real-world screening populations remains limited. Clinical implementation therefore requires external validation, screening-specific calibration, implemented reference standards, and workflow integration. Ultimately, multimodal AI may enable a "virtual biopsy" that combines imaging, molecular, pathological, and clinical data to deliver personalized, noninvasive prostate cancer assessment.

items.abstract: An increasing number of studies have identified a positive association between obesity and chronic diarrhea, although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We conducted quantitative proteomics on ileum tissues from obese people with chronic diarrhea (OD, n = 23), obese people without chronic diarrhea (OB, n = 8), and healthy controls (Control, n = 9). Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) in the OD vs. Control and OD vs. OB comparisons were significantly enriched in pathways related to macrophage cytokine production. Notably, down-regulated DEPs in OD vs. OB comparison were associated with mucin type O-glycan biosynthesis. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis identified 56 common DEPs, with formin-like protein 1 (FMNL1) emerging as a key candidate through machine learning algorithms. FMNL1, a component of macrophage podosomes, was significantly upregulated in OD patients, as validated by Western blot and co-immunofluorescence staining. Functionally, FMNL1 knockdown ameliorated palmitic acid-induced proinflammatory cytokine expression in THP-1-derived macrophages and improved tight junctions in the Caco-2/ THP-1 co-culture model. Collectively, our results suggest FMNL1 as a crucial role in OD pathogenesis through mediating macrophage inflammation, providing a molecular rationale for targeted therapeutic strategies in obesity-associated diarrhea.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is starting to transform pathology by enhancing diagnostic accuracy, prognostication, and therapeutic prediction through advanced computational analysis of histopathological images. This review explores key AI methodologies and their applications in lung cancer diagnostics. Supervised learning dominates current clinical AI tools, relying on annotated whole-slide images (WSIs) for tasks like tumor subtyping, quantitation of tissue-based parameters, prediction of driver alterations (e.g. EGFR and KRAS mutations, ALK rearrangement), and assessment of tumor microenvironment (TME) features. Meanwhile, weakly supervised and self-supervised learning (SSL) methods, such as multiple instance learning (MIL) and contrastive learning, reduce dependency on labor-intensive annotations and uncover novel prognostic morphologic patterns. AI demonstrates strong performance in predicting therapeutic responses, including immune checkpoint inhibitor efficacy and pathologic response to neoadjuvant therapy, while emerging techniques like spatial transcriptomics and multiplex immunofluorescence further leverage AI to decode complex spatial biology and generate novel biomarkers. Despite much progress, major challenges persist in validation, reliability, interpretability, regulatory approval, ethics and data privacy standards, cost and reimbursement, equity, and integration into clinical workflows. Adoption requires scalable digital pathology infrastructure, interdisciplinary collaboration, and suitable reimbursement frameworks. Regulatory efforts aim to address ethical and safety concerns, but global harmonization remains incomplete. We also consider the professional consequences of adoption, including cognitive deskilling, workforce displacement, and the conditions under which pathologist oversight remains meaningful rather than nominal, and argue that liability should follow the reality of control. As AI evolves, particularly with foundation models and large language models (LLMs), thoracic pathology stands to benefit from substantially extended diagnostic and predictive capabilities, pending resolution of implementation barriers.

items.abstract: Abstract Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) remains a leading healthcare-associated infection in intensive care units and is closely associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation, excessive antimicrobial exposure, higher costs, and poor clinical outcomes. Despite decades of clinical trials and guideline development, bedside diagnosis remains limited by the absence of a biological reference standard. Conventional criteria combine nonspecific clinical, radiographic, and microbiological findings and cannot reliably distinguish parenchymal infection from airway colonization, endotracheal tube biofilm, or sterile pulmonary inflammation. Syndromic multiplex polymerase chain reaction panels, metagenomic next-generation sequencing, and host response profiling have greatly increased analytical sensitivity and shortened the time to microbiological information. They have also exposed the amount of microbial and inflammatory noise present in the ventilated airway. Detection of an organism, a resistance determinant, or systemic inflammation does not by itself establish causality. This review examines the strengths and limitations of clinical scores, imaging, respiratory sampling, conventional culture, rapid molecular assays, antimicrobial resistance testing, systemic and alveolar biomarkers, host transcriptomics, breath analysis, and artificial intelligence-based models. It proposes that VAP should be approached as a time-updated probability of tissue invasive infection rather than a binary diagnosis. A practical host-pathogen attribution framework should integrate the timing and trajectory of respiratory deterioration, specimen quality, relative pathogen burden and dominance, resistance and virulence signals, local and systemic host responses, prior antimicrobial exposure, and competing diagnoses. Diagnostic tests should be ordered only when a predefined management decision is linked to the result, followed by structured reassessment at 48 to 72 hours. This approach may improve antimicrobial targeting while reducing treatment of colonization and other noninfectious mimics.

items.abstract: Accurate inference of gene regulatory networks (GRNs) from single-cell RNA-seq data remains challenging due to the complexity of transcription factor (TF)-target interactions and the difficulty in capturing both local and global regulatory dependencies. Here, we present GeneKAN, a novel deep learning framework that integrates multiscale graph convolution with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) for robust GRN inference. GeneKAN employs a kernel-based graph convolution module to hierarchically encode gene representations, while KANs model high-order, interpretable TF-target relationships through learnable spline activations. Benchmarking against eleven existing models, and seven scRNA-seq datasets from BEELINE, including diverse cell types, species, and ground-truth networks (ChIP-seq, STRING, LOF/GOF), demonstrates that our proposed GeneKAN achieves state-of-the-art performance in both AUROC and AUPRC. Ablation studies of the proposed model confirm the necessity of each component. Biological validation on human hepatocyte and lung cancer datasets reveals that GeneKAN not only recovers known regulatory interactions with high precision but also identifies functionally relevant hub genes and oncogenic pathways. GeneKAN thus offers a powerful, interpretable, and scalable solution for GRN reconstruction under real-world conditions of data sparsity and noise, with significant potential for advancing systems biology and precision medicine.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into veterinary diagnostic imaging, yet robust regulatory oversight, validation standards, and governance frameworks remain limited. This review examines the current landscape of veterinary radiology AI, emphasizing differences between AI-generated outputs and comprehensive radiologist interpretations. It highlights key sources of algorithmic and human cognitive bias, explains AI development and validation processes, and outlines common pitfalls in interpreting performance metrics. The article stresses that veterinarians retain responsibility for clinical decisions and should critically evaluate AI tools for transparency, intended use, validation, and clinical utility. Responsible implementation requires human oversight, documentation, education, and ongoing monitoring.

items.abstract: Brain metastases (BMs) require accurate delineation for treatment planning, yet magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) acquisition protocols vary substantially in clinical practice. Such protocol-level heterogeneity may affect the generalizability of deep learning-based segmentation models. This study evaluated the impact of heterogeneous T1-weighted MRI protocols on BM segmentation performance using two three-dimensional architectures, 3D Attention U-Net and DUCK-Net 3D. A retrospective dataset of 925 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI studies from 720 patients was analyzed. Models were trained under six sequence configurations, including multi-sequence, Black-Blood (BB), Non-Black-Blood (Non-BB), and three single-sequence cohorts. Independent test datasets consisted of three MRI cohorts: MPR Range, MPR Thick Range, and T1 SPACE 3D. Five-fold cross-validation was performed. Performance was evaluated using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), volumetric regression, and false discovery rate-corrected statistical comparisons. DUCK-Net 3D demonstrated more consistent performance across independent MRI cohorts, particularly under cross-sequence conditions. Multi-sequence training achieved the most stable cross-sequence performance, whereas single-sequence models showed greater sensitivity to protocol variability. Segmentation accuracy declined for small lesions (<0.4 mL) across both architectures. These findings suggest that MRI protocol heterogeneity affects segmentation performance and that sequence-diverse training may improve cross-sequence robustness in clinical settings.

items.abstract: Purpose Detection of new and enlarging lesions on longitudinal MRI is essential for monitoring disease activity in multiple sclerosis (MS) but is time-consuming and subject to inter-reader variability. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance and workflow impact of a CE-marked artificial intelligence (AI) platform compared with neuroradiologists of different experience. Methods In this retrospective study, 59 patients with relapsing-remitting MS underwent baseline and follow-up brain MRI including 3D FLAIR sequences. Two neuroradiologists independently assessed examinations for new or enlarging lesions, blinded to AI output. The reference standard was an AI-blinded consensus of the two readers, with discordant cases adjudicated by an independent third neuroradiologist. Patient-level diagnostic performance was evaluated for each reader alone, the AI alone, and each reader assisted by AI. Agreement was assessed with Cohen's kappa and reading times with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results Among unassisted assessments, the experienced reader achieved the highest accuracy (88.1%), followed by the less experienced reader (83.1%) and the AI alone (79.7%). AI assistance was associated with higher accuracy for both readers (94.9%, κ = 0.90, and 89.8%, κ = 0.80, respectively). AI assistance significantly reduced reading time for both readers (median within-patient reduction 0.9 and 1.0 min; p < 0.001), independently of baseline T2 lesion volume. Conclusion Against an AI-blinded consensus reference standard, AI assistance was associated with higher diagnostic performance of both readers, irrespective of experience, and significantly reduced reading time, supporting its role as a decision-support tool in the longitudinal MRI assessment of MS.

items.abstract: Thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy (TAO), an autoimmune inflammatory disease of the orbit, requires objective assessment of disease activity and severity to guide management. The Clinical Activity Score (CAS) is widely used for this purpose, but its reliability is limited by subjectivity and interobserver variability, and conventional structural imaging cannot reliably distinguish early inflammation from fibrotic remodeling. Orbital single-photon emission computed tomography/computed tomography (SPECT/CT) using 99mTc-DTPA-a small hydrophilic tracer that extravasates in proportion to inflammation-induced microvascular permeability-provides a noninvasive means of visualizing and quantifying orbital inflammatory activity. This review summarizes the imaging principles and quantitative methods of orbital SPECT/CT, from semi-quantitative uptake ratios to corrected SUVmax-based absolute quantification and multiparametric models, and critically appraises the evidence for its clinical applications in TAO activity stratification, prediction of glucocorticoid response, and longitudinal treatment monitoring. Emerging applications, including SPECT/CT radiomics with external validation and artificial intelligence-based image analysis, are also discussed. Throughout, established evidence is distinguished from exploratory applications that require prospective validation, providing a balanced basis for the further evaluation and potential clinical incorporation of orbital SPECT/CT in individualized TAO management.

items.abstract: To evaluate whether large language model (LLM)-assisted label cleaning can identify label-report discordance in CT-RATE, a large-scale public chest CT dataset. After report-level deduplication, 24,446 unique radiology reports from 20,209 unique patients were identified. Twelve reports were excluded from the primary GPT-5.4 analysis because of persistent content-safety filtering or unparsable output, leaving 24,434 reports and 439,812 label instances across 18 abnormality categories. GPT-5.4-derived binary labels were generated from report text using structured outputs and compared with the original CT-RATE labels. Discordant instances were adjudicated by radiologists. In addition, 100 randomly sampled reports were manually annotated as a development set to compare the original CT-RATE labels, individual LLM-derived labels, and three-LLM majority-vote labels against radiologist-annotated reference labels. These label sources were then evaluated against a prespecified, stratified confirmatory set of 250 reports independently annotated by two blinded radiologists, and run-to-run consistency was assessed by repeated runs. Overall agreement between GPT-5.4-derived and CT-RATE labels was 96.4%, with a Cohen's κ of 0.884. Lymphadenopathy showed the lowest agreement and κ. In the confirmatory set (pre-consensus inter-reader κ = 0.936), the majority vote achieved an unweighted label-macro-averaged F1 score of 95.6% and κ of 0.940, compared with 90.8% and 0.879 for the original labels (paired F1 difference, + 4.8 points; 95% CI, 3.6-6.2), and each individual LLM also outperformed the original labels. The instance-level flip rate across three repeated runs was 1.02% for the majority vote. LLM-assisted label cleaning identified substantial label-report discordance in CT-RATE, particularly for lymphadenopathy, and may provide a scalable approach to quality improvement of public imaging datasets. The refined report-aligned labels and associated code will be made publicly available upon acceptance. Because all labels were derived from report text, they reflect report alignment rather than image-level truth.

items.abstract: Tinnitus, or ringing in the ears, is a hearing disorder that affects approximately 15% of human adults globally. The neuroscientific understanding of this subjective disorder is limited at present, partly due to a lack of sufficient neuroimaging data to compensate for the heterogeneity in the disorder; neural data acquisition is often impeded by low patient counts and doubled costs against scanning ample controls. However, with the increase in data sharing practices, data scarcity can be overcome with harmonization methods if scans from independent sites and studies are pooled successfully. To achieve data harmonization for limited data from a tinnitus neuroimaging study, we merged a modest fMRI dataset acquired in our lab (n=35) with age- and gender-matched samples from another large dataset, the Lifespan Human Connectome Project Aging (n=377). We measured functional connectivity (FC) between brain regions based on resting-state fMRI session scans, and used deep learning architecture to systematically combine individual FCs across the datasets. We assembled and trained neural network modules to purge dataset-identifying information from FC maps, and retained patterns that can characterize tinnitus-related FC. Hallmark artifactual information of the datasets was significantly reduced while reconstructing resting state FC data. Relevant relationships in brain connectivity that discern the condition of tinnitus from controls were well-preserved in the reconstructed resting state FC data. In agreement with existing literature on brain networks of tinnitus, connectivity related to default mode, ventral attention and frontoparietal control networks were identified to be crucial for distinguishing the condition, as masking these networks connections severely impacted downstream classification prediction on reconstructed FC. The data harmonization model was successful in merging FC matrices from independently acquired fMRI datasets, without losing out on meaningful functional connectivity patterns of interest for the neuropsychological disorder of tinnitus. Our findings demonstrate the potential of data harmonization by integrating independently acquired datasets on healthy controls to overcome neuroimaging data scarcity while preserving disorder-relevant neural signatures, advancing research on understudied neurological disorders.

items.abstract: Abstract Background To evaluate the feasibility of deep learning-based prediction of mastectomy specimen and final reconstruction weights from three-dimensional CT and MRI, including multimodal and clinical-feature fusion. Methods This retrospective single-center study included 200 patients who underwent total mastectomy and TRAM (transverse rectus abdominis myocutaneous) flap breast reconstruction. Preoperative imaging was used for mastectomy-weight prediction and postoperative imaging for reconstruction-weight prediction. Three-dimensional deep learning models and CT-MRI feature fusion were evaluated with patient-level five-fold cross-validation, and clinical-feature fusion was additionally explored. Results The paired cohorts comprised 184 patients for mastectomy-weight prediction and 146 for reconstruction-weight prediction. MRI with ResNet3D-18 showed the lowest error for mastectomy weight (mean absolute error [MAE], 134.3 g; 95% confidence interval [CI], 119.2–151.4; weighted absolute percentage error, 28.3%), whereas CT-MRI fusion showed the lowest error for reconstruction weight (MAE, 123.0 g; 95% CI, 103.3–144.0; weighted absolute percentage error, 23.2%). Adding clinical features minimally affected mastectomy-weight prediction but numerically improved reconstruction-weight prediction (MAE, 123.0 to 108.2 g), although the 95% CI for the improvement crossed zero. Predictions tended toward the cohort mean at extreme weights. Conclusions Three-dimensional CT and MRI enabled direct deep learning-based prediction of measured surgical weights without explicit volumetric measurement, demonstrating the feasibility of direct image-to-weight prediction in breast reconstruction.

items.abstract: Abstract Purpose: To develop and validate magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based machine learning models integrating habitat analysis of peritumoral edema regions, Visually Accessible Rembrandt Images (VASARI) features and intratumoral heterogeneity (ITH) score for preoperative prediction of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) status in adult-type diffuse glioma. Methods: This retrospective study included 606 patients with adult-type diffuse glioma from two centers (376 for development; 230 for external validation). The peritumoral edema region was divided into two habitats (H1 and H2) using K -means clustering. Habitat-derived radiomics features, VASARI features, and the ITH score were used to construct five models: H1, H2, H1+H2, VASARI + ITH, and a comprehensive fusion model. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) method was employed for interpretability analysis. Results The H2 model outperformed H1 model (AUC, 0.884 vs 0.773). The VASARI + ITH model achieved an AUC of 0.841, whereas the H1 + H2 model achieved an AUC of 0.890. The comprehensive fusion model exhibited the best AUC (0.892), accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. SHAP analysis revealed that habitat-derived radiomic features contributed most to model prediction. Conclusion A fusion model combining habitat-derived radiomics features from the glioma peritumoral edema region, VASARI features, and the ITH score demonstrated favorable predictive performance for preoperative prediction of IDH status in adult-type diffuse glioma.

items.abstract: Abstract Background. Accurate differentiation between connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease (CTD-ILD) and idiopathic interstitial pneumonia (IIP) guides therapeutic decisions, yet substantial overlap in clinical and high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) features frequently complicates discrimination. Multidimensional diagnostic models integrating clinical, radiological, functional and serological markers remain scarce. Methods. This single-center retrospective cohort consecutively enrolled 64 patients with CTD-ILD and 68 with IIP. We compared baseline characteristics, modified Warrick HRCT scores, pulmonary function, echocardiographic parameters, serum KL‑6 and BNP. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors; model discrimination was assessed by ROC curves, with internal validation via 1 000 bootstrap resamples. Random Forest and SHAP analyses were applied for exploratory cross-validation of key predictors. Results.CTD-ILD patients were more often female (68.75% vs 33.82%) and less likely to have a smoking history (32.81% vs 52.94%). NSIP predominated in CTD-ILD and UIP in IIP; the modified Warrick score was higher in IIP (23.5 vs 12.75, P <0.05). After adjustment for sex and smoking, male sex (OR 0.20, 95%CI 0.08–0.46, P =0.0028) and higher Warrick score (OR 1.06, 95%CI 1.02–1.11, P =0.0037) independently predicted IIP, while DLCO% showed a borderline inverse association. The combined nomogram achieved an AUC of 0.808 (95%CI 0.728–0.888), with optimism-corrected AUC 0.779. DCA confirmed satisfactory net clinical benefit, and machine learning highlighted the importance of Warrick score and DLCO%. Conclusions. CTD-ILD and IIP share overlapping but distinguishable phenotypes. This multidimensional nomogram integrating clinical, quantitative HRCT and functional markers improves discrimination over single indicators. Only internal validation was performed; prospective external validation in independent cohorts is required prior to clinical use.

items.abstract: Background and Aims: Despite expanding therapeutic options for Crohn's disease (CD), treatment selection remains largely empiric. Identifying biomarkers linking inflammatory endotypes to treatment outcomes could inform first-line therapy selection. We sought to identify baseline plasma proteins associated with clinical, biochemical, and endoscopic outcomes in patients with CD receiving anti-TNF therapy. Methods: In this prospective multicenter cohort, children and young adults with CD initiating infliximab or adalimumab underwent plasma proteomic profiling at baseline and months 3 and 12 using SomaScan v4.1 (7,322 analytes) with deep remission (clinical and endoscopic) as the primary outcome. Rank-based composite correlation analysis identified candidate proteins associated with prespecified treatment outcomes, followed by functional enrichment analyses. Regularized machine learning models were used to derive and evaluate a candidate protein signature. Results: In a cohort of 80 participants, mean age 13.7 (SD 3.5) years, 42.5% female, and 90% White, composite rank analysis identified 73 candidate proteins associated with one or more outcomes. Seven candidate proteins (IFNA6, IGHM, MBL2, UBASH3A, REG1A, GABBR2, and NTS) were retained for evaluation. In an independent adult cohort (n=324), models based on whole-blood expression of the seven corresponding genes achieved mean AUPRCs of 0.71 (baseline) and 0.76 (week 14) for the cohort-defined primary response outcome. Conclusions: Plasma proteomic profiling identified a candidate 7-protein signature associated with anti-TNF treatment outcomes in CD. Cross-omic replication demonstrated consistent outcome-associated signals in an independent cohort. Although orthogonal validation of the protein signature is needed, these findings support the potential of proteomic biomarkers to guide biologically informed treatment selection.

items.abstract: Background Postoperative venous thromboembolism remains a major cause of preventable morbidity after surgery, and established risk scores may perform inconsistently across surgical populations. Methods MEDLINE, Embase and the Cochrane Library were searched for studies comparing machine learning with traditional risk models for postoperative venous thromboembolism prediction. Risk-of-bias was assessed with PROBAST + AI. The primary outcome was discrimination measured by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis estimated mean differences versus Caprini with 95% credible intervals. Best and worst-version analyses explored the impact of within-study multiplicity, with subgroup analyses by cancer surgery and procedure type. Results Eighteen studies including 177 656 validation patients were included. Meta-ensembles showed the largest improvement compared with Caprini in the best-version analysis (mean difference in AUROC, 0.232; 95% credible interval, 0.129-0.334), with a similar finding in the worst-version analysis (0.237; 0.123-0.351). Several other machine learning classes also had higher AUROC estimates than Caprini, whereas most traditional scores and surgeon judgement did not. Geneva showed lower performance than Caprini. Meta-ensembles ranked first overall, while Caprini and Geneva ranked 14th and last, respectively. Meta-ensembles and boosting models had higher AUROC than Caprini in both cancer surgery analyses; in general surgery, no model class showed higher performance than Caprini in the worst-version analysis. Conclusions Machine learning models, particularly meta-ensembles, showed higher reported discrimination than traditional scores, but evidence remains limited by heterogeneity, inconsistent calibration reporting, sparse decision-analytic evaluation and infrequent external validation. Clinical adoption requires external validation and demonstration of real-world net benefit.

items.abstract: Background/objective Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remains a major cause of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and the risk persists despite potent nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy. Current surveillance relies on broad clinical categories and conventional risk scores, although HCC risk in CHB is heterogeneous and changes over time. This review summarizes current approaches to HCC risk stratification in CHB, critically appraises machine learning (ML)-based models for individualized prediction, and discusses requirements for clinical implementation. Methods We searched PubMed/MEDLINE from inception to July 1, 2026 for studies that developed or validated an ML-based model for incident HCC in adults with CHB, and appraised the included models with a structured approach informed by PROBAST+AI and TRIPOD+AI. Results Conventional models are generally static and do not fully capture non-linear relationships, time-updated risk, or multimodal information. ML-based models using clinical, virological, treatment-related, post-seroclearance, and imaging-derived data can refine risk prediction across stages of CHB care. However, most appraised models were at high risk of bias in the analysis domain, and none has undergone prospective clinical validation. Future models should move toward dynamic prediction using longitudinal data and multimodal integration of clinical variables, liver stiffness, imaging, and viral or molecular biomarkers. Key requirements include external validation, calibration, interpretability, fairness, cost-effectiveness, and prospective impact studies. Conclusion ML-based models may complement conventional risk scores and support individualized surveillance in CHB. Future research should prioritize dynamic, multimodal, externally validated, and clinically implementable systems that improve surveillance decisions and patient outcomes.

items.abstract: Objective Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has an extremely dismal postoperative prognosis. Conventional TNM staging cannot adequately characterize tumor heterogeneity and microenvironment, leading to suboptimal risk stratification. This study aimed to develop and externally validate an integrated prognostic system for PDAC by combining deep learning (DL)-based radiomic features with guideline‑recommended clinicopathological variables. Materials and methods This multicenter retrospective study included 592 patients with PDAC who underwent R0 surgical resection. A Swin Transformer-assisted DL classifier (Outcome Prediction for PDAC, OP-PDAC) was built using multi-planar contrast-enhanced CT scans (axial, coronal, and sagittal planes). Radiogenomic analysis was conducted in 41 patients to elucidate the biological underpinnings of the OP-PDAC. Furthermore, the Intelligent Prognosis Stratification System (IPSS-PDAC) was developed by incorporating clinicopathological variables into the OP-PDAC framework. Results In the derivation and test cohorts, the C‑index of OP-PDAC for predicting 1‑year disease‑free survival (DFS) ranged from 0.807 to 0.844, which was significantly higher than that of the clinicopathological model (CP-PDAC; C‑index, 0.631-0.656). The IPSS-PDAC further enhanced predictive performance, yielding a C‑index of 0.836-0.871, and enabled effective stratification for both DFS and overall survival (all log‑rank p < 0.01). Radiogenomic analysis revealed that high‑risk patients exhibited an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, elevated stromal scores, activated oncogenic pathways, and reduced CD8 + T‑cell infiltration. Conclusion IPSS-PDAC is a non-invasive and robust prognostic stratification system that integrates imaging features and clinicopathological features. By sensitively reflecting tumor heterogeneity and TME, it provides references for clinical decision-making in the postoperative management of PDAC patients. Key points Question This study constructs an integrated prognostic model combining imaging signatures and guideline-recommended clinicopathological variables to address unmet clinical challenges in postoperative risk stratification for PDAC patients. Findings A multi-planar Swin Transformer-based deep learning model (IPSS-PDAC) achieves a C-index of 0.836-0.871 for disease-free survival prediction. Critical relevance statement High-risk patients stratified by the OP-PDAC model display a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, activation of core oncogenic signaling pathways, and reduced CD8 + T-cell infiltration.

items.abstract: The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and health care offers unprecedented opportunities to address global disparities in access to specialized epilepsy diagnosis and treatment, particularly in resource-limited settings. Advances in AI models, combined with increasing internet connectivity and smartphone usage in low-income and middle-income countries, offer promising solutions for epilepsy diagnosis and monitoring through AI-based analysis of electroencephalography recordings captured with affordable open-source systems, smartphone data and electronic health records. However, this technological revolution raises important questions about the preservation and expansion of clinical expertise, AI algorithm transparency and health-care equity. In this Review, we examine how AI can help to address disparities and improve global epilepsy care while maintaining high clinical standards and addressing systemic challenges.

items.abstract: Foundation models are advancing computational pathology by transferring knowledge from large datasets to diagnostic, prognostic and treatment response tasks. Most existing models, however, either operate at the patch level or learn slide-level representations using image-based objectives, coarse tissue labels or pathology reports that vary across institutions and reflect the subjectivity inherent in narrative reporting. Here we introduce THREADS, which instead learns general-purpose whole-slide representations by aligning tissue morphology with genomic or transcriptomic profiles. THREADS was pretrained on over 47,000 hematoxylin-and-eosin-stained tissue sections and evaluated across 107 oncology tasks spanning cancer subtyping and grading, tumor microenvironment characterization, treatment response prediction and survival analysis. THREADS consistently outperformed leading whole-slide foundation models and supervised baselines while demonstrating strong transfer across external cohorts and high label efficiency. These findings establish molecularly guided pretraining as an effective strategy for learning general-purpose whole-slide representations and motivate future extensions incorporating additional molecular, spatial and clinical modalities.

items.abstract: Objective Accurately distinguishing between epileptic seizures (ES) and nonepileptic seizures (NES) remains a significant clinical challenge, typically requiring resource-intensive inpatient video-EEG monitoring. We developed a multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based framework for automated extraction of semiological features from seizure videos, followed by classification of events as ES or NES. Methods We analyzed 90 seizure videos (45 ES, 45 NES) from 29 patients in an epilepsy monitoring unit. Each event was labeled using expert-reviewed video-EEG and annotated for 24 clinically relevant semiological features. An MLLM framework integrating open-source vision-language models (VLMs) and audio-language models (ALMs) was used to extract these features automatically. The extracted features were then used to train classifiers (K-Nearest Neighbors, XGBoost, and Deep Factorization Machine) to distinguish ES from NES. Model performance was evaluated using leave-one-patient-out (LOPO) cross-validation. Results Expert-annotated features yielded near-perfect classification using KNN (precision = 0.92, recall = 0.92, F1-score = 0.92, AUC = 0.99). Compared to expert annotations, the MLLM pipeline achieved a mean recall of 0.71, accuracy of 0.58, and F1-score of 0.51 for feature extraction. Using MLLM-extracted features, the KNN classifier (k = 7) achieved a precision of 0.77, recall of 0.76, F1-score of 0.76, and AUC of 0.76, correctly identifying 68 out of 90 events. Conclusion Multimodal large language models can extract clinically relevant semiological features from seizure videos and support interpretable classification of ES versus NES. This approach offers a scalable, explainable tool to assist in video-based epilepsy diagnosis.

items.abstract: Bispecific T-cell engagers (BiTEs) have transformed the treatment of hematologic malignancies, but real-world pharmacovigilance data on infection-related adverse events remain limited. This study analyzed data from the US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System from October 2014 to September 2025 for seven FDA-approved BiTEs targeting CD19, CD20, B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA), and G protein-coupled receptor class C group 5 member D (GPRC5D). Disproportionality analyses using the reporting odds ratio and Bayesian confidence propagation neural network identified safety signals at the MedDRA High-Level Term (HLT) level. Time to onset and the proportion of fatal outcomes were assessed. Comparisons with chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy were also performed. A total of 3,012 cases (22%) involved infections, with fatal outcomes reported in 33.3% of infection-related reports. At the HLT level, 37 distinct infection-related terms met the prespecified criteria for positive disproportionality signals. These terms included bacterial (n=14), viral (n=12), fungal (n=4), parasitic (n=2), organ-specific (n=3), and other infection-related HLTs (n=2). The median TTO was 36 days (interquartile range 7-124), ranging from 8 days for blinatumomab to 82 days for teclistamab. Bacterial categories showed the earliest median TTO (28 days), followed by fungal and viral categories. Compared with CAR-T, BiTE reported a higher proportion of infections in elderly patients (48% vs 39%) and a longer TTO (36 vs 6 days). Positive infection signals were largely concordant between BiTE and CAR-T. These findings demonstrate a broad spectrum of reported infection-related adverse events, variation in time to onset, and high fatal outcome proportions for certain pathogen-specific categories, highlighting the need for infection surveillance tailored to treatment, timing, and patient risk factors.

items.abstract: Biomimetic nanocarriers inspired by exosomes have emerged as a transformative strategy for precision drug delivery by combining the biological advantages of naturally derived extracellular vesicles with the scalability and tunability of synthetic nanotechnology. Native exosomes exhibit intrinsic immune evasion, membrane stability, ligand-mediated cellular tropism, and the ability to traverse complex biological barrier properties that conventional nanocarriers have struggled to replicate. This review systematically discusses the biological basis of exosomes, including their biogenesis, molecular composition, and intercellular communication roles, and translates these principles into engineering strategies for designing exosome-inspired biomimetic nanocarriers. We critically examine major biomimetic platforms such as cell membrane-coated nanoparticles, hybrid exosome-synthetic vesicles, lipid-based exosome mimetics, and polymeric biomimetic assemblies, with emphasis on fabrication techniques, drug loading approaches, targeting mechanisms, and advanced characterization methods. Recent therapeutic applications across oncology, central nervous system disorders, immunotherapy, gene and RNA delivery, and regenerative medicine are summarised with comparative insights into mechanistic performance. Furthermore, key challenges related to safety, manufacturing scalability, regulatory considerations, and quality control are discussed. Emerging trends, including microfluidic manufacturing, quality-by-design frameworks, and artificial intelligence-assisted nanocarrier optimization, are highlighted as future directions. Finally, we outline critical research gaps and propose a translational roadmap for clinical development of exosome-inspired biomimetic nanocarriers.

items.abstract: Non-typhoidal Salmonella enterica causes major foodborne illnesses worldwide. The traditional antigen-based method has difficulty distinguishing its lineages, while the core genome-based approach has limited discriminatory ability. Therefore, this study aims to investigate better machine learning techniques for analyzing virulent gene distribution patterns as a potential tool for serovar differentiation. A total of 14,176 clinical S. enterica isolates, representing four epidemiologically significant serovars (Enteritidis, Typhimurium, Infantis, Newport), were retrospectively collected from the NCBI Database. Virulence gene profiles, based on presence or absence, were filtered according to prevalence thresholds. At first, we evaluated Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), Decision Tree, Naïve Bayes, and Logistic Regression using stratified 5-fold cross-validation to determine the best interpretable approach for this study. The SVM and RF showed the highest cross-validation accuracy of ~91.7%. The final RF model achieved 91.6% accuracy and substantial agreement (κ = 0.89) for all four serovars. Mean decrease in Gini Index analysis identified lineage-specific virulence factors, with >96% sensitivity for Enteritidis and Typhimurium, and a significant overlap between Newport and Infantis/Typhimurium. SinH, sodC1, and sseK2, and lineage-associated genes such as gtgA, avrA, ybtP, and ybtQ were key predictor genes for the four serovars. Overall, the supervised random forest model accurately discriminated against four Salmonella serovars with biologically relevant virulence factors and complemented existing genomic surveillance tools. Further validation of this framework across diverse serovars, using incoming genomic data and functional testing, would advance this method as a potential tool.

items.abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313times and prefill latency by 6.9times at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5times and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.

items.abstract: We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method shows zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights. Project Page: https://nopeworld.github.io .

items.title: cmHC: Balancing Stream Mixing in Hyper-Connections via Geometric Contraction

items.abstract: Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extends residual connections to multiple streams and stabilizes residual propagation by constraining stream-mixing residual matrices to the Birkhoff polytope, the set of doubly stochastic matrices. In this work, we investigate how to effectively mix residual streams within the Birkhoff polytope. We reveal a mixing trade-off: when under-mixed residual matrices stay close to the vertices of the Birkhoff polytope, hyper-connections will degenerate into a set of nearly independent streams; when over-mixed residual matrices are concentrated around the uniform barycenter of the polytope, streams will become less distinguishable from each other. We theoretically validate our findings by bounding the cumulative residual mixing, stream difference and gradient difference of mixing coefficients across layers. Motivated by these findings, we propose Contraction for Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (cmHC), an exact doubly stochastic method which geometrically contracts the Birkhoff polytope toward its interior. This contraction mitigates under-mixing by forcing the residual matrices to explore deeper into the polytope, with a provable stream mixing bound and no new parameterization. Moreover, we apply a moderate contraction at the shallow layers to prevent over-mixing, enabling stable gradient propagation on extremely large-scale model pretraining. Extensive experiments across dense and mixture-of-experts models at various parameter scales demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of cmHC. We also develop fused operators for cmHC on Ascend NPUs, reducing hyper-connection execution latency by up to 44.8%.

items.abstract: Personalized long-form generation asks a language model to write new text the way a specific user would. The standard recipe, retrieval-augmented generation, places a few of the user's past texts in the prompt but leaves the model to decide what to take from them. We introduce StylePrism, a taxonomy of 28 stylistic aspects in seven categories, and SP-Refine, an inference-time method that makes style extraction an explicit step: the model first fills StylePrism with the user's patterns, quoted evidence, and habits to avoid, then drafts from the user's samples and revises the draft twice against this profile, guided by its own style scores. On the three long-form tasks of LongLaMP with three LLMs, SP-Refine outperforms LongLaMP's retrieval-augmented baseline in 25 of 27 ROUGE and METEOR comparisons, by 10.2% on average and by up to 35.8%. Annotating users' own texts with the extracted profiles shows that StylePrism captures concrete, checkable habits, from the order of rhetorical moves to a reviewer's sign-off. Ablations show that the profile helps as revision guidance, not as a replacement for the samples: writing from the profile alone is worse in all 27 comparisons, while a single implicit-inference call is a cheaper alternative that comes close. Oracle variants that let the reviser see the reference, together with reference-free controls, show that larger refinement gains require information unavailable at inference time.

items.title: Prune to Expand: Training Prompt Enhancers with Less to Imitate
items.summary: Prompt enhancement (PE) refines concise user prompts into detailed descriptions to improve the compositional aesthetics of generated images while preserving user intent. A common practice constructs supervised fine-tuning (SFT) pairs by deriving short, user-like prompts from dense captions, implicitly assuming that captions that improve image generation also provide effective supervision. items.abstract: Prompt enhancement (PE) refines concise user prompts into detailed descriptions to improve the compositional aesthetics of generated images while preserving user intent. A common practice constructs supervised fine-tuning (SFT) pairs by deriving short, user-like prompts from dense captions, implicitly assuming that captions that improve image generation also provide effective supervision. In this paper, however, we uncover a counterintuitive finding: PE models trained on caption pairs with substantial generation gains perform comparably to those trained on pairs with only marginal gains. We argue that dense captions can impose redundant supervision by requiring PE models to reproduce image-specific details weakly related to user intent. Motivated by this discrepancy, we introduce Prune to Expand (P2E), a simple text-only method that refines dense-caption supervision by selectively removing redundant sentences under a per-example deletion bound while preserving explicit user requirements and informative visual structure. Extensive experiments under identical training configurations demonstrate that P2E improves alignment with human preferences and visual quality over conventional dense-caption SFT across diverse image categories and visual generators.

items.abstract: Feeding each position's top-layer hidden state back into the next position's input improves Transformer performance. However, this feedback breaks speculative decoding, since verifying a drafted token requires the top-layer state from its preceding position, which forces the draft to rely on an approximate stand-in. Training the model to adapt to this stand-in can lower the exact-decoding performance ceiling, while using it at inference time further introduces approximation error. We propose Feedback Shortcut to address both bottlenecks. First, state alignment trains a lightweight projection from multi-token prediction head states to stand-ins, leaving base model training untouched. Second, pipelined correction re-evaluates each draft using its predecessor's newly computed state, a much closer proxy to true feedback. Running this correction inside the verification pass of subsequent drafts improves accuracy with zero extra calls. Across 135M and 780M scales, Feedback Shortcut stays within 10^{-4} bits per byte of the exact-decoding ceiling on Paloma and accelerates decoding by 2.4-2.8x with about 2% more training compute than the latent feedback Transformer. At large batch sizes, skipping correction still preserves Transformer speed and over 80% of latent feedback's gains.

items.abstract: RL post-training typically produces domain experts that must then be consolidated into one model, and as new experts keep arriving, this consolidation becomes a continual process. Weight merging and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) must re-consolidate the whole model whenever an expert is added, and can erode capabilities outside the target domains. We propose Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (CSPD), which keeps the pre-RL model frozen, distills each RL expert independently into a soft prompt, and composes experts by concatenating their prompts without joint training. A single soft prompt suffices to distill an RL expert, recovering at least 90% of the teacher's gain in 22 of 23 math, code, and agent settings. Independently trained prompts compose well. In a multi-expert setting, the average rises with every expert added, and the full composition matches MOPD (67.83 vs. 67.79). The composition generalizes best across six held-out benchmarks. Input-space adaptation adds little serving overhead, keeping throughput within 1.5% of the unadapted backbone and reaching 2.40x that of rank-4 LoRA. These results point toward continual post-training on a fixed backbone.

items.abstract: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) pipelines and vision-language models exhibit high accuracy on standard OCR and document-understanding benchmarks, yet they systematically underperform on document patterns that are operationally critical in financial workflows. These patterns include vertical or rotated text, logo-embedded vendor names, fine-print regulatory clauses, degraded scans, and complex multi-column layouts. While underrepresented in public datasets, they constitute a substantial portion of real-world failure cases. We introduce SAVIOR, a sample-efficient data curation methodology that targets such high-impact failure scenarios to adapt vision-language models for robust financial OCR. We further propose PaIRS, a structure-aware evaluation metric that measures layout fidelity by comparing pairwise spatial relationships between tokens. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct with SAVIOR-Train achieves a word recall of 0.93. When the resulting layout-aware OCR output is used as context for document question answering, it attains an F1 score of 0.89, outperforming both open- and closed-source models such as GPT-4o, Mistral-OCR, PaddleOCR-VL, and DeepSeek-OCR.

items.title: AutoPILOT: A Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay
items.summary: Multimodal foundation models can play video games well when the game waits for them, but often fail when it keeps running. We find that much of this gap lies in the harness, which decides what the model sees, what it remembers, and how its outputs become actions over time. items.abstract: Multimodal foundation models can play video games well when the game waits for them, but often fail when it keeps running. We find that much of this gap lies in the harness, which decides what the model sees, what it remembers, and how its outputs become actions over time. Existing harnesses such as VISTA improve the first two, yet turn each model call into at most one action, so the agent acts only as often as its model thinks. We introduce AutoPILOT, which changes the third: in each model call, the model can send a primitive action, start an open-loop macro, or write a closed-loop controller that keeps playing from the screen without further model calls until it hands control back. To evaluate agents in real-time games, we build AFK-Bench, 120 diverse browser games grouped by how they respond to inaction and playable in real time or with the clock paused. With GPT-6.1 Sol under the same budgets, AutoPILOT reaches 68.6% real-time success against 38.3% for VISTA, and on GameWorld it keeps 80.0% in real time while VISTA drops from 84.1% to 42.9%. Its gains hold across models, and it reaches VISTA's final success rate at a fifth of its API cost. Our results suggest that how a harness turns model outputs into actions over time is a central yet underexplored part of agent design, and we hope AutoPILOT and AFK-Bench will serve as a foundation for agents in a world that does not wait.

items.abstract: Most established instance-retrieval benchmarks emphasise landmarks; small sculptures from visually similar series offer a complementary challenge. We introduce Doppeldwarf-306: 1,691 openly licensed photographs of 306 bronze dwarf statues in Wrocław, Poland, many made in themed series that share one style, with the photographer of each image recorded. With no training, nearest-neighbour search over frozen DINOv2 features names the right statue first for 93.1% of leave-one-out queries, and the best of thirteen backbones from seven pretraining paradigms reaches 94.7%. Accuracy falls slowly as candidates are added: for DINOv2, by about 0.8 points each time their number doubles. A natural design for a phone guide compares a photograph only with statues near the user. In simulation this helps, but less than an equal number of randomly chosen statues does, so random subsampling overstates its value; a permutation test ties the penalty to the real layout (p = 0.005). Used as a weight instead of a filter, location raises DINOv2 from 93.4% to 98.7% for a simulated user 25 m from the statue. With the query's photographer withheld, learned local-feature matching raises DINOv2 accuracy from 81.8% to 85.5% and also improves DINOv3. Comparing the two best candidates cuts DINOv2's false acceptance of unknown statues from 38.3% to 19.6% at 90% known acceptance.

items.title: Learning Video Foresight Reasoning from Unlabeled Videos via On-Policy Self-Distillation
items.summary: Video foresight reasoning requires vision-language models to anticipate future events or next actions from currently observed videos. Existing methods fit future captions, rationales, or full visual states, but face two limitations. First, they rely on annotations or external large models for supervision, limiting scalability. We address this with an on-policy self-distillation framework that turns past-future video…
items.abstract: Video foresight reasoning requires vision-language models to anticipate future events or next actions from currently observed videos. Existing methods fit future captions, rationales, or full visual states, but face two limitations. First, they rely on annotations or external large models for supervision, limiting scalability. We address this with an on-policy self-distillation framework that turns past-future video pairs into a natural self-supervised signal without extra annotations or LLM supervision. Second, they treat the whole future clip as equally valuable, although most of it is irrelevant context information. We address this by defining a foresight score, from which we obtain a contrastive privilege advantage that drives the model to learn the most valuable future information. Since the score is intractable, we optimize a tractable lower-bound surrogate that interpolates this advantage, computed between the true and a random reference future, with a teacher-student distillation advantage; together, they amplify decision-relevant content information and suppress irrelevant context information. We call the resulting framework Future-OPSD. On open-ended prediction and closed-ended planning, Future-OPSD improves base models by up to 14.2 and 15.9 points without compromising general video understanding. Code will be available at https://jingchensun.github.io/future-opsd/

items.abstract: Background: /Objectives: ACTL6B encodes BAF53B, a neuron-enriched component of BRG1/BRM-associated factor (BAF) chromatin-remodeling complexes involved in neuronal differentiation and maturation. However, the biological and clinical significance of ACTL6B expression in glioma remains unknown. Here, we show that ACTL6B expression is linked to a neuronal differentiation-associated transcriptional program, favorable clinical outcome, and molecular features indicative of less aggressive glioma biology. Methods: Transcriptomic and clinical data from The Cancer Genome Atlas lower-grade glioma (TCGA-LGG) and Chinese Glioma Genome Atlas (CGGA) cohorts were analyzed. Survival, molecular and mutation-based comparisons, co-expression, Gene Ontology enrichment, and targeted transcriptional analyses were complemented by use of single-cell RNA sequencing data, and xCell, ESTIMATE, and Random Forest-based supervised machine learning analyses. Results: Higher ACTL6B expression was associated with favorable molecular characteristics, lower histological grade, and longer overall survival (OS) in both cohorts. In TCGA-LGG, the association persisted after adjustment for age, grade, and molecular subtype, although it was attenuated in a stratified sensitivity analysis. ACTL6B expression was positively associated with neuronal differentiation and synaptic genes and inversely associated with proliferation-related transcripts and ACTL6A. Functional enrichment highlighted neuronal and synaptic processes. Single-cell and tumor microenvironment analyses supported a malignant-cell contribution to ACTL6B expression and reduced immune/stromal transcriptional signatures. Machine learning accurately predicted ACTL6B expression from broader transcriptional patterns. Conclusions: ACTL6B expression identifies a neuronal differentiation-associated tran-scriptional program linked to favorable survival and less aggressive glioma biology. These findings extend emerging associations between neuronal transcriptional states and favorable glioma phe-notypes to chromatin-remodeling machinery.

items.abstract: Answering questions over days or weeks of video requires searching for scattered clues across long timelines. Existing video agents rely on complex memory graphs and fixed retrieval pipelines, which restrict how the agent can search. We propose VideoJSON, a minimal harness for ultra-long video understanding that keeps the memory simple and lets a coding agent write its own search programs. During indexing, a vision-language model turns each minute of video into a single JSON record containing a dense caption and structured fields such as events, entities, places, and speech transcripts. At query time, the agent writes Python or Bash programs in a sandboxed container to filter, link, and read these records over multiple steps, without task-specific training or raw video access. On four ultra-long video benchmarks, VideoJSON with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash outperforms MAGIC-Video by 7.0, 20.0, and 24.75 points on EgoLifeQA, Ego-R1-Bench, and MM-Lifelong Week, and beats the best prior EgoMemReason score by 12.6 points. Across four policy models of increasing capability, VideoJSON's average score rises by up to 11.58 points over the weakest model, compared with at most 5.50 points for MAGIC-Video. Ablations show that both agentic code search and the structured JSON records drive these gains, while adding hourly summaries, extra tools, or video access changes the average score by less than 1.5 points. In addition, fine-tuning Qwen-3.5-Flash on 64 VideoJSON trajectories from an unrelated 100-hour livestream improves its MM-Lifelong scores by up to 8.25 points. Code will be open-sourced after publication.

items.abstract: Agentic systems are increasingly being explored for automating experimental high-energy physics measurements, but the correctness of their results can today be reliably evaluated only via extensive expert review. To address this, we propose a method to perform detailed quantitative evaluations of agent-driven analyses through the use of blind analysis and injection tests, which are critical in a typical expert review. Agents develop a data analysis pipeline on a public dataset, while the evaluation is performed on programmatically generated sealed private datasets where signals are injected and simulation settings varied within realistic detector uncertainties. By requiring agents to provide a single workflow that is evaluated across these "sealed worlds", we are able to test the accuracy and robustness of the workflows. We demonstrate the approach on four tasks built from CMS open data and present it as a way to reliably benchmark scientific work in experimental high-energy physics. At the time of writing, the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, reaches 60% of the score of the expert reference analyses on average, ahead of GPT 6 Astra at 38% and Claude Opus 5.5 at 31%. In individual sessions on one of the tasks, Gemini 4 Argon exceeds the reference. The benchmark is hosted at https://hep-ex-bench.github.io

items.abstract: Transcription factor (TF)-based biosensors can report metabolite concentrations, but interpreting the effects of regulatory mutations remains challenging. Here, we characterized PP_2046, a putative LysR-type transcriptional regulator from Pseudomonas putida KT2440, and two adaptive laboratory evolution-derived variants, M1I and E34G, as 1,4-butanediol (1,4-BDO)-responsive reporters in Escherichia coli. We combined flow-cytometric dose-response measurements, constrained nonlinear regression, Western blotting, AlphaFold 3 structural modeling, and promoter substitution to compare regulatory behavior and sensor output. At 700 mM 1,4-BDO, M1I and E34G exhibited 3.24- and 2.10-fold endpoint fluorescence responses, respectively. Model fitting associated M1I's higher fold-change with lower basal reporter output, and Western blot analysis supported reduced PP_2046 abundance. Structural modeling suggested that E34G may alter DNA-contact geometry, although this prediction was not experimentally verified. Promoter substitution in the M1I background yielded an observed 5.07-fold response at 700 mM 1,4-BDO, but the difference in endpoint fold-change from the original promoter construct was not statistically significant (p = 0.054). Ligand profiling revealed cross-reactivity with related short-chain diols and γ-butyrolactone, while appreciable 1,4-BDO responses required concentrations of 300-700 mM. These findings establish a proof-of-concept PP_2046 reporter whose sensitivity and selectivity require further engineering.

items.abstract: Abstract Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis (ICI-M) is a rare but often fatal immune-related adverse event. Large language models (LLMs) have provided new opportunities for patient education, yet whether they can effectively support patient education in ICI-M remains unknown. In this study, we submitted 20 standardized ICI-M-related patient questions to five LLMs (ChatGPT-5.5, Gemini-3.5 Flash, DeepSeek-V4, Qwen 3.7, and Doubao), generating 100 responses. Model performance was evaluated using the Global Quality Score (GQS), modified DISCERN (mDISCERN), Quality Analysis of Medical Artificial Intelligence (QAMAI), Ensuring Quality Information for Patients (EQIP), Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool understandability and actionability scores (PEMAT-U and PEMAT-A), and six readability indices. Significant inter-model differences were observed across most quality and readability metrics, and no single model outperformed the others across all dimensions. DeepSeek-V4 achieved the highest mDISCERN score [5.00 (IQR, 4.00–5.00)], whereas ChatGPT-5.5 achieved the highest PEMAT-A score [40.00 (IQR, 35.00–45.00)]. Readability was suboptimal, with a mean FKGL of 16.60 ± 2.64. Correlation analyses demonstrated information quality, usability, and readability represented correlated but distinct evaluation dimensions. While LLMs may serve as adjunctive tools for ICI-M patient education, substantial optimization of content accessibility and actionability is required prior to clinical implementation.

items.title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions
items.summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. items.abstract: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.

items.title: Posterior Matching Distillation
items.summary: Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. items.abstract: Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. This matching is often driven by reverse-KL objectives, whose mode-seeking bias favors dominant teacher modes at the expense of diversity across samples. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), a new member of the distribution-based distillation family that combines mode-covering posterior sampling with any-step generation. At zero population loss, PMD recovers the teacher's full posterior of clean images at each trained noise level. Its stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without further training. To learn these posteriors, PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. Under Gaussian corruption, exponentially tilted posterior mean is a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input. We prove that, matching tilted means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior. PMD thus supervises the entire conditional distribution through a family of mean constraints, without any auxiliary student-score network. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods on both models, while maintaining competitive or leading performance across prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.

items.title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher
items.summary: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. items.abstract: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a target model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.

items.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the stage in which Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) advance their capability to reason over video. However, the VideoLLM also learns to answer from textual regularities of its training data, a shortcut that bypasses the video. The regularities behind the shortcut are hard to define at the data level, and the shortcut forms regardless of training epoch, data size, or backbone. The shortcut is hidden behind a rise in accuracy within the training distribution, yet it is not required for the rise and even costs SFT the gain the video offers under distribution shift. We therefore propose Video-Evidence Training via Orthogonal projection (VETO), which intervenes on the fine-tuning update where the shortcut is written rather than on the data. VETO calibrates the subspace that the text alone occupies in the activations of the base model and projects the update onto its orthogonal complement. The VideoLLM is thus left to ground its answer in the full input, with the shortcut suppressed as it forms and never defined. Across seven VideoLLMs, VETO preserves the gain of SFT on the training distribution and suppresses the shortcut. On six benchmarks under shift it gains more than SFT and answers from the full input rather than the shortcut. Code is available at https://github.com/Youngwoo-git/VETO.

items.title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience
items.summary: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. items.abstract: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.

By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. items.abstract: We present Depth Pro 2, an approach to estimating dense metric depth for images and video at full resolution. By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. To overcome this trade-off, we train a single, scalable network that processes both images and video and predicts depth maps at native resolution. Depth Pro 2 produces depth maps that are metrically accurate, sharp, and temporally consistent all at once, outperforming prior work in all of these dimensions. We release a family of models that define a new Pareto frontier in terms of metric accuracy, sharpness, temporal consistency, and runtime. We release code and weights at https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-depth-pro-2/

items.title: TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs
items.summary: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result.
