items.abstract: Full-duplex interaction models exhibit strong conversational agency, enabling natural, low-latency turn-taking, backchannels, and interruptions. However, completing tasks further requires task agency: timely tool invocation and argument revision following user corrections. Frontend-backend agents separate initiation from execution: the frontend decides whether and what to request, while the backend determines how. Execution can be offloaded, but unsent requests cannot be executed, and incomplete ones can misdirect the backend. On Full-Duplex-Bench v3 (FDB v3), most failures of Realtime-Venus-Audio + Harness in our streaming pipeline occur before a domain tool executes. We introduce Duopra, a full-duplex interaction model that learns task execution alongside conversational control. Duopra treats the backend as a tool, accepting a self-contained natural-language request. Direct calls and backend delegation share an action interface and requirements for faithful initiation and correct execution. Its three-stage training combines protocol SFT, full-duplex RL rewarding timely and complete execution, and projector-only repair of talker conditioning after thinker updates. With the same backend, Pass@1 rises from 4.7% to 44.7%; Duopra achieves 47.7% calling tools directly (26.0% after SFT) and 49.3% with a DeepSeek backend. It improves three FDB v1.0 takeover rates over the base model. These results show that task agency can coexist with key conversational agency.

items.title: DiLE: Discrimination-Aware Latent-Space Learning for Universal Multimodal Embeddings
items.summary: Multimodal large language models have greatly improved input understanding in universal multimodal embedding models. However, this understanding does not ensure that their embeddings preserve the evidence needed to distinguish relevant items from confusable alternatives. To preserve essential discriminative evidence in embeddings, this paper proposes DiLE, a discrimination-aware latent-space learning framework that…
items.abstract: Multimodal large language models have greatly improved input understanding in universal multimodal embedding models. However, this understanding does not ensure that their embeddings preserve the evidence needed to distinguish relevant items from confusable alternatives. To preserve essential discriminative evidence in embeddings, this paper proposes DiLE, a discrimination-aware latent-space learning framework that combines task guidance with on-policy retrieval feedback. Specifically, a few learnable queries are used to encode task-relevant information in a compact latent space. Reasoning instructions and auxiliary answer-generation supervision shape these representations to support both task understanding and retrieval discrimination. To address task-specific discriminative needs, we design shared-private expert adaptation that integrates cross-task knowledge sharing with task-specific representation learning. Building on this, the on-policy hard-negative distillation is introduced: the student retrieves confusable candidates, and a reverse KL divergence objective aligns its embedding-based similarity distribution with the teacher's fine-grained relevance distribution over these candidates. Candidates are periodically refreshed using updated student snapshots, tying teacher supervision to the student's evolving retrieval behavior and confusions. Across four model configurations that span two backbone generations, DiLE achieves state-of-the-art performance on MMEB-v2, UVRB, and MRMR, demonstrating its effectiveness across modalities and tasks.

items.title: ViDecide: Teaching Video Diffusion Models to Reason and Plan Step by Step
items.summary: Current leading video generation models can synthesize highly realistic videos, while still frequently violating physical and logical constraints in multi-step reasoning and planning, even after training with large-scale reasoning data or existing diffusion RL methods. We attribute these failures to the conventional video training paradigm, which treats a solution as a fixed-length clip rather than a chain of…
items.abstract: Current leading video generation models can synthesize highly realistic videos, while still frequently violating physical and logical constraints in multi-step reasoning and planning, even after training with large-scale reasoning data or existing diffusion RL methods. We attribute these failures to the conventional video training paradigm, which treats a solution as a fixed-length clip rather than a chain of decisions. We present ViDecide, a decision-centric framework that trains video diffusion models to predict state transitions causally and decide when to stop, with a decision-focused training schedule. We further propose Corrective Fine-tuning (CFT), which corrects failed decisions by mapping their noise to the model's own successful continuations, achieving stable improvement without policy-gradient optimization. Across abstract games, planning tasks, and a new benchmark of multi-step robot planning, ViDecide achieves an average strict success rate of 83.8%, far above 23.3% for standard fine-tuning and 67.8% for the strongest prior method, and generalizes to larger puzzles and unseen layouts. Our framework therefore unlocks greater potential for video generation models as reliable reasoners and planners in the visual world. Project page: https://kevin-thu.github.io/ViDecide.

items.title: UniVEP: Unifying Velocity and Endpoint Prediction for Robot Manipulation
items.summary: Flow-matching robot policies usually use one prediction target throughout action generation, even though recovering actions from noise and polishing nearly clean actions bring different challenges. We systematically compare velocity prediction (V), endpoint prediction (X), and velocity-weighted endpoint prediction (X--V) across multiple robot policies, benchmarks, and inference budgets. On StarVLA and LiLa-WAM, X--V…
items.abstract: Flow-matching robot policies usually use one prediction target throughout action generation, even though recovering actions from noise and polishing nearly clean actions bring different challenges. We systematically compare velocity prediction (V), endpoint prediction (X), and velocity-weighted endpoint prediction (X--V) across multiple robot policies, benchmarks, and inference budgets. On StarVLA and LiLa-WAM, X--V works best for few-step generation, while V gains more from iterative refinement. We further uncover their complementary strengths across noise levels: clean actions have concentrated covariance spectra, endpoint predictions stay more stable under high noise, and velocity predictions offer more accurate corrections near clean actions. Inspired by these findings, we introduce UniVEP, which learns both prediction targets together with consistency supervision and switches from endpoint recovery to velocity refinement as noise drops. Each step only needs one network run, and joint training also boosts single-step endpoint generation. Tests on simulated and real-world manipulation show better success rates and efficiency. On RoboTwin, UniVEP hits 61.36% success with one StarVLA run, beating the best single-target baseline at sixteen runs (59.96%). With LiLa-WAM, two runs outperform the best sixteen-step single-target baseline and cut inference latency by 77.1%.

items.title: Prism: Hierarchical Text Detection with Minimalist Design
items.summary: Hierarchical text detection aims to localize words, text lines, and paragraphs while parsing their structural relationships. It provides essential structural cues for visual text understanding. To maximize accuracy, existing methods typically rely on complex multi-scale feature fusion necks and heavy-weight heads, resulting in bloated architectures and low inference efficiency. In this paper, we argue that a…
items.abstract: Hierarchical text detection aims to localize words, text lines, and paragraphs while parsing their structural relationships. It provides essential structural cues for visual text understanding. To maximize accuracy, existing methods typically rely on complex multi-scale feature fusion necks and heavy-weight heads, resulting in bloated architectures and low inference efficiency. In this paper, we argue that a sufficiently pre-trained backbone can effectively replace these sophisticated external modules, while simple geometric inclusion suffices for hierarchical text structural parsing. Thus, we propose Prism, a minimalist framework for hierarchical text detection. Prism performs multi-granularity detection by attaching parallel lightweight heads to a single-scale backbone feature map, covering words, text lines, and paragraphs, and reconstructs the structural hierarchy via an efficient geometric inclusion algorithm. In addition, we systematically compare representative lightweight head archetypes and show that pixel-level regression offers the best accuracy-efficiency trade-off in this setting. Experiments on multiple public benchmarks show that our significantly simplified architecture achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with remarkable efficiency. Specifically, it runs 1.7times faster than LRANet on CTW1500 while achieving higher accuracy, and surpasses the current SOTA method, OmniParser V2, by over 6 PQ points on the hierarchical HierText dataset. Code will be released soon.

items.title: Fast-JEPA: Advancing the Success-Latency Frontier for Latent World Models
items.summary: Latent world models predict the outcomes of action sequences, but comparing candidate plans through recursive rollout remains expensive at test time. We introduce Fast-JEPA, a latent world model planning framework that advances the success-latency Pareto frontier of predictive search. Fast-JEPA reorganizes predictive computation to support effective action-sequence search at low planning cost. It constructs a…
items.abstract: Latent world models predict the outcomes of action sequences, but comparing candidate plans through recursive rollout remains expensive at test time. We introduce Fast-JEPA, a latent world model planning framework that advances the success-latency Pareto frontier of predictive search. Fast-JEPA reorganizes predictive computation to support effective action-sequence search at low planning cost. It constructs a goal-directed plan to guide search and directly predicts the outcomes of complete candidates for efficient comparison, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, Fast-JEPA achieves 96.50% average success rate with 2.41x faster planning than INTACT. Search-budget sweeps show that its competitive success and low latency extend across candidate counts and refinement depths. We further introduce DynaGoal, a benchmark for evaluating world-model planning under dynamic out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines, and controlled response delays. Fast-JEPA achieves average success rates of 73.83% on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoal-Deadline, demonstrating the practical value of low-latency predictive planning under changing control conditions and execution-time constraints. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sofilyzia/Fast-JEPA.

items.title: WeightCode: Installing New Capabilities into Neural Networks via Weight-Space Programming
items.summary: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write…
items.abstract: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23-14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs.

items.title: Plan4D: Generative Plannable 4D Worlds
items.summary: Most world models for future prediction prioritize aestetic quality of generated videos, but offer only weak physical grounding and limited geometric consistency over time, due to the lack of explicit 4D modeling. In this paper, we introduce plan4d, a possible next milestone towards building a generative plannable 4D world model that predicts future RGB videos together with dense 4D geometry, including depth,…
items.abstract: Most world models for future prediction prioritize aestetic quality of generated videos, but offer only weak physical grounding and limited geometric consistency over time, due to the lack of explicit 4D modeling. In this paper, we introduce plan4d, a possible next milestone towards building a generative plannable 4D world model that predicts future RGB videos together with dense 4D geometry, including depth, cameras, point clouds, and scene flow from an observed scene context and text-specified actions. Since training data with paired actions and dense 4D annotations is inherently scarce, plan4d leverages the complementary priors of foundational video generators and 3D reconstructors. Specifically, we propose a model-stitching architecture that couples Depth Anything 3 with LongCat-Video and augments it with an auxiliary DPT head for scene-flow prediction. The resulting model allows us to plan and generate complex, long-horizon, and fine-grained actions in a dynamic 3D scenes, while substantially improving both visual fidelity and geometric accuracy of the generated future videos. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that plan4d achieves state-of-the-art performance in generative 4D modeling of environmental reactions. Project Page: https://fogradio.github.io/plan4d-project

items.title: How Feedback-Free Self-Evolution Reshapes Agent Skills: A Systematic Study
items.summary: Agent skills are documents in which experts write down procedural knowledge, and models increasingly maintain them by rewriting them without feedback. Such rewriting could adapt a skill to the model that uses it or erode the expert knowledge that makes it useful, yet how skills evolve under this feedback-free self-evolution has not been studied. We let models rewrite expert skills round after round without any task,…
items.abstract: Agent skills are documents in which experts write down procedural knowledge, and models increasingly maintain them by rewriting them without feedback. Such rewriting could adapt a skill to the model that uses it or erode the expert knowledge that makes it useful, yet how skills evolve under this feedback-free self-evolution has not been studied. We let models rewrite expert skills round after round without any task, run or judgment and run agents built on the same models with the rewritten skills. Our experiments show that the skills lose value rather than improve, as every model we test performs worse with them on every benchmark, by 15 points on average on SkillsBench after thirty rounds. Sampling each model's prior with skills it writes from the topic alone, we find that rewriting pulls skills toward this prior and gives up first the knowledge outside it. Putting this knowledge back recovers much of the lost pass rate, so an expert's skill is valuable largely for what the model does not write on its own. Building on this insight, SkillDiff marks this knowledge in place and raises the pass rate on SkillsBench by 4.8 points on average without feedback or any change to the skill's text. Project repository: https://github.com/LitaoGuo/How-Self-Evolution-Reshapes-Skills.

items.title: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models
items.summary: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at…
items.abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.

Peptidomics and multi-step virtual screening identified three umami peptides-DNDLM, PHDP, and LDDDF-from Coprinus comatus trypsin hydrolysate. Recognition thresholds were 0.125 mg/mL (200-270 μM). Electronic-tongue (0.1 mg/mL) and human sensory (1.0 mg/mL) evaluations ranked DNDLM highest; PHDP and LDDDF did not…
items.abstract: Natural flavor ingredients derived from edible fungi offer sustainable routes to umami taste enrichment. Peptidomics and multi-step virtual screening identified three umami peptides-DNDLM, PHDP, and LDDDF-from Coprinus comatus trypsin hydrolysate. Recognition thresholds were 0.125 mg/mL (200-270 μM). Electronic-tongue (0.1 mg/mL) and human sensory (1.0 mg/mL) evaluations ranked DNDLM highest; PHDP and LDDDF did not differ significantly in the sensory panel. Docking to AlphaFold 3-modeled T1R1/T1R3 yielded rankings inconsistent with sensory responses. Subsequent 100-ns molecular dynamics (MD) and molecular mechanics/generalized Born surface area (MM/GBSA) analyses suggested DNDLM maintained persistent polar contacts, a dominant low-energy basin, and the most favorable estimated binding free energy (-79.18 ± 12.01 kcal/mol); LDDDF showed greater conformational heterogeneity. Energy decomposition identified Arg151, Arg277, and Arg307 as recurrent contributors; Arg281 additionally favored DNDLM binding. These findings identify previously unreported C. comatus-derived umami peptides and provide molecular-level insight into their predicted interactions with T1R1.

items.abstract: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.

items.title: Interpretable Prototype-Conditioned Adaptation for Weather Forecasting
items.summary: Data-driven weather forecasting requires distinguishing local states and their temporal evolution. However, learned patterns remain implicit in neural forecasters, making their influence difficult to interpret. Failing to distinguish local evolution can lead to similar forecasts for locations that develop differently, increasing prediction error. This motivates explicit references for distinguishing and interpreting…
items.abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting requires distinguishing local states and their temporal evolution. However, learned patterns remain implicit in neural forecasters, making their influence difficult to interpret. Failing to distinguish local evolution can lead to similar forecasts for locations that develop differently, increasing prediction error. This motivates explicit references for distinguishing and interpreting local patterns. Prototypes provide explicit pattern references, but sample- or task-level conditioning leaves open how to adapt to distinct locations and variable groups. To deal with this problem, we design ProtoCast, which uses group-specific prototype banks to adapt local features while accounting for cross-variable dependencies. Specifically, (1) we combine each group's historical features and temporal change with forecast context from cross-variable attention for evolution-aware prototype matching. (2) Sparse mixtures of prototype-specific low-rank operators tailor corrections to each group and location. A gated attention block then exchanges the corrected features across groups before prediction. Each group's correction decomposes into explicit prototype contributions before this fusion. (3) We jointly train the forecasting network and operators from scratch and refit each group's prototypes before every training epoch. Slot tracking preserves prototype-operator associations, making each prototype's contribution to local corrections more interpretable. Experiments on GlobalForecast and TyphoonTracking show improved forecasting accuracy, while prototype deletion links local feature contributions to changes in prediction error. This work advances the development of more accurate and interpretable data-driven weather forecasting models. Project page: https://zhixuanli.github.io/projects/li2026protocast

items.abstract: We report the development of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, a payment foundation model that integrates sequence, tabular, and graph representations for payment risk detection. The model contains approximately 7B parameters, with approximately 1.7B activated per task route. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer is pretrained to learn reusable behavioral and relational representations, primarily on Ant International's internal payment data. In a cross-business transfer experiment, pretraining improves the target business metric by 34.5% over the same architecture trained from scratch. With only 25% of the training labels, the pretrained model outperforms the full-label scratch baseline in Average Precision (AP) and Recall@0.5% on different merchant domains. In a four-month online experiment on Ant International's billion-scale payment platform, the model reduced the overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to XGB-Online.

items.title: LoopedWAM: Looped World Action Models for Elastic Inference
items.summary: World action models (WAMs) couple generative video modeling with robotic action prediction but typically require large video and action transformers, limiting deployment efficiency. We present LoopedWAM, a compact WAM that recurrently applies a shared six-block core in each expert, executing 30 transformer layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert. To account for their asymmetric inference costs, the video and…
items.abstract: World action models (WAMs) couple generative video modeling with robotic action prediction but typically require large video and action transformers, limiting deployment efficiency. We present LoopedWAM, a compact WAM that recurrently applies a shared six-block core in each expert, executing 30 transformer layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert. To account for their asymmetric inference costs, the video and action experts can operate at different depths: visual features are computed once per query, whereas action computation repeats at every sampling step. We further propose elastic self-distillation, which trains a single elastic checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, across action-depth and sampling-step budgets. With only 0.58B policy parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM achieves 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, while using 7.4times less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched inference measurements. On LIBERO, LoopedWAM-E achieves 96.0% success in 27.6 ms or 95.2% in 24.7 ms on an H100, providing multiple accuracy-latency operating points from a single checkpoint; with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of LoopedWAM on all three benchmarks. Ablations demonstrate that weight-shared depth preserves competitive performance, while aggressive action-depth reduction requires explicit budget-aware training. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, LoopedWAM succeeds in 71.3% of 80 trials across four tasks.

items.title: Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences
items.summary: Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations and cash constraints because empty shelves hide lost walk-in demand, short-shipped customers quietly shrink future orders weeks later, and emergency buying drains working capital. We introduce SMB Bench, a calibrated 90-day…
items.abstract: Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations and cash constraints because empty shelves hide lost walk-in demand, short-shipped customers quietly shrink future orders weeks later, and emergency buying drains working capital. We introduce SMB Bench, a calibrated 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run frontier trace dataset, to ask what experience and learning signal make an agent better at noticing, attributing, and acting on the delayed consequences of its own decisions in unseen businesses. Across 16 frontier models, only 3 outperform a fixed buying rule; models often record a relevant diagnosis in their notes without changing later purchases in time, showing that diagnosing a problem, changing behavior, and improving a business are separate achievements. To study how experience improves those failures in an open model (Qwen3.8-27B), we used training-business records to identify operational rules and archived frontier quarters as starting states to continue from rather than transcripts to copy. On an unseen test business under identical evaluation instructions, the trained policy followed customer-protection commitments more consistently and reduced severe-loss quarters, while the additional profit benefit remained uncertain. Carrying those commitments through the quarter exposed the cost of fulfilling them, as early-quarter stocking habits left the buyer relying on emergency supply and a deteriorating supplier. The results separate recognizing a delayed effect, acting on it consistently, and coordinating surrounding decisions so that the response improves profit. SMB Bench connects these observations to a learning method by turning archived decisions and their consequences into reusable training experience.

items.summary: Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B active parameters, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Beam delivers frontier level reasoning, while requiring 3-4x less inference compute than many models of its class. Pretrained on 23.8T diverse, curated, high-quality tokens, Beam features a 1M-token context window achieved through a…
items.abstract: Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B active parameters, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Beam delivers frontier level reasoning, while requiring 3-4x less inference compute than many models of its class. Pretrained on 23.8T diverse, curated, high-quality tokens, Beam features a 1M-token context window achieved through a novel two-stage midtraining phase, built on verifiable, correctness-anchored data. Post-training leveraged a large-scale, fully asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) campaign across 10.5K GB300 GPUs, generating over 100M rollouts over 4 weeks of training. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date. Across our evaluation suite, capabilities continued to improve as we increased RL compute, with no sign of a plateau. Supported by deep hardware-model co-design, FP8/NVFP4 quantization, and a 1.93B-parameter speculative decoding drafter (DFlash 2), Beam maximizes serving throughput with efficient, flexible deployment. Averaged across conversation turns and harm categories, Beam refuses or pivots on 88.9% of harmful requests while complying with 81.5% of harmless requests, achieving the highest refusal/pivot rate on harmful requests among open-weight models on the Pareto frontier.

items.abstract: Vision-Language Models increasingly rely on textual reasoning to solve advanced multimodal tasks. Despite its effectiveness, this paradigm faces two fundamental limitations. First, relying on textual reasoning alone can limit perceptual ability in vision-centric questions, where accurate answers depend on interpreting task-relevant visual evidence. Second, applying textual reasoning uniformly across inputs overlooks question-dependent variation in both reasoning modality and depth, often producing verbose and unnecessary traces when little logical inference is required. To this end, we propose Adaptive Visual-Textual Reasoning (AVTR), which introduces visual imagination as a complementary reasoning modality to textual thinking, enabling the model to revisit its visual observations and distill the salient evidence through generative visual reflection. Furthermore, we formulate reasoning-modality selection as a learned routing problem, allowing a single policy to adaptively harness the complementary strengths of visual reflection and textual reasoning in response to the perceptual and inferential demands of the input. Across 16 benchmarks, AVTR improves the average score by 4.5 points over Qwen3.5 baseline, while reducing inference latency by 33\%. It also scales effectively into a smaller size backbone, outperforming the evaluated 2B-scale baselines.

items.abstract: Adapting a film into a game requires selecting source elements and translating them into player actions, rules, and feedback. We introduce Movie2Game-Bench (M2G-bench), a benchmark for evaluating film-to-game adaptation beyond playability. M2G-bench combines general evaluation, movie-specific evaluation, and playtesting by three GUI model players. The protocol connects source content to gameplay steps and implementation evidence, capturing both content preservation and interactive realization. The benchmark comprises 22 films and 658 source-specific reference items. Evaluating 14 models on the same films with their selected primary harnesses reveals complementary strengths in game quality, adaptation, and player experience. A shared weakness concerns playable sequences: this category has the lowest content-presence mean in all 14 models, averaging 37.9 out of 100 compared with 54.8 for iconic elements. Among judgments of retained emotionaldevelopment content, narrative choices account for 60.0% and scenario operation for 7.2%. These findings identify two linked priorities for film-to-game adaptation: preserving source situations that can support gameplay and connecting retained content to player actions and consequences.

items.abstract: Generating physically based rendering (PBR) texture maps for a 3D mesh from a single reference image is highly ambiguous, as the observed appearance entangles material identity, surface reflectance, and illumination. While current generative methods produce realistic albedo maps, they still struggle to infer accurate metallic and roughness attributes for relighting. We present UltraTex, a cascaded multi-view framework that moves beyond appearance matching by integrating physical knowledge into multi-view diffusion-based PBR generation. UltraTex first jointly predicts albedo and world-space shading normals to generate more detailed albedo maps, and then predicts metallic-roughness (MR) maps conditioned on the generated albedo, reference image, and material semantic priors. To inject material semantics, a lightweight adapter transforms hidden-layer features of a vision-language model (VLM) into intrinsic material representation tokens, providing part-level knowledge anchors for MR estimation. To model material-light interaction, photometric representation alignment guides intermediate diffusion features toward ground-truth material renderings under controlled lighting. This makes metallic and roughness variations observable through highlight intensity, specular sharpness, and local reflectance contrast, providing stronger guidance for fine-grained material prediction without explicit lighting supervision. Extensive experiments show that UltraTex generates high-quality textures and outperforms existing open-source and commercial methods in visual fidelity, material accuracy, and physical plausibility.

items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). Model developers use the attacks discovered during internal red-teaming to harden agents through adversarial training before deployment, a collaborative offensive-defensive process known in cybersecurity as purple-teaming. However, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee robustness gains from subsequent adversarial training. Specifically, we find that two state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, suffer from mode collapse, repeatedly discovering similar attack strategies whose additional successes add no additional robustness improvements to adversarial training. To address this gap, we introduce PIPETTE, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that effectively converts red-teaming discoveries into defender robustness improvements. PIPETTE employs a dictionary learning-based reward that encourages broader coverage of attack strategies during red-teaming. It also integrates an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to IPI defense, enabling agents to resist attacks while completing legitimate user tasks. Extensive evaluations across agentic benchmarks (AgentDojo and ASB) demonstrate that PIPETTE produces defenders that achieve near-zero attack success rates on static attacks and can withstand strong adaptive attacks, while maintaining benign task utility close to that of the undefended baseline.

items.summary: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. items.abstract: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.

items.summary: Personalized vision-language assistants use visual observations and personal memories to provide advice tailored to the user. items.abstract: Personalized vision-language assistants use visual observations and personal memories to provide advice tailored to the user. When the observed scene contains a physical hazard, personal context, such as allergies, medical conditions, or mobility constraints, can change what help is appropriate. Responding appropriately therefore requires recognizing the visible hazard and applying the relevant person's information. We introduce PReMind-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that evaluates this combination across diverse hazards and personal-memory conditions. It separately measures memory access, grounding, abstention, and hazard response, and assesses joint success on interdependency cases. Existing models often satisfy one requirement while failing the other, and training only for safety or personalization leaves a gap in joint success. We therefore propose PReMind, a two-phase reinforcement learning framework that combines on-demand and forced-call interactions (memory always retrieved) to jointly train grounded memory use and hazard response. At 4B, PReMind raises joint success from 12.9% to 28.6% over its base on the interdependency set and improves hazard adequacy and correct abstention on the main test. Joint-success gains persist under forced-call evaluation and under a second LLM judge across three Phase II seeds; averaged over these seeds, joint success also improves on unseen hazard groups. These findings highlight the need to evaluate and train personal assistants to connect visual evidence with the relevant person's context.

items.abstract: Looped language models deepen reasoning at a compact parameter count by iterating a shared layer stack T times per token, turning recurrence depth directly into sequential decoding latency. Conventional early-exit decoding halts after initial passes without cache completion, truncating cached key-value states of past tokens to shallow depth. We study the opposite strategy, late entry, where new tokens skip initial passes and enter directly into the final K < T passes over a deep context cache. Once lightweight fine-tuning resolves hidden-state norm mismatch at the entry boundary, deep cached context substitutes for skipped token-local passes, allowing late entry to outperform matched early exit across model families and pass budgets. To turn this asymmetry into wall-clock speedups without stalling to build deep caches, candidate blocks verify through only the final K passes on the critical path while previously committed tokens complete passes 1 -> T alongside subsequent steps at zero extra serial calls. Projecting these finished T-pass wake states inside the existing output GEMM (Wake verification, governed by logit-margin tolerance tau in [0, inf]) unifies greedy-exact T-pass decoding (tau = 0, matching K = T block decoding within bf16 reduction order), margin-gated verification (tau > 0), and non-rollback lossy late entry (tau = inf) inside a single static CUDA graph. On Ouro-2.6B (T = 4), K = 2 Wake reaches 5.2x greedy-exact speedup at tau = 0 (+26% over K = 4 block decoding on GSM8K) and 6.8x at tau = inf (+16.9 points over trained early exit at matched speed). Scaling test-time recurrence across T in {8, 16, 32, 64} on Huginn-3.5B cuts K = T/4 rollbacks 21.5x with depth, driving greedy-exact (tau = 0) speedups to 6.1x (T = 32) and 8.4x (T = 64, +153% over K = 64 block) and tau = inf speedups to 10.6 to 12.5x.

items.summary: Video rough-cut is a core stage in media production workflows, organizing raw media materials into an initial video cut. items.abstract: Video rough-cut is a core stage in media production workflows, organizing raw media materials into an initial video cut. Despite recent advances in large vision-language models (LVLMs) for video-related tasks, automatic rough-cut remains underexplored, without a comprehensive benchmark for evaluation or mature workflows for producing executable cut plans. To address the evaluation gap, we introduce RoughCut-Bench, which covers two practical settings: (1) a visually driven setting over video cases, covering highlight detection and selection, source-video ordering, and adherence to user requirements when provided; and (2) a speech-driven setting over automatic speech recognition (ASR) transcripts, covering filler removal, expression deduplication, and low-value content trimming. Across these settings, the benchmark contains 101 visually driven cases, including 831 raw videos with 1,476 highlight annotations. It also includes 84 speech-driven cases, each consisting of an ASR transcript with annotated cleanup spans. The evaluation compares cut plans with these annotations in both settings and additionally uses a human-aligned agentic evaluator to assess rendered-cut quality in the visual setting. To apply LVLMs to automatic rough-cut, we further propose agentic workflows that guide them to produce structured cut plans from input materials. Experiments show that current LVLMs remain limited in producing expert-aligned cut plans. Our benchmark, code, and prompts are released at https://whalesong-zrs.github.io/RoughCut-Bench-Project-Page.

items.title: DrawScore: Evaluating Generated CAD Models against Engineering Drawings
items.summary: Automatic CAD generation is commonly evaluated with volumetric IoU, Chamfer Distance, and surface F-score, which barely penalize local errors that occupy only a small fraction of a part's volume or surface area, such as a misplaced hole or a slot on the wrong face, even though such errors are critical to manufacturing. items.abstract: Automatic CAD generation is commonly evaluated with volumetric IoU, Chamfer Distance, and surface F-score, which barely penalize local errors that occupy only a small fraction of a part's volume or surface area, such as a misplaced hole or a slot on the wrong face, even though such errors are critical to manufacturing. We formalize these metrics in a unified integral form and show that the weight of a local error decays as the (k+q)-th power of its size, where k is the dimension of the integration domain and q is determined by the penalty function. Guided by this analysis, we propose DrawScore, which projects both models into three orthographic views with visible and hidden lines, as in engineering drawings, and applies a saturating penalty along the projected curves, so that the weight of a local error decays only linearly. Controlled experiments confirm the predicted decay orders, and on outputs of existing CAD generation agents, DrawScore exposes errors in outputs that IoU rates as nearly perfect. DrawScore further improves generation as a reinforcement learning reward and, for CAD generation from engineering drawings, serves as a test-time verifier without 3D ground truth or an additional reward model. Our code is available at https://github.com/UESTC-Simon/DrawScore.

items.title: Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models

items.abstract: Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in a trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for a question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. We present Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), which augments terminal outcome rewards with a training-only auxiliary signal measuring how retrieved documents improve the likelihood of a reference answer. Rather than scoring the full dialogue prefix, ECA queries a frozen snapshot of the current policy under an evidence-only prompt containing solely the question and the deduplicated documents observed so far, isolating the utility of retrieved passages from surface variations in generated thoughts or search queries. Within this framework, we compare two return formulations, ECA-Step (which accumulates step-clipped potential increments) and ECA-Horizon (which preserves the telescoping horizon gain in potential), paired with cross-fold group normalization, novelty gating, and search-local token assignment. Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over an outcome-only GRPO baseline by 1.03 and 4.80 percentage points on Qwen2.5-3B- and 7B-Instruct, respectively, outperforming both RLOO and GiGPO. Zero-shot evaluation on MultiHop-RAG further demonstrates strong transfer to multi-hop inference queries.

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to infer psychological attributes, predict individual behaviour, and simulate human populations. items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to infer psychological attributes, predict individual behaviour, and simulate human populations. However, despite generating plausible responses, they often misrepresent individuals and distort population statistics. Here we introduce Chiron, a foundation model to measure and predict human behaviour. We jointly fine-tune an LLM to represent psychological constructs, predict individual behaviour, and align population response distributions with human statistics. The training and evaluation data span 36 behavioural domains and 78 social science experiments, comprising 288,307 person records, 1,411,750 atomic behavioural decisions, and 99,953 psychometric assessments over 109 psychological constructs. In our evaluations, Chiron's psychological measurements agree more closely with human self-reports and exhibit fewer biases that undermine psychometric validity. It predicts individual behaviour more accurately than frontier LLMs (up to 28.4% relative improvement). In simulations of social science experiments, it more accurately captures the direction and magnitude of human experimental effects (82.2--94.3% lower effect-size estimation error). Together, these results establish Chiron as a unified computational instrument for measuring and predicting human behaviour.

items.abstract: NPU design-space exploration for LLM inference mainly relies on an expensive simulator that often returns only scalar feedback such as latency and power. Such feedback can rank evaluated configurations, but gives little information for deciding why a configuration is slow or which architecture parameter should be changed next. This limitation is especially severe because prefill and decode workloads can be limited by different resources, including compute throughput and HBM bandwidth. We propose CriticNPU, a sample-efficient DSE framework built around an online-calibrated mechanistic critic for NPU architecture design. The critic uses explicit hardware limits to evaluate NPU configurations: before simulation, it estimates whether a proposed configuration is likely to improve over the current best and filters weak candidates; after simulation, it aggregates operator-level runtimes into prefill/decode bottleneck summaries and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. We instantiate the critic with a Roofline-style model that derives compute and memory limits from architecture parameters and calibrates per-operator-type effective limits using simulator observations. And CriticNPU combines this critic with a workload extractor and an architecture planner to propose configurations. Across six LLM workloads and 16 deployment configurations per model, CriticNPU achieves best-or-tied-best latency in 74% of prefill and 87.5% of decode settings while using roughly half the simulator calls of competitive DSE baselines. We conduct extensive ablation studies and detailed analyses to validate the effectiveness of our method from multiple perspectives. Our code is available at https://github.com/bruno686/CriticNPU.

items.abstract: System One models such as Jev return decisions through fast, parallel prediction. In this paper, we introduce Jeveration, showing that the same decision paradigm can also generate high-quality images in a single forward pass. Jeveration builds on a frozen vision-language model, repurposing its visual-semantic knowledge for holistic image generation. The key challenge is to maintain global consistency. A single prompt admits many valid images, yet parallel predictions must converge on a coherent whole. We therefore condition all positions on a shared random state to coordinate parallel predictions, so that each draw yields a different but coherent image. Since the model tends to ignore this state under direct image supervision, we first learn a distribution over discrete image codes to guide single-pass generation. Beyond text-to-image generation, we further unify image-to-image generation and dense prediction within the same architecture, so that one checkpoint supports all three tasks, each in one forward pass. Experiments show that Jeveration generates a 512x512 image in 78 ms, up to 122x faster than existing unified models, while maintaining competitive image quality and dense prediction performance.

items.title: Game2Player: Scaling Gameplay Experience for Visual Agents through Environment-Player Co-Development
items.summary: Games are a rich testbed for visual agents, demanding perception, long-horizon planning, and precise control. However, collecting human gameplay is costly, and learning from gameplay videos requires inferring missing actions. Existing datasets also cover a limited range of games, often without explicit tasks or verifiable outcomes. To address these gaps, we introduce Game2Player, a framework that co-develops game…
items.abstract: Games are a rich testbed for visual agents, demanding perception, long-horizon planning, and precise control. However, collecting human gameplay is costly, and learning from gameplay videos requires inferring missing actions. Existing datasets also cover a limited range of games, often without explicit tasks or verifiable outcomes. To address these gaps, we introduce Game2Player, a framework that co-develops game environments and players to collect diverse and verifiable gameplay experience at scale. In the Game2Player loop, a Builder agent adapts existing web games, exposes their internal state, and defines tasks with state-based progress measures and success checks. A Coding Player and a VLM Player then attempt the tasks and report problems to the Builder for repair, so that play serves as both environment validation and training data collection. With Game2Player, we build 568 verified web games with 3,436 tasks, collect 15.7K trajectories (307 hours of gameplay), and hold out 50 games as the benchmark PlayerBench. To evaluate the collected experience as training data, we train VLM agents with progress-weighted SFT, assigning greater weight to steps that advance task progress. Game2Player-9B improves progress from 14.3% to 31.2% on PlayerBench and from 30.0% to 53.1% on the external GameWorld benchmark. More broadly, our work suggests a path for visual agents to scale their gameplay experience by building, verifying, and learning from existing game worlds.

items.title: Recurrent Domain Incremental Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models
items.summary: Pretrained Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) provide strong representations for downstream classification tasks. Yet adapting a TSFM under changing operating conditions remains challenging. A model must improve on each newly observed condition without sacrificing conditions it has already learned, often from only a small labeled calibration set and without knowing the operating condition at inference time. items.abstract: Pretrained Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) provide strong representations for downstream classification tasks. Yet adapting a TSFM under changing operating conditions remains challenging. A model must improve on each newly observed condition without sacrificing conditions it has already learned, often from only a small labeled calibration set and without knowing the operating condition at inference time. We find that this difficulty has an important geometric structure. Under an operating-condition shift, the embedding space of a TSFM does not move uniformly: some local regions change substantially, while others remain nearly unchanged. Consequently, a global adaptation can unnecessarily move embeddings that were already correctly classified. To address this, we propose the novel PACT (Piecewise Adaptation via Chart Transport). PACT partitions the frozen source embedding space into local charts and learns lightweight residual transports for the regions affected by each new condition. An explicit identity path is always retained, and a learned gate softly selects among the identity and accumulated transports for each input. The pretrained TSFM encoder, classifier head, and previously learned transports remain fixed. With only 5% labeled calibration data per arriving condition and no condition identity at test time, PACT maintains an average macro-F1 above 0.95 across a four-condition bearing-fault stream. Under homogeneous tasks and label spaces, similar retention-adaptation behavior is observed across public benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Sachithx/PACT.

items.title: IDEA: Intent-Dominance Evidence Audit for Inference-Time Backdoor Detection in GUI Agents
items.summary: Organizations increasingly deploy downloaded open-weight GUI agents. A backdoored agent passes acceptance tests on clean data and misbehaves only when a visual trigger appears on screen, turning an unvetted checkpoint into a supply-chain risk. However, existing sample-level detectors target image classifiers and CLIP-style encoders, leaving step-level backdoor detection for GUI agents unaddressed. On clean steps,…
items.abstract: Organizations increasingly deploy downloaded open-weight GUI agents. A backdoored agent passes acceptance tests on clean data and misbehaves only when a visual trigger appears on screen, turning an unvetted checkpoint into a supply-chain risk. However, existing sample-level detectors target image classifiers and CLIP-style encoders, leaving step-level backdoor detection for GUI agents unaddressed. On clean steps, the instruction drives the action; when an unreferenced screen region hijacks the step, the instruction loses control over the decision state or that region dictates it instead. We term this signature intent--evidence dominance inversion and propose IDEA (Intent-Dominance Evidence Audit) to detect backdoor activation at inference time for each step without trigger knowledge or attack data. Specifically, Intent Counterfactual Probing (ICP) measures how far redirected instructions move the decision state, and Region Causal Audit (RCA) quantifies how far ablating a candidate region moves it. A gated conformal score compares both displacements against clean steps at the same distance from the clean manifold, providing a finite-sample false-positive guarantee. Extensive experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B across five attack families show that IDEA consistently detects backdoor activation under a controlled false-positive rate and outperforms state-of-the-art detection methods, while localizing the trigger region for every alarm and adding only modest inference overhead.

items.summary: Abstract Predicting drug-target interactions (DTIs) with deep learning offers opportunities to accelerate drug discovery, yet performance is often constrained by the scarcity of target-specific training data. Transfer learning relieves this limitation but requires choosing a relevant source task, a choice usually made ad hoc. Here we use the Enzyme Commission (EC) classification hierarchy as a systematic criterion…
items.abstract: Abstract Predicting drug-target interactions (DTIs) with deep learning offers opportunities to accelerate drug discovery, yet performance is often constrained by the scarcity of target-specific training data. Transfer learning relieves this limitation but requires choosing a relevant source task, a choice usually made ad hoc. Here we use the Enzyme Commission (EC) classification hierarchy as a systematic criterion for source selection, ascending the EC tree from the target enzyme until a related family carries sufficient ChEMBL bioactivity data to pre-train a deep feedforward network, which is then fine-tuned on the scarce target. We applied this approach to SHMT2 and MTHFD2, two pharmacologically understudied enzymes of the mitochondrial one-carbon (1C) pathway, which is implicated in cancer and fibrosis and supports fibroblast collagen production through glycine synthesis. With 29 active compounds for MTHFD2 and only 6 for SHMT2 which has no ligands of its own, the six coming from its paralogue SHMT1 in the same EC class. EC-guided transfer learning produced usable models in a system where training from scratch failed (Matthews correlation coefficient 0.00 for SHMT2). Virtual screening of the DrugBank library identified six candidates, three of which, carbimazole, crizotinib, and GSK-2018682, reduced TGF-β-induced collagen production and glycine accumulation in human lung fibroblasts. The methodology, datasets, and code are released as a reusable template for enzyme targets with scarce bioactivity coverage.

items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence for science (AI4S) is often discussed as a unified transformation, although scientific domains differ markedly in how model outputs are tested, validated, and justified. We map an audited corpus of N=2,784 records (2014–2025) retrieved from Crossref and screened with a frozen, versioned rulebook, and compare evidence regimes in protein science, materials design, drug discovery, closed-loop experimentation, and mathematical reasoning. Using term co-occurrence, reference co-citation, burst detection, growth models, and collaboration networks, we identify three robust patterns: (i) rapid but decelerating growth (Poisson rate 1.381, 95% CI 1.361–1.402, declining from 1.537 in 2014–2019 to 1.320 in 2019–2025); (ii) a coherent term-co-occurrence structure (75 nodes, modularity Q=0.404 ) organized around four measured streams—representation learning, generative and inverse design, closed-loop experimentation, and neuro-symbolic reasoning—with the generative stream acting as the connecting hub; and (iii) a right-boundary rise in large language model terminology (burst state 3) that a year-by-year backtest shows is not a last-observation artefact. The maps are sensitive to metadata availability: abstract coverage is 50.6%, reference coverage 84.3%, and a title-only variant changes the network partition substantially (adjusted Rand index 0.762), so the maps describe the screened open-metadata corpus rather than the total AI4S literature. Cross-domain analysis shows that AI most consequentially shifts scientific bottlenecks from representation and candidate generation toward experimental or formal validation, provenance, and responsibility for claims. We contribute an auditable, open-metadata science-mapping workflow designed for reproducibility and an evidence-regime framework for analysing how epistemic labour is redistributed across models, instruments, formal verifiers, infrastructures, and human experts.

items.abstract: Introduction The root vole (Microtus oeconomus), a small mammal native to the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, is adapted to chronic high-altitude hypoxia and exhibits a polygynous mating system. whereas the prairie vole (Microtus ochrogaster) from North American grasslands is a model of social monogamy. Oxytocin (OXT) and its receptor (OXTR) play central to prosocial behaviors including pair bonding, yet their sequences and evolutionary implications in the root vole remain unclear. Methods we retrieved cytochrome b, OXT, and OXTR sequences from 21 species via GenBank. Coding and regulatory regions of the OXT and OXTR in the root vole were cloned by PCR, nucleotide and amino acid sequences were aligned using DNAMAN 6 and Multalin tool. Phylogenetic trees were constructed in MEGA X using the neighbor-joining (NJ) method. The three-dimensional (3D) structures of the OXT-OXTR complexes for mouse, M. oeconomus, and M. ochrogaster were predicted with AlphaFold 3. and Hydrogen bonds were analyzed in ChimeraX (1.11.1). Results We cloned the OXT and OXTR coding and regulatory regions from hypothalamus of M. oeconomus. Phylogenetic trees placed M. oeconomus, M. ochrogaster, and Mus musculus in a single major clade, with the two-vole species sharing the same branch. Species-specific sequence variations between the two voles were identified. Predicted 3D structures revealed differences in ligand-receptor binding interfaces and in hydrogen-bond networks across species. Notably, the M. ochrogaster complex contained the greatest number of hydrogen bonds, suggesting a tighter ligand-receptor interaction. Conclusion We propose that variation in the OXT-OXTR hydrogen-bond network, the ligand-binding pocket (TM4), and the intracellular loops IC1 and IC3 may be related to underlie species differences in ligand-receptor binding affinity and, consequently, in pair-bonding behavior.

items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for de novo small-molecule design, but the practical and translational utility of generated candidates depends on the configuration of the entire discovery workflow rather than on generative model architecture alone. This review adopts a workflow-based perspective on generative molecular design, tracing the process from existing molecular data sets, preprocessing and representation, to molecule generation, conditioning, candidate prioritization, evaluation, and iterative refinement. It examines how generative AI model families, constraints, and predictive oracles interact within this pipeline, and evaluates generated candidates using intrinsic metrics, computational assessments, and experimental and translational evidence. Active learning, computational and experimental feedback, and human expert input are further discussed as mechanisms for closed-loop refinement. Across these stages, we identify data construction and representation choices, oracle quality, evaluation protocols, and the availability of informative feedback as major determinants of how model performance should be interpreted and whether generated structures progress toward biologically and translationally meaningful candidates, with selected examples. In conclusion, reliable generative drug discovery requires coordinated design across the entire workflow rather than isolated advances in individual components.

items.abstract: Background Stanford type A aortic dissection (AAD) is a life-threatening vascular emergency characterized by high mortality and a lack of targeted pharmacological interventions. Cuproptosis, a recently defined copper-dependent regulated cell death modality, has been implicated in various cardiovascular pathologies, yet its specific molecular role in the development of AAD remains largely unexplored. Methods We performed an integrated bioinformatics analysis using three independent GEO datasets (GSE107844, GSE147026, and GSE190635) to identify cuproptosis-related differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in AAD tissues. A panel of diagnostic biomarkers was selected using three machine learning algorithms: Random Forest, Support Vector Machine-Recursive Feature Elimination (SVM-RFE), and Boruta. The expression of identified hub genes was validated in clinical patient samples and a BAPN/Ang II-induced AAD mouse model via qRT-PCR and histological staining. Potential therapeutic agents were identified through the Drug-Gene Interaction Database (DGIdb) and validated using molecular docking. Results A total of 31 cuproptosis-related DEGs were identified. Six key genes were identified via PPI and machine learning algorithms. The differential expression patterns of these genes were validated by qRT-PCR in both AAD mouse model and clinical tissues. Subsequently, clinical correlation analysis revealed that MT1G and NLRP3 expression correlated significantly with inflammatory (white blood cell count, IL-6) and coagulation markers (D-dimer). The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for MT1G and NLRP3 was comparable to that of D-dimer, indicating their potential value as biomarkers. Via screening using the DGIdb and validation by molecular docking, compounds such as Buthionine sulfoximine (targeting MT1G), dapansutrile (targeting NLRP3), and ARP100 (targeting DBT) demonstrated favorable binding affinity to their targets. Conclusion Our findings suggest that cuproptosis-related genes may play a role in AAD pathogenesis and provide candidate biomarkers and therapeutic leads for further investigation.

items.abstract: Purpose: To develop a data-efficient, clinically guided transfer-learning framework for hyperacute neurological outcome prediction from head CT in patients undergoing extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) after cardiac arrest by leveraging free-text radiology report. Methods: . This retrospective study included 683 patients with available CT examination and radiology reports from December 2015 to November 2025. The primary outcome distinguished favorable neurological outcomes (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 1-2) from neurological death due to brain death or cerebral herniation (CPC 5). A cross-attention adaptor jointly learned to predict neurological outcome and five report-derived manifestations of brain injury from a frozen pretrained head CT encoder. Outcome prediction used CT images alone at inference. The manifestation-guided adaptor, trained with and without additional patients who contributed only manifestation labels, was compared with outcome-only adaptor and two pooled-feature baselines. Performance was summarized as mean ± SD across five held-out folds. Results: . Of 683 patients, 197 were eligible for outcome evaluation (63 with favorable outcomes and 134 with neurological death), and 486 formed the manifestation-only cohort. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.918 ± 0.044 for the outcome-only adaptor. The manifestation-guided adaptor achieved an AUROC of 0.927 ± 0.042. With additional manifestation-only training data, the adaptor achieved the mean AUROC (0.929 ± 0.037), specificity (93.7% ± 6.5%), with a sensitivity of 79.9% ± 9.2%. Conclusion: Manifestation-guided adaptation outperforms outcome-only adaptation for neurological outcome prediction from hyperacute head CT after ECPR. Report-derived manifestation labels enabled training with additional examinations without eligible outcome labels while preserving CT-only prediction.

items.abstract: Background: MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) provides minimally invasive option for surgical treatment of recurrent brain tumors. While patient-specific prediction of thermal dose distributions would improve treatment planning, no quantitative methods currently exist for this purpose. Although conventional numerical solvers are being widely investigated, these methods are computationally expensive and often limited by accuracy and reliability. Purpose: Here we propose DeepoLITT, a rapid and accurate model to predict quantitatively heat propagation in LITT procedures. This study represents the first phase of the investigation which focuses on training and validating synthetic datasets to test model , s accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency. Methods: We built DeepoLITT on a branch–trunk neural network architecture, where the first branch extracts feature from tumor images, the second branch encodes laser parameters (power, duration, and probe orientation), and the trunk models the mapping from spatial coordinates to the resulting temperature field. To train and test the model, we generated synthetic datasets with different noise levels (0~20%) to mimic LITT procedures with two distinct laser probe types (FullFire and SideFire [Monteris, Inc.]) by a FEM (finite element method) solver. The dataset consisted of 400 samples, of which 90% were used for training and validation and 10% for testing. To evaluate spatial similarity of predicted thermal dose distribution against the ground truth, we employed Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and Hausdorff Distance (HD) computed on CEM43 (Cumulative Equivalent Minutes at 43 °C) isodose contours at thresholds of 2, 10, and 60 minutes. Finally, we evaluated the model , s inference speed with a representative image grid. Results: For the FullFire laser probe, the DeepoLITT model achieved temperature prediction error with average values ranging from 1.16±0.40% to 2.92±0.25%, and peak values ranging from 4.26±1.31% to 14.94±0.43% as data noise increased from 0% to 20%. For the SideFire laser probe, the model achieved temperature prediction error with average values ranging from 3.79±0.53% to 5.13±1.00% and peak values ranging from 15.18±7.15% to 20.75±2.84%. For thermal dose assessment, at the noise-free level for the FullFire laser probe, the model exhibited strong spatial agreement with FEM references, yielding DSCs of 0.96±0.02, 0.97±0.21, and 0.96±0.21 with corresponding HDs of 0.09±0.08 mm, 0.07±0.07 mm, and 0.06±0.08 mm at 2–, 10–, and 60–minute CEM43 thresholds. For the SideFire laser probe, the model achieved DSCs of 0.96±0.02, 0.97±0.21, and 0.96±0.21, with corresponding HDs of 0.20±0.31mm, 0.11±0.30 mm, and 0.15±0.31 mm, respectively. As the noise level increases, these DSC values show a decreasing trend, and the HD values increase. In terms of computational efficiency, the DeepoLITT model inferences temperature maps with 0.04±0.05 seconds per 3D sample ([31 × 31 × 3] grid), compared to 24.32±2.12 seconds required by the FEM solver. Conclusions: The study with synthetic data demonstrates the proposed model is an accurate and rapid method in predicting thermal dose. After testing clinical data, the method has high feasibility to be deployed in real clinical environment.

items.abstract: Cognitive reserve concerns why the same aging causes less decline in some individuals than others, a question that digital twin brains can address by aging each individual in silico. Here we present Brain-VRNN, a connectome-constrained variational recurrent neural network trained on longitudinal multitask functional MRI. Its regenerated brain signals reproduced four functional aging markers of unseen individuals (r = 0.93–0.96) and identified each person (accuracy 0.98). Without cognitive scores, its global latent learned a trait dimension stable within each person, which helped predict future cognition. Crucially, when every individual underwent the same counterfactual aging, those with a lower trait value declined more, yet recovered up to 1.6 times as much with a reduction in body mass index, a modifiable dementia risk factor. Aging single regions showed that different markers decline through different regions, with a lateral temporal–angular region shared by all. Brain-VRNN brings within-person simulation to cognitive reserve.

items.abstract: Abstract Pseudoprogression, transient radiographic worsening caused by treatment-related inflammation rather than tumor growth, is a well-recognized pitfall after chemoradiotherapy for glioblastoma and is becoming more relevant as checkpoint inhibitors and cellular immunotherapies such as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells enter clinical testing. Conventional structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) cannot reliably separate pseudoprogression from true progression, exposing patients to premature treatment discontinuation or unnecessary intensification. Quantitative, artificial-intelligence-based imaging analysis (radiomics, and its molecular extension radiogenomics) is an emerging candidate solution. In this narrative review we synthesize the evidence on radiomics and radiogenomics for differentiating pseudoprogression from true progression in glioblastoma, with emphasis on the immunotherapy and cellular-therapy context. We summarize the pathobiology and reported frequency of pseudoprogression after standard and immune-based therapies, outline the limitations of current response criteria (RANO, iRANO, RANO 2.0), and review representative studies of texture analysis, hand-crafted radiomics, deep-learning radiomics, and radiogenomics. Although several studies report promising discrimination (reported area-under-the-curve values of approximately 0.88-0.92 in different cohorts), the evidence is limited by small sample sizes, retrospective designs, inconsistent definitions and protocols, and infrequent external validation. Progress will require prospective multicenter cohorts with standardized acquisition and segmentation, adherence to TRIPOD and CLAIM reporting standards, transparent and interpretable models, and integration with clinical, molecular, and liquid-biopsy data. A dedicated evidence base specific to cellular immunotherapy is urgently needed.

items.abstract: Abstract Ring artifacts, caused by detector pixels whose gain or offset is slightly wrong, appear in reconstructed computed tomography (CT) slices as concentric circles around the rotation centre. They can hide small features and break threshold-based segmentation. Classical ring removal relies on hand-tuned filters, and real scans have no ground truth for measuring how well a method works. This project builds a synthetic CT pipeline (phantom, parallel-beam projection, Poisson noise, detector gain and offset error, filtered back-projection) in which the true ring is known for every image, and trains a two-head U-Net that predicts the ring image, which is subtracted from the input, and a ring mask. On 1000 training, 100 validation and 100 test slices of 256 × 256 pixels, where the test slices come from a phantom family never seen in training, the U-Net raises the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) from 33.11 dB to 39.54 dB and the structural similarity (SSIM) from 0.868 to 0.957. A radial-profile classical baseline tuned on the validation set gains 0.77 dB on validation but loses 0.56 dB on the unseen family. The U-Net gain depends on ring type, from +13.9 dB for dead_hot rings to +0.4 dB for faint band rings. Training with 100, 500 and 1000 images gives 35.29, 38.42 and 39.54 dB; three random seeds give 39.40 ± 0.15 dB; removing the Dice term from the loss raises PSNR to 39.89 dB but lowers mask Dice from 0.640 to 0.605. The mask head is the weaker output (Dice 0.640 overall, 0.07 on band rings). Because all data are simulated, the sim-to-real gap remains the main open question.
