items.abstract: Abstract Advances in whole-brain ex vivo imaging enable large-scale, cellular-resolution mapping of macaque brain architecture and connectivity. However, the seamless integration of multimodal datasets at scale remains challenging due to substantial tissue deformation, cross-modal contrast discrepancies, and individual morphological variability. Here, we present Macaca-Star, a high-throughput, fully automated framework for cross-modal whole-brain mapping in macaques. Macaca-Star synergizes modality-specific preprocessing, deep learning–based cross-modal translation, and optional subject-specific in vivo MRI guidance to achieve robust spatial and modal alignment. This end-to-end system reconciles these disparities, eliminates manual intervention and reduces the processing time from weeks to hours while maintaining high anatomical fidelity. It effectively maps both 3D volumetric and 2D section-based optical data into a unified anatomical space, enabling precise spatial integration of cytoarchitectural features, axonal projections, and neuronal somata. To demonstrate its discovery potential, we applied Macaca-Star to integrate fMOST-derived anterograde tracing with section-based retrograde tracing data. This integration resolved subregional connectivity patterns within the temporoparietal and insular areas that were previously difficult to unify across disparate imaging scales. Overall, Macaca-Star offers a versatile platform for multimodal data fusion, advancing comprehensive connectivity and atlas-based analysis in the primate brain.

items.abstract: The use of computed tomography (CT scans) images is increasing in forensic anthropology to address ethical, logistical, and preservation challenges related to physical cadaveric collections. However, preparing large volumes of medical images for artificial intelligence (AI) applications remains challenging, particularly in terms of standardisation and data privacy. The aim of this study is to develop an automated preprocessing workflow for CT images to support machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) applications in forensic anthropology research and education. Methodology A Python-based pipeline was designed in three stages: data de-identification and sorting, patient table removal, and bone windowing. A script was developed for de-identification, and a custom U-Net architecture was developed for both patient table removal and bone windowing. The workflow was developed and applied to CT thorax. Model performance was evaluated using standard metrics and compared with ground-truth models. Results DICOM metadata de-identification was performed as part of preprocessing; all predefined identifying attributes were successfully processed in the 200 DICOM files examined. The patient table removal model removed the table successfully in 96% of datasets (192/200) and achieved 99.94% accuracy on the original, non-augmented test images. The bone segmentation model achieved a Dice score of 93.12% and a precision of approximately 90%. The segmented 3D models showed high agreement with the ground-truth model, with minimal geometric deviation. Conclusions We have proposed an integrated workflow that provides an ethical, efficient and standardised solution for de-identifying and preprocessing CT imaging data. It also enables the preprocessing of a scalable dataset for AI applications, thereby supporting the development of methodologies for the modern population, with future expansion to full-body scans and other imaging modalities.

items.abstract: Purpose of review Image-guided and augmented-reality (AR)-assisted robotic surgery is moving from static preoperative visualization toward dynamic, automated navigation. This review summarizes evidence from the past 12-18 months on three-dimensional (3D) virtual models, AR, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted registration in robotic urology, focusing on which applications have moved to comparative and randomized evidence, and on how far this rationale now generalizes beyond the centers that first described it. Recent findings In radical prostatectomy, a randomized trial of AI-driven 3D-AR guidance vs. cognitive MRI guidance showed lower overall positive margins, less postoperative radiotherapy, and better 12-month continence. In partial nephrectomy, 3D models have progressed from anatomical planning to perfusion-mapped clamping and automated AI-based registration, with favorable outcomes across comparative, meta-analytic, and propensity-matched series, including in horseshoe kidneys and totally endophytic tumors. Independent European groups have reported automated registration, segmentation, and nephrometry tools, and small series have extended image guidance to kidney transplantation, vena cava thrombectomy, upper tract urothelial carcinoma, and testicular cancer surgery. Summary Randomized evidence in prostatectomy, a maturing pathway in partial nephrectomy, and growing independent replication support an expanding but still procedure-limited role for image-guided robotic surgery. Standardized protocols, objective accuracy metrics, multicenter validation, and structured training remain necessary before wider adoption.

items.abstract: Purpose of review In this review, we outline the role coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) plays in the diagnosis of coronary artery disease (CAD) and in facilitating risk assessment. Plaque quantification and phenotyping using CCTA is a promising approach in guiding cardiovascular preventive management. Recent findings There is growing interest in how artificial intelligence-based quantitative plaque analysis using CCTA (AI-CPA) can guide preventive therapy. The review summarizes studies that show prognostic utility of CCTA-derived plaque quantification and phenotyping as well as outlines more recent studies that show the impact of AI-CPA in patient management decisions, allowing a more individualized approach to preventive strategies. Summary CCTA provides a comprehensive assessment extending beyond coronary luminal stenosis to include plaque quantification, plaque phenotyping, functional assessment of stenotic lesions and vascular inflammation, further refining traditional approaches of risk prediction.In summary, the growing evidence highlights the importance of incorporating CCTA-based plaque volume and plaque phenotype analysis in better informing physicians about individual's risk and in guiding preventive management.

items.summary: The microscopic structure of human tissues encodes molecular information that is not directly accessible by visual inspection. items.abstract: The microscopic structure of human tissues encodes molecular information that is not directly accessible by visual inspection. Current pathology foundation models improve histological interpretation but operate at multicellular resolution. It remains unclear whether routine histology contains structured molecular and cellular information recoverable at single-cell resolution, which biological properties are associated with this recoverability, and where its limits lie. Here, we introduce Loki2, a single-cell pathology foundation model trained on UniSeg, a pan-tissue resource integrating 15 million cells with segmentation, lineage annotations and measured or histology-inferred transcriptomic profiles. We examine the above question across cellular representation, molecular recoverability, and patient-level relevance. Loki2 captures cellular identity and continuous morphological variation, with interpretable latent dimensions linked to physical nuclear phenotypes through DAPI validation. Transcriptomic retrieval and in silico protein staining test molecular recoverability, with gene-level analyses revealing the strongest recovery for genes associated with morphologically distinct cellular identities and functions. Then, patient staging and biomarker discovery connect cellular morphology representations to clinical relevance. Together, these findings establish Loki2 as a biologically interpretable single-cell pathology foundation model and provide the opportunities of recovering cellular and molecular information from routine H&E histology at single-cell resolution.

items.abstract: De novo peptide sequencing reads peptides directly from tandem mass spectra, but none of the released deep learning models can sequence peptides labeled with isobaric tags such as TMTpro, which are widely used for multiplexed quantitative proteomics. We extended the residue vocabulary of Casanovo with TMTpro tags and phosphorylation, fine-tuned it on 21 million spectra from our laboratory, most of them TMTpro-labeled, and re-ranked the candidates in the beam by their agreement with the measured precursor mass. The resulting model, Casanovo-TMT, predicted the exact peptidoform for 84.7% of the TMTpro-labeled spectra in our test set and for 87.4 and 79.6% of the spectra in two public global-proteome datasets from other laboratories, whereas the extended vocabulary without fine-tuning gave 0.3%. Discarding the lowest-scoring predictions raised precision to 95% while retaining 81.7% of the test spectra. Casanovo-TMT also predicted the exact peptidoform for 69.2% of the spectra in a public phosphopeptide-enriched dataset and for 66 to 72% of the phosphopeptide spectra in three phosphoproteomic studies from our laboratory that were not used for training. In these studies, it identified numbers of phosphopeptides comparable to or larger than those of database search engines, and proportionally more where database search identified fewer. For the phosphopeptides identified only by Casanovo-TMT, entrapment estimated that more than 90% were correct, and an independent search engine assigned the same sequence to 95 to 98% of the spectra that it identified with confidence. Casanovo-TMT can therefore extend database search in TMTpro-based quantitative proteomics, particularly in studies in which database search identifies few phosphopeptides.

items.abstract: Missense variants in the KCNQ family of voltage-gated potassium channel genes are associated with a broad spectrum of neurological and cardiac disorders for which computational tools capable of differentiating benign and pathogenic variants are essential. Here, we present, to our knowledge, the first application of quantum machine learning (QML) to missense pathogenicity prediction. We employ a hybrid quantum framework combining data re-uploading quantum neural networks with quantum support vector machines and applied it to pathogenicity classification across the full KCNQ gene family. Systematic exploration of circuit architectures revealed that optimal hyperparameter choices enable the proposed quantum model to achieve predictive performance superior to or comparable to state-of-the-art classical machine learning approaches, reaching AUC-ROC values of approximately 0.94 across the full dataset. Although no clear quantum advantage is observed at present, these results demonstrate that quantum feature representations can effectively capture biologically relevant patterns in variant data and establish QML as a viable framework for future applications in computational genomics and precision medicine.

items.abstract: Background Advances in proteomics assays enable measurement of thousands of plasma proteins, which could facilitate machine learning-based approaches to enhance risk prediction of disease. Methods We measured plasma levels of >9500 proteins among 4000 Chinese adults (1937 myocardial infarction [MI] cases and 2026 subcohort), using both Olink Explore (2923 proteins) and SomaScan (6597 proteins) platforms. Protein-based risk prediction models were constructed, using conventional and machine learning approaches, with model performance assessed via discrimination (C-statistic), classification (net reclassification index; NRI) and calibration. Protein scores were compared and combined with conventional risk factors and polygenic scores (PGS), and externally validated in 37,187 Europeans (630 MI cases) in UK Biobank. Findings Overall, 451 Olink and 530 SomaScan proteins were significantly associated (5% false discovery rate) with MI risk after adjustment for conventional risk factors. The protein prediction models based on Olink, SomaScan, or both platforms combined, outperformed conventional risk factors and PGS using discrimination, classification and calibration. The protein score using 23 Boruta-selected (Olink/SomaScan: 11/12) proteins yielded a 3.3-fold difference in 10-year cumulative incidence of MI between the top and bottom 20% risk groups (3.6 [95%CI: 3.1-4.1] vs 1.1 [0.9-1.2] per 100), compared with 2.5-fold (2.5 [2.2-2.9] vs 1.0 [0.9-1.2]) and 1.5-fold (1.9 [1.6-2.1] vs 1.3 [1.1-1.4]) differences for conventional and PGS, respectively. Adding this protein score to conventional risk factors increased C-statistics from 0.846 (0.829-0.862) to 0.864 (0.849-0.879), yielding an NRI of 72%. External validation in 37,187 participants in UK Biobank by adding 23 Boruta-selected proteins to conventional risk factors yielded comparable improvement in C-statistics for MI (from 0.710 [0.688-0.731] to 0.733 [0.710-0.756]) and 45% improvement in NRI (NRI 45%). Conclusions Machine learning identified subsets of proteins for improved MI risk prediction beyond conventional risk factors and PGS, showing the potential for developing small panel proteomics assays to improve disease risk prediction.

items.abstract: The National Genomics Data Center (NGDC), as part of the China National Center for Bioinformation (CNCB), provides a family of database resources and web services to both academic and industrial communities worldwide. Given the rapid growth of multi-omics data and the intrinsic dependence of artificial intelligence on high-quality curated data, CNCB-NGDC continues to enhance data integrity, usability, and accessibility, facilitate knowledge discovery, and support data-driven research. Over the past year, CNCB-NGDC has expanded and updated its core database resources and strengthened data exchange and sharing with international collaborators. Thirteen new resources have been released, covering genome and variation (HLA and NMVR), health and disease (PWAS Atlas, CoVAR-KG, HONOR, IBDkb, and MTB-ImmunogenKG), biodiversity and biosynthesis (iCellOmics, iPangolin, SesbaniaOmics, and Vita Taxonomy), and tools (π-OmicsKit and DeepSeMS). All resources and services are publicly accessible at https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn.

items.abstract: Inborn errors of immunity (IEIs), such as Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD), impose a disproportionately severe clinical burden in populations with high rates of consanguinity. CGD is caused by defects in the phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex, frequently due to mutations in the NCF1 gene encoding the p47phox protein. While the functional domains of NCF1 are well characterized, the quantitative architectural constraints governing its structural stability remain elusive. This study aimed to decipher the multidimensional quantitative signatures of NCF1, across diverse organisms in order to understand its conserved spatial sequence architecture and the structural basis of variant severity. We analyzed 41 NCF1 sequences using ten distinct quantitative features, integrating primary sequence metrics, biophysical chemistry, and abstract topological geometry. The synthesis of these features revealed a lack of a unified proximity matrix, demonstrating that NCF1 is defined by feature-dependent, multidimensional individual signatures. Primary sequence metrics exhibited rigid phylogenetic conservation, revealing invariant zero-entropy blocks that correlated strictly with severe CGD-causing mutations, while topological metrics exposed a deep spatial architectural convergence. These multidimensional baselines confirmed that the protein requires a highly specific spatial packing to assemble the NADPH oxidase complex; pathogenic mutations therefore disrupt precise structural signatures rather than globally destroying the protein. Consistent with this, the AlphaFold model places the folded PX and tandem SH3 domains in a high-confidence core and the regulatory C-terminal tail in an exposed, low-confidence region, supporting a tail-mediated autoinhibitory mechanism. Ultimately, this quantitative framework offers a useful perspective on NCF1 architecture and may serve as a supportive tool for evaluating the severity of clinical variants, contributing to precision medicine efforts for NCF1-associated diseases.

items.abstract: Abstract Automated white blood cell (WBC) classification in peripheral blood smears supports morphological assessment of hematological disorders, but most deep learning classifiers treat cell categories as independent labels and do not account for hematopoietic maturation. We propose a hyperbolic classification framework that combines a ResNet-18 feature extractor with a prototype-based classifier in the Poincaré ball, allowing biologically related cell states to be represented in a geometry suited to hierarchical structure. The model was evaluated on a curated dataset of 129,174 annotated single-cell images mapped to 14 blood cell classes, including leukocyte subtypes, hematopoietic precursor states, and multiple stages of granulocytic maturation. To reduce acquisition-level information leakage, we used a grouped evaluation protocol that keeps linked multi-focus acquisitions within the same subset. Across the six top-ranked grouped-split configurations, the hyperbolic model improved macro-averaged F1-score from 0.812 ± 0.005 to 0.819 ± 0.004 relative to the Euclidean baseline, while overall accuracy remained slightly lower (0.826 ± 0.002 vs 0.830 ± 0.006). Recall gains were most pronounced for promyelocytes, immature WBCs, and metamyelocytes. These results suggest that hyperbolic representation learning can improve class-balanced classification of WBCs and related hematopoietic cell states while maintaining competitive overall accuracy.

items.abstract: Syphilis is a multistage sexually transmitted infection caused by the highly invasive and immunoevasive spirochete Treponema pallidum (TPA). TPA depends on the import of many host-derived nutrients to sustain its auxotrophic lifestyle. Moreover, its invasive nature requires interactions with diverse host molecules to successfully disseminate and persist. The outer membrane proteins (OMPs) mediating these processes remain largely uncharacterized. In other bacteria, 8-stranded β-barrels (8SβBs) perform such functions, including nutrient uptake and host interactions. Here, we investigated the composition, structural diversity and evolutionary dynamics of the 8SβB family in TPA. Reexamination of the TPA OMPeome revealed four previously unrecognized members in addition to the four known 8SBs, expanding the family to eight members. Based on RNAseq, all eight were transcribed in treponemes harvested from rabbit testes. Predicted structures revealed substantial differences in channel properties and extracellular loop (ECL) architecture, consistent with functional diversification. AlphaFold 3 modeling predicted interactions with diverse host molecules implicated in nutrient uptake, adherence, and immune regulation, providing testable hypotheses for the functional specialization of individual 8SBBBs. Despite containing predicted B-cell epitopes, most TPA 8SβB ECLs exhibited limited antigenicity during rabbit infection. Analysis of global clinical strains revealed distinct patterns of sequence variation across the 8SβB family, although most were highly conserved and appeared to be under purifying selection. Variation within hypermutable intragenic polyguanosine tracts emerged as an additional potential mechanism for modulating 8SβB repertoire composition. Our findings highlight the 8SβB family as an important component of the molecular architecture underlying TPA stealth pathogenicity and reveal an ongoing mechanism through which the spirochete diversifies its OMP repertoire within circulating populations.

items.abstract: Background: Apolipoprotein A1 (ApoA1), the main protein component of high-density lipoprotein, suppresses chemokine-driven leukocyte migration. This effect is usually attributed to indirect mechanisms such as cholesterol efflux, changes in lipid rafts, and altered receptor expression. Whether ApoA1 interacts with chemokine receptors directly is not known. Methods: We combined in silico rigid-body docking of AlphaFold-predicted structures (GRAMM-X, with interface analysis by PDBePISA) and surface plasmon resonance (SPR). In SPR experiments, ApoA1 was immobilized on the sensor, and CCR1, CCR5, CX3CR1, CXCR2, and CXCR4 were incorporated into proteoliposomes and injected as analytes. Mock proteoliposomes lacking any receptor served as a negative control. Kinetics were fitted with a 1:1 Langmuir model. Results: Docking predicted favorable interfaces between ApoA1 and all five receptors. CCR1 had the most favorable docking interaction, and CCR5 had the largest predicted interface (3716.7 A;iG -62.8 kcal/mol). Mock proteoliposomes showed no detectable binding to ApoA1, whereas all five receptors bound to ApoA1 in the SPR experiments. The apparent equilibrium dissociation constants (KD) were 3.44x10^-8 M for CXCR4, 3.96x10^-8 M for CXCR2, 5.26x10^-8 M for CCR5, 4.35x10^-7 M for CCR1, and 1.23x10^-6 M for CX3CR1. Conclusions: ApoA1 appears to bind chemokine receptors directly, with the highest apparent affinities for CXCR4, CXCR2, and CCR5. These findings suggest a candidate mechanism, complementary to cholesterol efflux and receptor expression regulation, by which ApoA1 may influence chemokine signaling. However, whether binding alters receptor signaling, internalization, or cell migration remains to be determined.

items.abstract: Protein design campaigns are often run as multi-stage pipelines with a generative backbone model, an inverse-folding model, and a structure predictor chained together in that order. The stages differ by one to two orders of magnitude in cost per candidate, and the allocation of sampling effort across them is fixed before a campaign begins. Such a filter cascade can only discard candidates. It cannot redirect sampling toward the regions of design space a model stack can reach, and for targets whose constraints are far from the generative model's training distribution it may return no solution at any practical sample count. We present IMPRESS (Integrated Machine-learning for PRotein Structures at Scale), a framework in which design pipelines are stateful objects that halt, continue, resample, or branch at runtime from their own accumulated results. Adaptive decisions are evaluated asynchronously with respect to execution, so a campaign refines itself without global synchronization. We apply IMPRESS to three problems: backbone generation on discontinuous enzyme active-site motifs, de novo small molecule binder design, and PDZ binder redesign. Adaptive parameterization solves active-site motifs carried on three or more discontinuous residue islands that a fixed cascade does not solve, shifts the realized task mix toward inexpensive sequence exploration, and produces sequence ensembles that explore broadly but stay near their inputs. All comparisons reported here are between in silico metrics. We expect that adaptive parameterization will matter most for targets furthest from the training distributions of the underlying models, and that the same primitives will accommodate experimental measurement as a steering signal.

items.abstract: Rationale: Point of care lung ultrasound is portable and radiation free and could extend tuberculosis screening to settings without chest radiography, but no standardized criteria exist for interpreting it for tuberculosis. Objectives: To develop and internally evaluate deep learning models that classify pulmonary tuberculosis from lung ultrasound images, alone and combined with routine clinical variables, and to derive an abbreviated scanning protocol. Methods: In a prospective study in Kampala, Uganda (2023 to 2025), we enrolled people aged 13 years or older with microbiologically confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis, their household contacts, and symptomatic people with other respiratory conditions. One still frame from each of 12 lung ultrasound zones was analyzed with an attention-based multiple-instance learning network. We compared clinical-only (random forest), ultrasound only, and combined models and derived a 6 zone protocol from training set attention weights. Participants were allocated to training (n = 223), validation (n = 20), and held-out test (n = 73) sets. Results: Of 318 enrolled participants, 316 were analyzed (118 with and 198 without tuberculosis). In the test set, areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve were 0.88 (95% confidence interval, 0.80 to 0.95) for the clinical-only model; 0.93 (0.86 to 0.97) and 0.95 (0.89 to 0.99) for the 12 zone ultrasound-only and combined models; and 0.91 (0.83 to 0.97) and 0.93 (0.86 to 0.99) for the corresponding 6-zone models. At 90% sensitivity, specificity was 82.2% (34.9 to 97.8) for the 12-zone combined model and 91.1% (25.0 to 98.0) for the 6-zone combined model. Point estimates for all 12-zone models and the 6-zone combined model met the 2025 World Health Organization minimum accuracy targets for a high-sensitivity screening test (≥90% sensitivity, ≥60% specificity). Conclusion: Lung ultrasound analyzed with attention-based deep learning and combined with clinical variables showed high internal discrimination for pulmonary tuberculosis, and a simplified 6-zone protocol retained most of this performance. External validation in intended-use screening populations is needed

items.abstract: Objective: Biopsies are examined under the microscope by a pathologist, giving a diagnosis, which guides treatment and predicts prognosis. A shortage of pathologists and increasing workload leads to diagnostic delays, while for duodenal (small intestinal) biopsies, variable diagnostic concordance between pathologists limits accuracy. These challenges have motivated us to develop an artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated approach for the automated diagnosis of up to 80% of duodenal biopsies (i.e., most cases of the two most frequent diagnoses: coeliac disease and normal). We set out to understand patient, carer and stakeholder views regarding the adoption of such technology. Methods and Analysis: We conducted mixed-methods stakeholder engagement (February 2024 to June 2026). We ran a national online patients and carers questionnaire (n=231 respondents) and four UK focus-group workshops, one of which additionally captured Likert-scale attitudes1 immediately before and after a structured educational session (n=34 matched pairs). Healthcare professionals completed an online questionnaire (n=37) and took part in a structured workshop. Quantitative data were summarised descriptively; free-text and workshop data were analysed thematically and triangulated across all sources. Results: Most patients and carers supported AI-reliant diagnosis (68.4%) and would strongly trust systems with formal regulatory approval (66.7%). Most wanted to be informed if AI was used (73.6%), but only 52.4% felt explicit permission was necessary. Qualitative themes centred on clear and available evidence of accuracy, human oversight, transparent communication and clear terminology, with the term machine learning being preferred to artificial intelligence. Agreement (agree or strongly agree combined) with statements relating to trust, acceptance and perceived benefit of AI was significantly higher after a structured educational session (38.2% to 67.6%, 85.3% to 97.1%, and 52.9% to 97.1% respectively; all p<0.003). Healthcare professionals favoured an AI assistant model over full automation, citing the need for validation, explainability, data governance and workflow integration. Patients also preferred some level of human oversight. Conclusion: Patients and healthcare professionals are cautiously supportive of AI-assisted diagnosis of duodenal biopsies, conditional upon demonstration of accuracy, appropriate human oversight and transparent communication. Attitudes towards AI-assisted diagnosis were more favourable after structured explanation.

items.abstract: Abstract Background Cobb angle and vertebral slip measurements are clinically vali-dated techniques that are time-intensive and prone to inter-observer variation. Objective To develop a comprehensive deep learning approach for auto-mated measurements and grading of scoliosis and spondylolisthesis cases using a single-center hospital radiograph dataset. Methods In this retrospective study, 2,500 anonymized spinal radiographs from one participating hospital were used, including 1,635 scoliosis and 865 spondy-lolisthesis radiographs. Researchers had access only to radiographs without any patient identifiers, demographic information, and clinical data. Radiographs were preprocessed by applying Gaussian denoising, CLAHE contrast adjust-ment, intensity standardization, and scaling to 224 x 224 pixels. Vertebral landmark-based vertebral angles were computed for scoliosis analysis, and verte-bral body localization-based slip percentages were calculated for spondylolisthesis detection. Two networks, DenseNet201, and ResNet152, were fine-tuned with two-stage ImageNet transfer learning approach. Results DenseNet201 obtained an accuracy of 87.5% for scoliosis and 88.4% for spondylolisthesis on hold-out test subsets. Cobb-angle MAE was 1.845° and slip percentage MAE was 1.8 percentage point. The corresponding ICC values were 0.962 and 0.958, and macro-AUC values were 0.83 and 0.84. Conclusion The proposed method demonstrated strong internal validity in terms of spinal deformity measurement and grading within the context of a single-center study. Since patient matching was not possible, patient-level independence of the image split could not be confirmed. These results, therefore, constitute internal validation at the level of the image and need to be externally validated independently. Clinical trial registration Not applicable. This study was retrospective and did not involve a clinical trial or prospective intervention.

items.abstract: Abstract Structural heart disease (SHD) often goes undiagnosed, and echocardiography, the standard test, cannot be offered to every patient promptly. AI analysis of routine electrocardiograms (ECGs) could help prioritize who is scanned first. ECG foundation models promise broad applicability across ECG tasks, but SHD abnormalities are novel targets, defined by echocardiography and outside the labels on which these models were pretrained, so how best to use them is unclear. Rather than adapting the foundation model to these targets, we propose GS-ECG, a synergistic generalist–specialist approach that keeps it frozen and pairs it with a compact specialist, DGRNet, trained on novel SHD targets. In this setup, the generalist summarizes each recording in long-context features, while DGRNet focuses on SHD-specific waveform morphology at beat-level resolution, with a receptive field of about two cardiac cycles per feature. We evaluated GS-ECG in two health systems: MIMIC-IV-Ext-SHD (49,229 patients), a new public benchmark, and the EchoNext-Mini Dataset (36,286 patients). Full fine-tuning of the foundation model improved mean AUPRC by only 1.3–3.6% over freezing it, whereas DGRNet alone exceeded fine-tuning by 6.1–6.4%. Combining the frozen generalist with DGRNet in GS-ECG performed best, exceeding fine-tuning by 8.1% in both datasets while training 4.9% as many parameters; its composite SHD AUROC was 0.825 and 0.839. Against the published EchoNext-Mini Model on its own dataset, GS-ECG found 17–25% more patients with aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation or tricuspid regurgitation among the top 5% ranked for echocardiography. Pairing frozen foundation models with purpose-built specialists offers an efficient route to clinical targets that lie beyond pretraining labels.

items.abstract: Abstract Background Difficult airway is an important cause of serious perioperative adverse events. Conventional preoperative assessment is simple but partly operator dependent and has limited predictive accuracy. We developed machine learning models combining clinical measurements and airway ultrasound parameters to support preoperative difficult airway assessment. Methods Seven predictors were collected from 1,000 adults undergoing elective surgery under general anesthesia: body mass index, neck circumference, mouth opening, sternomental distance, skin-to-epiglottis distance, tongue thickness, and hyomental distance ratio. Data were split into training (n = 800) and test (n = 200) sets. Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), generalized additive model (GAM), and Naive Bayes were tuned by stratified 5-fold cross-validation using ROC-AUC. The principal metrics were the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC), average precision (AP), accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), balanced accuracy, and F1 score. Results Mean cross-validation ROC-AUC values were 0.818 for Random Forest, 0.797 for XGBoost, 0.790 for GAM, 0.786 for Logistic Regression, and 0.770 for Naive Bayes. The test set included 24 difficult airway cases. Test-set ROC-AUC values were 0.802 for GAM, 0.783 for XGBoost, 0.777 for Random Forest, and 0.771 for Logistic Regression. At the 0.5 threshold, Logistic Regression had the highest sensitivity (0.542) and a negative predictive value of 0.930; XGBoost had sensitivity 0.458, specificity 0.892, and F1 score 0.407. Conclusions Models combining clinical and airway ultrasound measurements showed some discrimination for difficult airway prediction. Given its sensitivity, negative predictive value, and interpretability, Logistic Regression is a candidate for calibration, threshold optimization, and external validation.

items.abstract: Abstract Background Medical students often struggle transitioning from preclinical coursework to clinical environments. Simulation-based training can bridge this gap but can be resource intensive. Large language models (LLMs) provide a scalable resource that can augment traditional training. However, their effects on learning outcomes and student perceptions are currently not understood. This study aims to evaluate medical student knowledge acquisition and perception of the utility of simplified LLM-based clinical simulation. Methods Using the RISE framework, a structured simulation was designed to assess medical student knowledge of acute asthma exacerbation management. ZotGPT, an institutional GPT-4 based platform was utilized. Medical students completed pre- and post-simulation assessments assessing knowledge, confidence, and perceptions of simulation utility. Subgroup analysis was stratified by time spent completing the simulation. Statistical analyses included Wilcoxon signal-rank and McNemar tests. Results A total of 155 students participated. The simulation significantly improved perceived understanding of key treatment steps, including initial bronchodilator and steroid therapy (p = 0.001), magnesium sulfate escalation (p = 0.002), refractory management (p = 0.021), and discharge planning (p = 0.005). Students rated the simulation as more useful than non-simulation learning tools (p = 0.017) and noninferior to in-person simulation (p = 0.226). Confidence in asthma management increased (p < 0.001), but objective knowledge gains were not observed, with balanced correct-to-incorrect and incorrect-to-correct responses for intermediate steps. Longer engagement (> 600 seconds) was associated with greater perceived benefit. Simulations were deemed helpful for learning (94.7%), and most students preferred immediate feedback (68.4%). Conclusions LLM-based clinical simulations were well accepted, improved medical student confidence, and were perceived as educationally useful. However, objective knowledge gains were limited. LLMs thus may serve as an adjunctive educational tool but require improved prompt design, structured feedback, and guided implementation to optimize outcomes.

items.abstract: BackgroundHealthcare's digital transformation depends on artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC), yet no healthcare-specific framework consolidates the competences required for their adoption.ObjectiveTo identify, classify and synthesise the competences healthcare professionals need to implement AI and HPC in clinical practice.MethodsFollowing PRISMA 2020, six databases (PubMed, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, EBSCOhost, Emerald Insight, Taylor & Francis Online) were searched in June-July 2025 for 2020-2025. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data; three reviewers categorised competences by inductive thematic synthesis. Methodological quality was appraised with design-specific instruments (AMSTAR 2, CASP, JBI, CREDES), and a sensitivity analysis excluding low-quality studies tested robustness.ResultsOf 2255 records, 17 studies were included, yielding 22 competence categories. The most frequent were AI fundamentals (88.2%), ethical and legal issues (70.6%), data analysis and interpretation (64.7%) and evaluation of AI tools (58.8%). No HPC-related competence was reported in any included study, despite HPC terms in the search strategy.ConclusionsThe 22 competences are consolidated into four dimensions (technical and data-centric, ethical and legal, human-centred and interpersonal, and organisational and cognitive leadership), mapped to three proficiency levels and to defined target groups. The absence of HPC competences is a distinct research gap.

items.abstract: While geospatial technologies in psychiatric epidemiology have advanced, the literature remains fragmented. Guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), we reviewed English-language research in Scopus and Web of Science published between 1982 and 2024. We included 114 studies applying geospatial tools for public health research on mental health outcomes, all of which were published between 2012 and 2024. Findings indicate a significant transition from static, area-based descriptive mapping toward dynamic computational mental health epidemiology. Key advancements include artificial intelligence (AI)-based street-view assessments and Global Positioning System (GPS) mobile sensing to address the Uncertain Geographic Context Problem (UGCoP), a spatial exposure misclassification issue. However, critical gaps persists: physical environment are extensively mapped, whereas dynamic social interactions are largely unexplored. The focus remains heavily skewed toward clinical pathology, rendering positive adaptation under-researched. Additionally, research is predominantly conducted in high-income countries and specific middle-income nations like China, leaving populations in the Global South largely underrepresented. To advance the field, future research must prioritize longitudinal designs to establish robust causal relationships. Investigating positive psychological constructs is essential to shift the focus from merely mitigating pathology to actively promoting resilience. Furthermore, developing standardized environmental indices is critical to ensure cross-study comparability and translate spatial data into actionable public health and spatial planning policies. Crucially, there is an urgent need to address geographic disparities by expanding research within the Global South and translating geospatial insights into actionable policies that foster mental health equity and build resilient communities.

items.abstract: Purposeof the research: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy induces progressive gait deterioration, yet most Machine Learning (ML)-based gait studies rely on binary classification frameworks that fail to capture the stage-wise biomechanical changes occurring across the diabetes neuropathy continuum. To identify stage-consistent and stage-specific gait biomarkers across three clinical groups healthy controls (N), diabetes without neuropathy (D), and diabetes with peripheral neuropathy (DPN) using an interpretable machine learning framework.MethodsGait data were collected from 394 participants (N = 109, D = 163, DPN = 122) using the Zebris FDM platform. Spatiotemporal, plantar pressure, and symmetry parameters were extracted. Four pairwise classification tasks (N vs D, D vs DPN, N vs DPN, Healthy vs Diseased) were evaluated using Results: Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Logistic Regression under stratified five-fold cross-validation. Cross-validated SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based feature selection and a final XGBoost model were used for biomarker identification and interpretation. SVM achieved the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) across all tasks (N vs D: 0.80, D vs DPN: 0.75, N vs DPN: 0.91, Healthy vs Diseased: 0.85). SHAP analysis identified bilateral heel contact time and step length as stage-consistent core biomarkers, present across all four classification tasks. Stage-specific discriminators included forefoot load-timing disruption in early diabetes, midfoot unloading and lateral symmetry reversal at the neuropathic transition, and posterior Centre of Pressure (CoP) displacement in established neuropathy.ConclusionsDiabetic gait pathology progresses in a measurable, stage-ordered sequence from early forefoot load-timing disruption through midfoot redistribution and symmetry reversal at the neuropathic transition, to global spatiotemporal deterioration in established neuropathy. The stage-wise biomarker framework presented here provides an interpretable, clinically grounded basis for gait-based screening of diabetic neuropathic progression, warranting prospective validation.

items.abstract: AimPatients with migraine, especially those with aura, have a higher risk of stroke and other vascular events. However, the underlying mechanisms are complex, multifactorial, and may require integration of multimodal data for comprehensive characterization. We have conducted prior analyses on how artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled electrocardiogram (ECG), specifically the atrial fibrillation prediction model and age estimation model output, echocardiogram parameters, and detailed migraine characteristics separately predict vascular events. Herein, we aim to investigate the relative importance and combined effects of all three modalities for vascular risk prediction.MethodsIn this retrospective cohort study, we developed a multimodality prediction risk score to evaluate the vascular risks in patients with migraine based on the coefficients of variables extracted from our prior studies, including comprehensive AI-ECG atrial fibrillation prediction model output and computed delta age (ECG estimated age minus chronological age), echocardiogram parameters, and migraine characteristics. We then included patients with at least one 12-lead ECG, transthoracic echocardiogram, and a visit with a headache specialist at any Mayo Clinic site within three years to evaluate the risk score. The outcome is a composite endpoint of acute ischemic stroke, acute myocardial infarction, venous thromboembolism, and all-cause mortality. We selected 20 risk parameters, including demographics, comorbidities, AI-ECG outputs, echocardiogram features, and migraine characteristics found to be predictive of vascular events. Each variable was assigned a different risk score according to the hazard ratio (HR) and beta coefficient from prior Cox regression analysis for each modality. We used Contal and Q'Quigley's method to find the optimal cut-off, and an additional multivariate Cox regression was conducted to assess the relative risk of each parameter category in the final cohort. We investigated the added value of each modality by net reclassification improvement rate.ResultsA total of 29,928 patients, 12,778 patients, and 6819 patients were included to investigate how AI-ECG outputs, echocardiogram parameters, and migraine characteristics, respectively, predicted adverse vascular outcomes, and the results were used to develop a multimodal risk score. A total of 297 patients with migraine included in previous analyses, of whom 247 (83.2%) were female and 109 (36.7%) had aura, were used for proof-of-concept evaluation of the developed risk score. The mean (standard deviation, SD) age was 39.0 (13.3) and follow-up period was 68.9 (60.9) months. Thirty-five patients (11.8%) developed the composite endpoint. Those with a risk score ≥15 had a significantly shorter vascular event-free survival (HR [95% Confidence Interval (CI)], 3.83 [1.89-7.76]; p < 0.001) compared to those with a risk score <15 in our cohort of 297 patients. Furthermore, comorbidity (HR, 1.17 [1.06-1.30]; p = 0.003) and migraine characteristics (HR, 1.33 [1.06-1.67]; p = 0.014) were significantly predictive of the composite endpoint, whereas other categories were not. Net reclassification improvement was 17.7% (95% CI, 15.9-19.9%; p < 0.001) for AI-ECG model output, 16.9% (95% CI, 14.1-19.5%; p < 0.001) for echocardiogram, and 22.1% (95% CI, 16.7-26.9%; p < 0.001) for migraine characteristics, suggesting significant contribution from each modality.ConclusionThis pilot evaluation study supports the use of combined AI-ECG output, echocardiogram, and migraine characteristics for vascular risk prediction. Although future external validation and real-world clinical assessment is necessary, our preliminary results suggest significant added value of each modality and indicate the importance of obtaining detailed migraine features for vascular risk stratification.

items.title: Bidirectional multi-scale implicit neural representation network for topology-aware lung 4D-CT registration.
items.summary: Objective. Precise lung 4D-CT registration is extremely challenging due to large respiratory excursions. To capture such large-magnitude motion, existing deep learning methods typically adopt a unidirectional coarse-to-fine cascade strategy, which is vulnerable to error propagation because uncorrected coarse-level misalignments degrade subsequent finer-scale stages and often lead to spatially inconsistent…
items.abstract: Objective. Precise lung 4D-CT registration is extremely challenging due to large respiratory excursions. To capture such large-magnitude motion, existing deep learning methods typically adopt a unidirectional coarse-to-fine cascade strategy, which is vulnerable to error propagation because uncorrected coarse-level misalignments degrade subsequent finer-scale stages and often lead to spatially inconsistent deformations. While implicit neural representations (INRs) support continuous coordinate-based deformation modeling, traditional instance-specific INRs lack clinical efficiency and struggle to converge on global large deformations because of the absence of multi-scale semantic guidance. This study aims to bridge these gaps by developing a bidirectional multi-scale INR network that jointly handles large deformation modeling and localized structural fidelity. Approach. We propose a bidirectional multi-scale INR network. First, a generalized conditional INR framework is introduced to enable continuous deformation modeling without the need for retraining. Crucially, a bidirectional feature feedback mechanism built upon Swin Transformer injects high-level semantic priors into low-resolution streams, correcting coarse-level biases through top-down interaction. Furthermore, an anatomy-aware structural constraint is incorporated to promote anatomical consistency and local boundary alignment. Main results. Under the within-subject phase-held-out DIR-Lab protocol, the proposed method achieved a mean TRE of 1.28 mm and a folding rate of 0.0090%. A leave-one-case-out evaluation assessed subject-independent generalization, yielding a mean TRE of 1.53 mm and a folding rate of 0.0195%. On the independent POPI dataset, the method achieved a mean TRE of 1.84 mm and a folding rate of 0.0806%, demonstrating competitive cross-center performance. Inference took 0.33 s per case. Significance. The proposed framework effectively combines continuous coordinate modeling with deep learning efficiency, overcoming error propagation inherent in discrete coarse-to-fine strategies and preserving both global deformation consistency and local anatomical precision. Its sub-second inference and performance under leave-one-case-out and independent external testing support its potential for efficient image-guided radiation therapy workflows.

items.abstract: Fine-grained questions about long videos ask how many times an action occurs, in what order events unfold, or exactly when a state changes. Answering them can require finding brief moments scattered across hours of footage. Agentic models that decide when and where to look promise to find these moments, yet this ability is hard both to measure and to learn. Sparse supporting evidence may establish that an action occurred without establishing its total count; verifying timeline-wide claims requires checking for missed occurrences and double counting. Answer-only supervision, in turn, does not explicitly supervise the search for evidence. We present NexSight, which builds verifiable tasks to both evaluate and train agentic long-video understanding. Its agentic pipeline, SightForge, accepts a task only if a verifier blind to the draft answer can reconstruct it from evidence densely reacquired from the raw video and counterexample checks fail to refute it. This yields SightLine, 310 evidence-traceable tasks from 108 long videos, evaluated through SightLoop, a shared multiscale harness supporting temporal exploration, local inspection, evidence integration, and revisiting while recording returned observations. On disjoint videos, solver trajectories on verified tasks become step-level supervision for observation decisions. The strongest model reaches only 54.52% on SightLine, yet 79.35% when given the annotated evidence. With under 6K examples, Sight-35B nearly doubles its base model's interactive accuracy (21.29% to 42.26%), outperforms the 397B model of its family, begins using explicit spatial inspection after post-training, which its base model never uses, and gains over 8 points on two external long-video benchmarks.

items.abstract: The goal of this paper is to reduce the input token cost of Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) at inference time. Omni-LLMs reason jointly over audio, video and text, but the cost of the three streams is highly unbalanced: visual tokens account for the vast majority of the input, and are highly redundant. In this paper, we propose ReMo, a training-free framework that compresses visual tokens by redistributing their information across modalities: a visual token is kept only if its information appears nowhere else. ReMo achieves this in two ways: (i) it aligns audio and video in a shared space via closed-form calibration, and removes visual tokens already explained by the audio or by other visual tokens; and (ii) it replaces object-level visual tokens, identified by a lightweight object detector, with compact text proxies, short descriptions of each object and its location, conveying the same content in far fewer tokens. On Qwen2.5-Omni at two model scales, ReMo removes 54% of the input tokens with comparable accuracy. It performs comparably to the full-token model, reaching 101.2% and 101.4% of its average accuracy over five audio-visual benchmarks.

items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

items.abstract: Visual proxies decouple explicit world-state simulation from photorealistic video synthesis, offering a controllable interface for both offline clip creation and real-time interactive streaming. Yet a practical renderer must address two challenges. Upstream proxies vary from coarse layouts to fine articulated geometry depending on the interaction, and streaming inference must operate in a few causal steps without accumulating drift across self-generated history. We present Invoker-Render, pairing a bidirectional creation model with a causal four-step streaming model under a shared conditioning interface over structural proxies, an appearance reference, and language. Trained on an aligned approximately 200-hour multi-granularity corpus, Invoker-Render honors fine geometric constraints when supplied while synthesizing plausible local motion under coarse proxies, enabling runtime selection of input detail. To bridge bidirectional creation and real-time streaming without compounding step compression and rollout drift, we introduce Progressive Forcing (ProForcing). ProForcing first trains a causal predictor and distills it into a four-step renderer using histories derived from training videos. Training then shifts to continuous self-generated rollouts. A pipelined serving stack supports efficient streaming inference. Experiments show versatile control across proxy families, granularities, and camera paths, consistent gains over recent streaming baselines, and stable 30-minute racing rollouts that preserve scene and subject appearance.

items.title: Let Samples Sing in Chorus: Mitigating Spurious Correlations via Cross-view Consensus
items.summary: Deep models often rely on spurious correlations that fail on underrepresented groups. Existing methods either correct human-specified bias attributes or infer unknown biases from the learned representation space. However, annotated attributes may differ from the shortcuts actually used by a model, while a single representation provides incomplete and potentially noisy evidence. Our key insight is that a bias…
items.abstract: Deep models often rely on spurious correlations that fail on underrepresented groups. Existing methods either correct human-specified bias attributes or infer unknown biases from the learned representation space. However, annotated attributes may differ from the shortcuts actually used by a model, while a single representation provides incomplete and potentially noisy evidence. Our key insight is that a bias obscured in one feature space may be clearer in another. In this work, we propose CHORD (Cross-view Harmonic Outlier Reversal for Debiasing), a multi-view framework that allows samples to "sing in chorus" across diverse representation spaces to achieve robust cross-view consensus. CHORD aggregates aggregates within-class partitions in each view, which is a proxy for specifying candidate biases, to debias the target representation and classifier without bias supervision. Experiments on seven benchmarks across vision, language, speech, and medical imaging show consistent improvements in worst-group accuracy. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/davelee-uestc/chord_debiasing_public .

items.title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
items.summary: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose…
items.abstract: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.

items.title: Decoding Without a Decoder: Direct Pixel Prediction from Diffusion Transformers
items.summary: Latent diffusion models rely on a decoder to map denoised latents to pixels, adding complexity and inference cost. We introduce Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), which lets a finetuned diffusion transformer produce final pixels directly through a linear head. items.abstract: Latent diffusion models rely on a decoder to map denoised latents to pixels, adding complexity and inference cost. We introduce Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), which lets a finetuned diffusion transformer produce final pixels directly through a linear head. Unlike previous methods, where the denoising output leads to final pixels, DWD separates the two roles: the original denoising head continues to drive sampling, then the new DWD head predicts the pixels at the final step. We extend pretrained latent models with DWD efficiently by finetuning only the last few transformer blocks, training the DWD head with pixel quality losses while anchoring the denoising head to the pretrained model to preserve the sample trajectory. Across latent image and video generators, DWD removes the decoder and reduces inference cost while maintaining or even improving pixel quality. On Wan video generation, it visibly reduces detail distortion and flickering, lowering warping error by 23%. Remarkably, the same separation also improves pixel diffusion models that do not even use a decoder: a final-step DWD head produces substantially better texture detail in text-to-image generation, and improves ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43, a new state of the art among pixel flow models.

items.title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
items.summary: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds…
items.abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.

items.abstract: Attention scores candidate supports of an answer, which we call witnesses, and reads the scores at a temperature. We build a higher-order attention layer whose state lives on pairs of items: for a pair (a, b), each third item k is a witness judged through its legs (a, k) and (k, b). It reads witnesses at zero temperature, keeping the best and the number tied with it, passes on only bits comparing such counts, rebuilds its pair state from the input and these bits at every loop, and is trained from answers alone. Each choice removes one way soft attention fails at size: dispersed weight, unresolved gaps between learned scores, and a drifting soft state. In maximum retrieval it is right on at least 99.95% of sets 1,000 times larger than in training, on all ten seeds; trained with a soft count, the same network falls to 42% at 4,096 items. On CLRS-30 without hints, a general form of the layer (half its channels read at zero temperature, numbers embedded, state carried) beats the best published model, which uses hints on some tasks; the full cold layer is exact on every test input of 9 of the 12 tasks whose answers depend on numbers only through comparisons. From yes-or-no answers it decides 2-SAT and two-colouring exactly at 500 variables and, as our theory predicts, not parity equations. Beside a frozen 7B language model it chains family relations exactly at 1,000 statements after training on 16, where the model alone falls to 44%; finite checks on the weights prove every block that learned correct at every size, on acyclic contexts and given what the model reads. On CLUTRR it is right on every story of five to ten relations given the graphs, learning the 62 rules exactly; from text, with the model frozen, no hand-written rule and only a small read-in trained, it lifts an open 7B model from 33% to 65%, above every system we found without hand-written rules except frontier reasoning models.

items.title: GameRealm: Grounding Visual Learning in Interactive Games
items.summary: Visual foundation models are central to physical intelligence, yet their development remains constrained by fragmented training datasets, inconsistent annotation quality, and limited multimodal supervision. To address these challenges, we introduce GameRealm, a large-scale, richly annotated dataset that grounds visual observations in synchronized, game-native supervision. GameRealm encompasses over 120 million RGB…
items.abstract: Visual foundation models are central to physical intelligence, yet their development remains constrained by fragmented training datasets, inconsistent annotation quality, and limited multimodal supervision. To address these challenges, we introduce GameRealm, a large-scale, richly annotated dataset that grounds visual observations in synchronized, game-native supervision. GameRealm encompasses over 120 million RGB frames and 1,000 hours of gameplay footage across all views. Beyond its unprecedented scale, GameRealm provides rich multimodal supervision, including metric depth, camera parameters, synchronized audio, control inputs, and 3D point trajectories. Its diversity further extends to flexible view configurations, spanning single-view, stereo, multi-view, and panoramic recordings. To enable scalable acquisition across diverse game environments, we develop a unified data collection pipeline that combines human-operated interaction with agentic exploration. Extensive experiments across diverse visual learning tasks demonstrate that GameRealm consistently strengthens visual foundation models in both visual generation and geometric learning. These results establish GameRealm as a versatile and valuable data resource, unlocking new opportunities for advancing visual intelligence.

items.title: CADMAGEDDON: High-Fidelity CAD Reconstruction with Local Inference
items.summary: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. For individuals and small companies, bringing this work in-house also requires computational resources they can afford. We introduce CADMAGEDDON, an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD from meshes and can run locally on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops. The method decomposes this…
items.abstract: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. For individuals and small companies, bringing this work in-house also requires computational resources they can afford. We introduce CADMAGEDDON, an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD from meshes and can run locally on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops. The method decomposes this complex task into a chain of simple visual decisions about what to construct and what to correct. Geometric tools support precise construction, allowing the agent to focus on visual reasoning. Using the mid-sized Qwen3.8-27B model, CADMAGEDDON outperforms prior approaches, including systems based on frontier models, in reconstruction quality on all the main benchmarks. CADMAGEDDON integrates with FreeCAD, bringing its reconstructions into practitioners' existing CAD workflows. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/cadmageddon

items.abstract: Turning a CAD model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and geometric precision. Language models can generate such workflows by writing geometry and toolpath code for each part, but this makes numerical execution part of the model's task. We introduce MillBill, an agent that separates machining decisions from their geometric execution and verification. Given a boundary-representation part, stock, and material, a locally hosted, mid-sized open model proposes operations and cutting parameters for indexed three-axis machining. A geometric harness generates toolpaths, simulates material removal, and returns feedback for plan refinement. Setup planning accounts for what the available cutters can physically reach, rather than visibility alone. We evaluate the resulting programs by the fraction of the target surface area within the specified tolerance after simulated machining. With Qwen3.8-27B, MillBill outperforms frontier-model approaches that construct their own geometry and toolpath workflows on the evaluated machining tasks. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/millbill

items.abstract: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) enables a single student to absorb the skills of several domain teachers by learning from its own generated responses. We present Multimodal Model Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation Reasoner (M3OPD-Reasoner), a fully open recipe for post-training vision-language models (VLMs) over three reasoning domains: image STEM, image perception, and video. We curate two datasets, M3OPD-SFT-1.35M for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and M3OPD-RL-193K for reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards. On these data, we compare post-training recipes that start from Qwen3.5-9B: training one model on the mixed data of all domains (MixSFT and MixRL), and training one teacher per domain with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), directly or after an SFT warm-up, and distilling the teachers into one student with MOPD. We evaluate on 21 image STEM, image perception, and video reasoning benchmarks after we decontaminate the training data against them. The comparison establishes MOPD of teachers trained with GSPO directly from Qwen3.5-9B as the best recipe: the student closely matches each teacher on its own domain and is on average above the mixed-training baselines on the same prompts. Since MOPD already merges the domain capabilities that MixRL would otherwise have to learn, its student is a stronger starting point for RL, and we ask whether the same data can carry the model further from there: we add MixRL on top of the MOPD student, on the same prompts and with the same settings, which, to our knowledge, no prior VLM recipe has studied. The same prompts still improve the MOPD student, with no collapse, and give our main model, M3OPD-Reasoner-9B. MOPD and MixRL can therefore work as consecutive stages that get more out of the same data. We release all data, the training code, and the checkpoints of every stage.

items.abstract: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of a Transformer into N parallel streams, and manifold-constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes them at scale. However, mHC benefits little from more than four streams, partly because each sublayer writes a single output to all streams, limiting how differently they can be updated. In this work, we propose TPHC, which integrates tensor-parallel (TP) shards with HC streams to promote greater independence across streams. Specifically, we route a separate mixture of the residual streams to each TP shard and keep the individual shard outputs separate during write-back, so each stream can receive a different mixture of those outputs. This design makes the residual-stream updates more expressive without adding parameters or FLOPs to the attention or FFN sublayers. With native support for stream sharding under TP, TPHC requires only 9% more training time than mHC on an 8B model when both use four streams. Increasing the number of streams from four to sixteen raises its training time by only 19%. On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC reduces validation loss by 0.7-1.0% and raises average zero-shot accuracy across six commonsense reasoning benchmarks by 0.3-0.7 percentage points relative to mHC at matched stream counts Nin{4,8,16}. Our code is available at https://github.com/wuyou2002/TPHC.

items.abstract: Training coding agents for long-horizon tasks requires environments with verifiable feedback. Existing pipelines often follow a linear process that ends with validation, establishing usability but providing little guidance on improving training value. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) often requires model rollouts or model training followed by downstream evaluation, with costs and feedback delays amplified on long-horizon tasks. How can we use timely, reliable proxy signals to improve training value and synthesize environments at scale? We present RepoFactory, an automated pipeline that converts real repositories into verifiable environments where agents build complete projects from scratch given a language specification. Its Environment Evolution Loop optimizes a multiplicative objective combining validity, structural coupling, and implementation scope through proxy feedback. RepoFactory produces 10,159 environments across 17 software domains. Training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on these environments yields RepoHorizen-35B-A3B, which achieves gains of 22.6 percentage points on NL2Repo-Bench and 8.5 points on average across five benchmarks covering long-horizon coding and agentic tasks in real-world production settings, compared with 17.5 and 6.4 points without environment evolution. These results highlight the training value of RepoFactory environments and the additional gains from the Environment Evolution Loop.

items.abstract: Learned lossless codecs make smaller files than common classical codecs, yet the images we archive and train on still use classical codecs. A main reason is time: a learned codec takes seconds to decode a photo that a classical codec opens in milliseconds, and their faster variants give up most of their gain in size. We argue that much of this time is spent waiting, not computing: the network waits for the values it conditions on, and the arithmetic decoder reads them one at a time. We introduce FMT (Fixed-step Multiscale Tree), a lossless image format whose decoding order and entropy coder are designed together so that neither wait grows with the image. FMT stores an image as a coarse-to-fine tree whose steps hold independent values: a GPU predicts each step at once and decodes it in parallel rANS lanes that carry their states from step to step, so an image of any size decodes in a fixed number of sequential steps. On this tree we build a family of bit-exact codecs, from a rule with no network to large networks, and no codec we ran on the same GPU beats any of them on both size and speed. Without a network, FMT beats NVIDIA's HTJ2K on size and speed; with a large one, it decodes Kodak photos 9 to 61X faster than learned codecs we ran on the same A100, at the same size or smaller.

items.abstract: After sparking a revolution in protein structure prediction, machine learning (ML), and artificial intelligence (AI) are now reshaping the modeling of protein conformational ensembles and dynamics. A fast, scalable, and accurate representation of protein conformational ensembles could enable genome-scale studies of protein function, with broad applications in drug discovery and protein engineering. The challenges associated with this goal, however, are far greater than those involved in single structure prediction because of the broad timescales spanned by protein motion, the complex relationship between sequence and dynamics, and the scarcity of datasets with experimental measurements. Despite these difficulties, many promising solutions have emerged in recent years, ranging from accelerated molecular dynamics to direct sampling of the conformational distribution, as well as some hybrid methods. Here, we review recent AI-powered approaches to tackle protein dynamics and conformational sampling, and outline their current limitations.

items.abstract: Most genetic variants associated with human traits and diseases lie in non-coding DNA, where they can alter gene regulation in specific cell types and states. Single-cell atlases chart these states across tissues and development, but rarely profile enough donors to associate variants with expression directly. Deep learning models could bridge this gap by predicting variant effects from DNA sequence, yet they poorly distinguish related cell states and require fine-tuning for new datasets. Here we present AlphaGenome 2 (AG2), which substantially advances cell-type-specific prediction of regulatory activity and variant effects for gene expression and chromatin accessibility. Trained on organism-wide human and mouse single-cell atlases and bulk functional genomics data, AG2 takes as input a 1-Mb DNA sequence and a condition specifying a target tissue, cell type, or cell state. Conditioning enables AG2 to impute unmeasured epigenomic tracks and predict multimodal variant effects across cell types. Inferring this condition directly from gene expression extends AG2 to unseen datasets and cell states without fine-tuning. AG2 outperforms fine-tuned AlphaGenome 1 and specialized models trained on target datasets, doubling recall of causal single-cell eQTLs at 90% precision. AG2 also achieves state-of-the-art enhancer-gene linking and can pinpoint causal variants at complex trait loci. Across hundreds of human cell types, we generated an atlas of enhancer-gene links and scores for 7 million common variants. As single-cell profiling expands across development, tissues, and disease cohorts, AG2 provides a blueprint for turning observational atlases into variant effect maps.

items.abstract: Pathology classification of cancer tumor subtypes and benign tumors can be difficult due to cellular heterogeneity and similar morphological features. Renal Cell Cancer (RCC) poses a major challenge for uropathologists as advanced RCC is often incidentally diagnosed with complex histological characteristics. We hypothesised that molecular profiling of RCC and benign tumor specimen by mass spectrometry with machine learning methods enable accurate tumor classification and identification of candidate RCC biomarkers. MALDI-MSI and quantitative proteomics (LC-MS) provided peptide and protein profiles of RCC neoplasms and benign tumors presented in tissue microarray (TMA) format of 541 tissue cores from 126 patients. Machine learning models classified RCC subtypes: Clear cell RCC (ccRCC), Chromophobe RCC (chRCC), papillary RCC (pRCC), and oncocytoma (OC). Known and novel candidate protein biomarker panels for discrimination of RCC subtypes were identified. RCC peptide mapping, evaluated using patient-level cross-validation, reliably classified ccRCC and healthy tissue, but did not reliably discriminate the diagnostically challenging RCC subtypes chRCC vs OC. Quantitative proteomics identified over 5000 proteins and classified all four RCC subtypes with 95.5% patient-level accuracy, including robust discrimination of chRCC from oncocytoma. We report new candidate protein biomarkers for ccRCC and pRCC and distinguish histologically similar subtypes OC (benign) and chRCC (malignant), as demonstrated by mass spectrometry-based immunohistochemistry. Candidate prognostic biomarkers for ccRCC contribute to risk of relapse (CDK6, ATM) and risk of metastasis (DDB2, MK03). Digital histo-molecular differentiation of cancer tumor subtypes and benign tumors by mass spectrometry and macbine learning enables retrospective and prospective studies. Identified candidate protein biomarkers complement existing protocols in tumor pathology.
