items.abstract: Objectives To estimate standalone artificial intelligence (AI) diagnostic performance in temporomandibular joint (TMJ) imaging across input modality-target pairings. Methods Four databases were searched through 18 June 2026. Eligible studies assessed standalone imaging AI and supplied an exact test-set 2 × 2 table in the report or after author contact. Four pairings were analysed by bivariate meta-regression. Two reviewers applied QUADAS-3 at estimate level. Results Sixteen studies contributed 17 estimates. For disc displacement, magnetic resonance imaging input yielded pooled sensitivity 0.924 (95% CI, 0.859-0.960) and specificity 0.812 (0.709-0.885), compared with 0.765 (0.618-0.867) and 0.741 (0.592-0.850) for panoramic or cone-beam computed tomography input. The sensitivity difference was 0.159 and remained 0.152-0.198 in leave-one-out and replicate analyses; the omnibus pairing test was not significant (χ²(6) = 10.38, P = .110). Reference-standard relation and pairing partitioned the disc-displacement evidence identically. No estimate had low overall risk of bias, and several otherwise eligible estimates lacked exact published 2 × 2 data. Conclusions Sensitivity was higher when disc displacement was depicted directly on magnetic resonance imaging than when inferred from imaging that does not depict the disc. However, the cross-domain group contained only three estimates, the omnibus pairing test was not significant, and design factors were entangled. Performance should therefore be interpreted by pairing, while direct depiction versus proxy inference requires prospective testing. Advances in knowledge TMJ imaging AI performance should be interpreted in the context of the input modality-target pairing rather than as a property of the algorithm alone; exact test-set confusion matrices are essential for verification.

items.abstract: Generalist manipulation policies can benefit from the complementary experience of humans, real robots, and simulated agents. However, differences in morphology, sensing, and control interfaces make it difficult to learn effectively from their combined demonstrations. We introduce EgoX, an egocentric cross-embodiment learning framework that organizes heterogeneous demonstrations through semantically corresponding observation and action modalities. EgoX pretrains a Modularized Cross-Embodiment Transformer with Embodiment Dreaming (MXT+) on this mixture and fine-tunes it on target-embodiment demonstrations. Within each embodiment, MXT+ assigns a dedicated tokenizer to each observation modality and a dedicated expert to each action modality, with a Transformer trunk shared across embodiments. A training-only embodiment-dreaming objective predicts latent representations of future visual and proprioceptive states, encouraging the shared trunk to model each embodiment's dynamics. Across 13 task-embodiment pairs spanning five tasks and six robot embodiments, including five physical robots and one simulated humanoid, cross-embodiment pretraining raises MXT+'s average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 over training from scratch. The gains are particularly pronounced under out-of-distribution conditions, where average task progress increases from 0.53 to 0.77. Ablations demonstrate the benefits of broader pretraining mixtures, modular interfaces, and embodiment dreaming, with dreaming producing more similar latent geometry across embodiments. Project page: egox-dream.github.io.

items.abstract: Frontier video generation models work in a VAE latent space that compresses video in both space and time. This compression made training tractable, but now limits high-resolution, controllable, and interactive generation -- doubling resolution quadruples token count, conditions apply to groups of frames rather than individual ones, and each response must wait for the rest of its multi-frame block. We present PixVid, a simple yet effective method that lifts a pretrained latent video model to directly generate every frame in pixel space. PixVid keeps the diffusion transformer and replaces the VAE decoder with a convolutional head that renders its outputs into pixels. We find that predicting clean video rather than velocity, together with a larger noise shift, is key to quality. Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B, PixVid is competitive with the latent baseline within sim 1.3M training clips. Working framewise in pixels, it generates at 2times higher resolution with the same per-frame token count, keeps depth-conditioned video editing aligned under fast motion, and responds to each action at the next frame. Project page: https://chenshuo20.github.io/PixVid/

items.title: Consensus Capture in Reference-Based UAV Video Stabilization: A Benchmark on Dynamic Urban Scenes
items.summary: Reference-frame stabilization registers every frame of a hovering-drone video onto one reference frame, keeping object positions comparable. The registration pipelines it relies on are selected on feature-matching benchmarks in which only the camera moves. items.abstract: Reference-frame stabilization registers every frame of a hovering-drone video onto one reference frame, keeping object positions comparable. The registration pipelines it relies on are selected on feature-matching benchmarks in which only the camera moves. Over a busy intersection, vehicles moving together supply mutually consistent correspondences that can draw the robust homography estimate toward their motion: consensus capture, which inlier statistics cannot flag. A two-part benchmark measures it and the object masking meant to prevent it. A static protocol scores ten pipelines under exactly known homographies on 4K aerial frames, tuned on a site-disjoint split at a matched resolution and feature budget. A dynamic protocol scores them at an offline and a real-time budget on hovers selected from the video alone to span the amount and coherence of moving foreground, plus a stationary control. It measures background alignment, object position error and the share of a moving group's displacement an estimate follows, against a pseudo-ground-truth reference audited with manually annotated ground control points, which also score every candidate. On static scenes, tuned AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT and BRISK lead, retuning the matcher thresholds raises the mean average accuracy (mAA) by at most 0.0062, and masking costs less than 0.005. Unmasked ORB is captured on 28 of 304 real-time dynamic pairs and on 6 offline; its real-time captured estimates have a median corner error of 18.8 px yet typical inlier counts and ratios. Masking removes capture for every pipeline and leaves the leading pipelines unchanged. Code, data and results are released.

items.title: The Value of Thinking: Learning When to Reason in Hybrid Decision Models
items.summary: Existing adaptive-reasoning methods shorten the explicit reasoning a model writes, or skip it by switching modes; either way the answer is still written out token by token. Rather than deciding how much to think, we explore a different paradigm, zero-or-T thinking: a single model either answers from the implicit thinking inside one forward pass, generating no token, or performs full autoregressive reasoning at a…
items.abstract: Existing adaptive-reasoning methods shorten the explicit reasoning a model writes, or skip it by switching modes; either way the answer is still written out token by token. Rather than deciding how much to think, we explore a different paradigm, zero-or-T thinking: a single model either answers from the implicit thinking inside one forward pass, generating no token, or performs full autoregressive reasoning at a cost of T tokens when that is worth paying. We realise it in a hybrid decision model (HDM), where one frozen backbone serves both modes and a lightweight self-routing block chooses between them. The block estimates the value of thinking, the utility the slow mode is expected to add over the fast one, from what that implicit thinking has already produced, and the slow mode runs only where that value exceeds a price λ set per request. Where no per-decision label exists, as in episodic agentic tasks, we introduce Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation (CDPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that trains the block from episode-level returns. We evaluate HDM on MMLU-Pro, AGIEval, GPQA-Diamond, JevBench, BANKING77 and MiniWoB. Specifically, on JevBench HDM-4B scores 0.857 against Jev's 0.851 (+0.7%) at a median 0.179\,s against 0.652 (-72.5%). On the agentic venue MiniWoB HDM-27B cuts token cost by 80.1%.

items.title: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding
items.summary: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the…
items.abstract: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.

items.title: Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement
items.summary: It is common to train Large Language Models (LLMs) for agentic tasks with Reinforcement Learning (RL) from scalar rewards. However, this throws away the fine-grained information about the environment that the agent experienced during the trial (e.g., error logs). To utilize this rich information, recent works wrap the agent in a harness that refines its own inputs through reflection or compaction and hands past…
items.abstract: It is common to train Large Language Models (LLMs) for agentic tasks with Reinforcement Learning (RL) from scalar rewards. However, this throws away the fine-grained information about the environment that the agent experienced during the trial (e.g., error logs). To utilize this rich information, recent works wrap the agent in a harness that refines its own inputs through reflection or compaction and hands past experience to future rollouts, but the construction of the handed-off artifacts (e.g., a playbook) is itself not learned. We want the best of both worlds: gradient updates from a scalar reward, while also utilizing environment information to hand off experience. As a concrete testbed, we fix the Agentic Context Engineering () harness and train one model to act, reflect, and curate task-local playbooks. Our method, , evaluates candidate experience-handoff artifacts by their downstream effect on future actor rollouts, and co-optimizes the role-specific behaviors (action generator, insight reflector, and playbook curator) under a fixed scaffold. Across agentic benchmarks, achieves higher held-out performance than baseline methods. The results suggest that agent training should optimize not only the actions in the current rollout, but also the model-written experience that future rollouts inherit.

items.title: DeepStress: Stress-Testing Deep Search Agents
items.summary: While search agents demonstrate impressive capabilities in multi-step question answering, their robustness to poor-quality evidence remains under-explored. Such evidence is rare in benchmark corpora, and resulting failures are hard to reproduce. We propose DeepStress, a dynamic stress-testing framework that subjects agents to degraded evidence at controlled rates. It replaces the retrieval module with a synthetic…
items.abstract: While search agents demonstrate impressive capabilities in multi-step question answering, their robustness to poor-quality evidence remains under-explored. Such evidence is rare in benchmark corpora, and resulting failures are hard to reproduce. We propose DeepStress, a dynamic stress-testing framework that subjects agents to degraded evidence at controlled rates. It replaces the retrieval module with a synthetic environment where documents are generated dynamically for each query, under independent control of their trustworthiness, relevance, and factuality. To characterize behavior under stress, we go beyond binary accuracy with a five-way classification of final-answer outcomes and two new reliability-aware metrics, RAS and CoPRAS, which credit cautious behavior and account for computational cost. Evaluating 12 systems on questions from HotpotQA and BrowseComp-Plus, we find that several open-weight agents answer confidently when sources contain obvious credibility red flags, and that many HotpotQA questions are answered from parametric knowledge even when all returned documents are factually wrong.

items.title: TTB: Test-time Baking for Efficient Rendering of Decoder-only View Synthesis Models
items.summary: Decoder-only Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) with KV-cache have recently achieved state-of-the-art quality by regressing novel views from neural networks without reconstructing 3D geometry, while Test-Time Training (TTT) layers save computation but sacrifice quality. We propose Test-Time Baking (TTB), a strategy that learns to bake global scene information from cross-view attention into a lightweight MLP,…
items.abstract: Decoder-only Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) with KV-cache have recently achieved state-of-the-art quality by regressing novel views from neural networks without reconstructing 3D geometry, while Test-Time Training (TTT) layers save computation but sacrifice quality. We propose Test-Time Baking (TTB), a strategy that learns to bake global scene information from cross-view attention into a lightweight MLP, enabling fast and high-fidelity novel-view decoding. The first key is to repurpose the fast-weight MLP of TTT to learn the cross-view attention mapping explicitly from its input-output pairs, rather than replacing attention entirely, achieving the same rendering efficiency as TTT while delivering substantially higher quality. The second key addresses a modality misalignment between context prefilling and novel-view rendering: we disentangle context tokens into camera-only context rendering tokens to serve as TTB input, and context ground-truth tokens with image content to serve as the TTB mapping target, ensuring the baked MLPs are relieved of the modality generalization challenge between context and novel-view processing. Our method achieves up to **23x** rendering speedup with quality on par with the state-of-the-art across several benchmarks. Project page: https://test-time-baking.github.io

items.title: Ropedia Xperience 2: A Gold Standard for Scaling Physical AI Environments and Behaviors
items.summary: Large foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 have recently been shown to control robots directly from visual observations. They nevertheless remain brittle on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks in real-world environments. Further progress depends on two complementary resources: demonstrations of human behavior that supervise how tasks are performed, and interactive environments in which policies…
items.abstract: Large foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 have recently been shown to control robots directly from visual observations. They nevertheless remain brittle on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks in real-world environments. Further progress depends on two complementary resources: demonstrations of human behavior that supervise how tasks are performed, and interactive environments in which policies can be rolled out, evaluated, and improved in closed loop. Language models have advanced along well-characterized scaling laws; the corresponding question for physical AI is how capability scales with environments and behaviors, which first requires identifying which data to scale and how to produce and reuse such data continuously. To address this question, we introduce Ropedia Xperience 2, comprising 1,589 released metric-scale 3D scans and a collection of 4,230 egocentric recordings of 74 tasks (131 hours). We further show that each capture can be repurposed for robot learning: scenes are converted into physically interactive simulation environments, human motion is retargeted to whole-body robot trajectories, and additional robot behaviors are obtained through virtual teleoperation and automated long-horizon trajectory generation. We propose this joint capture of environments and behaviors as a gold standard for physical AI data collection, laying a data foundation for establishing scaling laws over environments and behaviors.

items.title: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents
items.summary: Decision models answer a question with a typed output, such as a choice among options with a probability for each, so one model can choose an agent's actions, evaluate actions already taken, or score every action to teach a policy with reinforcement learning. Prior work has studied them mainly as actors, judging their usefulness by how well they act. We ask whether a decision model that acts poorly can still teach…
items.abstract: Decision models answer a question with a typed output, such as a choice among options with a probability for each, so one model can choose an agent's actions, evaluate actions already taken, or score every action to teach a policy with reinforcement learning. Prior work has studied them mainly as actors, judging their usefulness by how well they act. We ask whether a decision model that acts poorly can still teach well. We compare three decision models and three general LLMs as actors and judges on ALFWorld, and use JEV as a teacher on ALFWorld and WebShop. As actors, all six models are pulled away from a subgoal that must come first by an easier one. As judges that see the whole trajectory, the same models credit the steps toward that subgoal, and asking whether each action helped, rather than whether the task will succeed, separates useful from useless actions. As a teacher, JEV raises a Qwen2.5-1.5B policy over GRPO from 72.8% to 82.9% success on ALFWorld and from 56.8% to 71.4% on WebShop. These results suggest that a poor actor can still teach well, because judging an action after the episode ends reveals the consequences that acting must anticipate. Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/decision-agents.

items.title: Factored One-sided Adam-Moment for Practical and Scalable SOAP
items.summary: Second-order optimizers (e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper,…
items.abstract: Second-order optimizers (e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP's dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP's dense second moment, and we measure only a 15-20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP's optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP's gains need not require SOAP's cost. Code: https://github.com/naver-ai/foam

items.summary: Cytokine receptors are important therapeutic targets in anti-inflammatory therapy. Point mutations in the interleukin-6 receptor and the interleukin-11 receptor are associated with inflammatory disorders and developmental defects of the skull, respectively. In silico methods to determine whether a novel point mutation found in a patient is pathogenic and thus the likely cause for the patients' disease are therefore…
items.abstract: Cytokine receptors are important therapeutic targets in anti-inflammatory therapy. Point mutations in the interleukin-6 receptor and the interleukin-11 receptor are associated with inflammatory disorders and developmental defects of the skull, respectively. In silico methods to determine whether a novel point mutation found in a patient is pathogenic and thus the likely cause for the patients' disease are therefore of high diagnostic interest. There is an ongoing discussion about whether AlphaFold 3 (AF3) is a suitable tool to understand the influence of point mutations on the structure and hence function of a protein. In this study, by analyzing all interleukin-6 receptor and interleukin-11 receptor variants that are known to be disease associated, we find that the structural models generated by AF3 are more similar to solved crystal structures of the wild-type (WT) cytokine receptors than the corresponding WT models. We show that this over-accordance is caused by template bias of AF3, whereby the best-fitting template is not used for the WT models, but is used when a single amino acid is altered in the input sequence. Our results suggest that AF3 should be used with extreme caution when comparing WT proteins and single-point mutations to assess structural changes underlying disease association.

items.abstract: Juvenile Paget's disease (JPD) is an ultra-rare autosomal recessive skeletal disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in TNFRSF11B, which encodes osteoprotegerin (OPG), resulting in enhanced osteoclastic bone resorption. Purpose To describe the clinical, genetic, and therapeutic features of two patients with a clinical diagnosis of JPD who carried distinct homozygous TNFRSF11B variants. Methods Clinical and longitudinal follow-up analyses of two unrelated Chinese pedigrees with JPD were performed. Clinical assessment, biochemical testing, skeletal imaging, Sanger sequencing of TNFRSF11B with familial segregation, in silico pathogenicity prediction, and AlphaFold-based structural analysis were undertaken. Results Patient 1 (P1), a 3-year-old boy, had severe early-onset disease with recurrent fractures, macrocephaly, long-bone bowing, markedly elevated bone turnover markers, and diffuse skeletal involvement on imaging. Patient 2 (P2), a 35-year-old woman, had a milder but progressive deforming phenotype with scoliosis, profound hearing loss, low lumbar spine bone mineral density (BMD), persistent biochemical hyperturnover, and extensive polyostotic skeletal disease on imaging. Sanger sequencing identified two novel homozygous TNFRSF11B missense variants: c.544 G > T (p. Asp182Tyr) in P1 and c.307 C > T (p. Arg103Cys) in P2; both families showed heterozygous parental carrier status. Both variants were classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS) by the genetic testing laboratory. Zoledronic acid in P1 rapidly reduced alkaline phosphatase (ALP) from 5069 to 1917 U/L at 6 weeks and improved skeletal mineralization, but was complicated by hungry bone syndrome. Denosumab in P2 markedly suppressed bone turnover markers, reduced pain, improved mobility, prevented new fractures during the 1-year follow-up, and increased lumbar spine BMD by 17.5% at 6 months. Conclusion This study expanded the genotypic and phenotypic spectrum of OPG-deficient JPD and confirmed that both zoledronic acid and denosumab were effective treatments, although response and safety differed according to age and baseline disease activity, supporting individualized antiresorptive management.

items.abstract: Translating candidate gene panels into objective physiological trait interpretations remains a major hurdle in exercise genomics. Conventional total genotype scoring suffers from severe panel-composition bias, fails to evaluate unannotated or novel variants, and frequently fosters inflated claims regarding individual athletic prediction. Here, we present a population-calibrated, multi-tiered computational framework that evaluates genomic variation across six evidence streams integrating deep learning protein and genomic language models (ESM-2, Evo 2), missense and splice predictors (AlphaMissense, SpliceAI), and regional pathogenic-density metrics to generate a continuous Variant Priority Score (VPS; 1-10 scale). By dynamically renormalizing missing evidence streams rather than zero-filling them, the framework robustly scores unannotated variants lacking empirical database entries. Individual trait burden across 344 genes (spanning 17 physiological traits in Aerobic, Anaerobic, and Recovery domains) is aggregated and normalized against ancestry-matched expectations derived from gnomAD South Asian and an in-house reference cohort (N > 13,000). When applied to 960 South Indian individuals (584 male, 376 female; whole-exome sequencing), this normalization removed the dependence of expected trait burden on panel size by construction, and gene count explained only 2.7% of the variance in the resulting capacity scores (six traits interrogated by 16 to 33 genes). Variance partitioning of 4,764 individual-by-trait scores (six of the 17 traits: one aerobic, two anaerobic and three recovery) revealed that score variation was predominantly trait-driven (45.5%) rather than individual-driven (11.1%, p = 0.386), a pattern reproduced independently in males and females and with no statistically significant gender difference in capacity scores, indicating that, in this cohort, the candidate panel resolved differences between physiological traits but did not detect differences between individuals in capacity scores (no athletic phenotype was measured). Benchmarking against ClinVar classifications achieved an AUC of 0.74, which fell to 0.62 when archive-dependent streams were excluded, directly quantifying the role of shared data provenance. Replacing the in-house frequency reference with gnomAD South Asian shifted absolute scores (median fold change 0.73) but preserved trait ordering (Spearman 0.96), so scores are positions against a stated, population-specific reference. This framework provides an auditable, evidence-traceable baseline for trait-level research and functional variant prioritization while offering a critical methodological safeguard against over-interpreting unvalidated individual performance predictions.

items.abstract: Esophageal cancer (EC), comprising esophageal squamous cell carcinoma and esophageal adenocarcinoma, remains a highly aggressive malignancy characterized by substantial intratumoral heterogeneity, cellular plasticity, therapeutic resistance, and poor clinical outcomes. Increasing evidence indicates that EC progression is governed not only by tumor-intrinsic genetic alterations but also by dynamic interactions among signaling networks, metabolic and epigenetic programs, cancer stem-like states, stromal and immune cells, extracellular matrix, vasculature, neural components, and the microbiome. In this review, we synthesize advances in the cellular and molecular biology of EC and discuss their implications for precision therapeutic strategies, with emphasis on oncogenic signaling, pathway rewiring, tumor–microenvironment interactions, cancer stem-cell plasticity, and emerging biomarker platforms, including multi-omics, liquid biopsy, extracellular vesicles, single-cell sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics. We further examine patient-derived organoids, organoid–immune co-culture systems, three-dimensional bioprinted tumor models, and computational approaches as functional platforms for investigating tumor heterogeneity, therapeutic response, and treatment resistance. Beyond tumor control, tissue-engineering and regenerative strategies for repairing treatment-associated mucosal injury, fibrosis, stricture, and tissue loss are discussed. Importantly, regenerative interventions require careful oncologic consideration because pathways involved in tissue repair, stem-cell activation, angiogenesis, and extracellular-matrix remodeling may influence residual malignant cells. Finally, we highlight the convergence of precision oncology, functional tumor modeling, regenerative medicine, and artificial intelligence, while addressing challenges in standardization, validation, scalability, regulation, and clinical translation.

items.abstract: While a differentiation hierarchy with leukemia-initiating stem cells (LICs) at the apex is well documented for acute myeloid leukemia, the existence of LICs and their trajectories in B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) are debated. This study aims to investigate the hierarchical landscape of two B-ALL cases by combining barcoding and multiome single-cell data to unveil the differentiation architecture and temporal dynamics of leukemic differentiation at clonal and single-cell resolution in vivo. Single-cell transcriptome and AbSeq analysis of lentiviral barcoded and transplanted patient-derived B-ALL cells revealed interconnected subpopulations, which could be prospectively isolated via surface markers and exhibited distinct leukemogenicity. Barcode tracking demonstrated the ability of cells to differentiate from a source cluster into differentiated progeny. Using machine learning, we identified expression patterns predicting the differentiation potential of each barcoded cell within the immature cell compartment. To determine the dynamical properties of clones, we developed a mathematical model that simulates the development of these subpopulations from a clonally diverse stem cell compartment. The model confirmed the most likely cluster of origin, supporting our functional data, and revealed the variability in dynamical properties between clones, while largely excluding plasticity. Hence, our work demonstrates unidirectional differentiation in selected B-ALL cases.

items.abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), the most common subtype of non-small cell lung cancer, exhibits profound histological and molecular heterogeneity. While genomic profiling has identified key oncogenic drivers and immune signatures, its use is limited by cost, technical demands and tissue availability. In addition, spatial transcriptomics provides spatially resolved molecular insights but remains challenging and time-consuming. To address this gap, we developed XpressO-Lung, an explanatory deep learning model that predicts gene expression heterogeneity spatially in tumor and its microenvironment on hematoxylin and eosin based diagnostic (Dx) whole-slide images (WSIs) by learning associations between tissue morphology and the corresponding bulk-transcriptomic data. Utilizing 200 LUAD cases from The Cancer Genome Atlas, XpressO-Lung predicted spatial expression patterns of NAPSA, TP53I3, CD8A, TTF1, KRT7, CDKN2A, FOXO1, KEAP1, RB1 and TP53 on Dx-WSIs with AUCs ranging from 0.64 to 0.92. The predicted spatial gene expression patterns aligned with the known morphologic interactions of the tumor and its microenvironment, capturing biological events directly on Dx-WSIs. These spatio-morpho-molecular associations were further validated using immunohistochemistry on an external set of clinical samples at Dartmouth Health, demonstrating concordance between model-predicted spatial patterns and observed histomorphologic features. By coupling predictive performance with spatial interpretability of gene expression on Dx-WSIs, the XpressO-Lung model bridges histopathology and bulk-transcriptomics, enabling explainable spatio-morpho-genomic analyses to advance biomarker discovery, therapeutic stratification and precision oncology in LUAD.

items.abstract: Single-cell RNA technologies enable the routine acquisition of transcriptomic atlases. However, these molecular profiles are influenced by overlapping sources of variation. Since these covariates confound comparisons, data integration is the first step in most analyses. Three challenges remain: correcting strong batch effects, scaling to millions of cells, and modeling how covariates influence gene expression. To address these challenges, we developed PIANO, probabilistic inference autoencoder networks for multi-omics, a deep learning framework whose central feature is a generative model of gene expression data. Additionally, PIANO achieves robust integrations and trains 10× faster than previous methods. PIANO accurately integrates single-cell data across species and across single-cell and spatial transcriptomics modalities. As practical applications, PIANO models spatially resolved gene expression during Alzheimer's disease progression in human brains and integrates over 100 million cancer cells to model drug perturbations. In summary, PIANO's integration and generative modeling capabilities will empower novel insights for a wide range of future studies.

items.abstract: Accurate battery modeling is essential for reliable state estimation in modern applications, such as predicting the remaining discharge time and remaining discharge energy in battery management systems. Existing approaches face several limitations: model-based methods require a large number of physical parameters; data-driven methods rely heavily on labeled datasets; and current physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often lack aging adaptation, still depend on many physical parameters, or require continuous state regeneration. In this work, we propose SeqBattNet, a discrete-state PINN with built-in aging adaptation for battery modeling to predict terminal voltage during the discharge process. SeqBattNet consists of two components: (i) an encoder, implemented as the proposed Hierarchical Reasoning-GRU deep learning module, which generates cycle-specific aging adaptation parameters; and (ii) a decoder, based on the equivalent circuit model (ECM) combined with deep learning, which uses these parameters together with the input current to predict voltage. The model requires only a small number of readily available physical battery parameters and, when trained on data from a single cell, demonstrates promising predictive performance on unseen battery cells within the evaluated datasets. Experimental results on three benchmark datasets (TRI, RT-Batt, and NASA) show that SeqBattNet consistently outperforms classical sequence models and recent PINN baselines. On the NASA dataset, SeqBattNet reduces the RMSE from 0.0382 to 0.0257 for battery RW4 and from 0.0406 to 0.0253 for battery RW5 compared with the state-of-the-art PDB-Net, corresponding to relative improvements of approximately 32.7% and 37.7%.

items.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits high clinical and biological heterogeneity, which complicates the development of one-size-fits-all therapeutic strategies. Standard trial designs can mask subgroup-specific effects, highlighting the need to move towards precision neurology entailing multisystem genomics, biomarkers, and artificial intelligence (AI) integrative signals. The aim of the study is to critically synthesize and evaluate emerging strategies for drug optimization and individual therapeutic algorithms informed by genomic architecture, pharmacogenomics (PGx), and polygenic risk scores (PRS) with the opinion to resolve the controversy and unanswered question. Amplify the convergence into amyloid processing, lipid metabolism, and innate immunity seen from monogenic mutations and over 80 GWAS risk loci. Genotyping of CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 variants permits pharmacogenomic stratifications for the optimization of cholinesterase inhibitor and psychotropic dosing, thereby reducing adverse events. Variants of the alleles APOE ε4 and immune-related factors (e.g., FCGR3A) are significant in predicting the effects of ARIA associated with amyloid on anti-amyloid immunotherapy outcomes. PRS and deep phenotyping (including digital and fluid-based biomarkers) allow for the identification of unique biological endotypes (e.g., tau-dominant vs. vascular-inflammatory) that improve clinical trial enrichment and prognostication. This framework delineates molecular endotypes and translates CYP2D6 or APOE stratification into drug dosing and ARIA risk predictions. These biomarker-driven strategies shift AD management from a passive, reactive therapeutic scheme to an active, personalized one. Utilization of high-dimensional data streams via AI-driven learning health systems converts AD management from a reactive, symptom-based model to that which is proactive and hallmark biomarker-driven precision.

items.abstract: Abstract Background: Deltoid muscle volume varies across anatomical regions and population groups, with potential implications for intramuscular injection site selection. Evidence comparing middle and posterior deltoid volumes in vaccine-eligible populations is limited. Purpose: To compare middle and posterior deltoid muscle volumes by vaccine eligibility group, sex, and side. Methods: Deltoid muscles were manually segmented into anterior, middle and posterior regions in 43 UK Biobank Dixon MRI scans. A MONAI deep learning model trained on the annotations (Dice score = 0.78) segmented deltoid muscles of 5,239 participants, categorised by UK flu vaccination eligibility: A (≥65 years without risk conditions, n=1,760), B (≥65 years with risk conditions, n=1,744), and C (<65 with risk conditions, n=1,735). Bilateral-average posterior and middle volumes were compared using a paired t-test. A linear mixed-effects model assessed posterior-middle differences by group, sex and side. Results: Mean age was 66.7 ± 7.2 years and body mass index was 27.5 ± 5.7 kg/m2 (mean ± SD). Posterior deltoid volume exceeded the middle deltoid volume by 55.36 ml (95% CI, 54.14-56.58, p<0.0001). Posterior-middle differences were largest in Group A, followed by B and then C, greater in men, and greater on the right side (all p<0.0001). Mean segmentation-quality score was 4.27 ± 0.73 on a five-point Likert scale and weighted inter-observer kappa was 0.583 (95% CI, 0.452 - 0.713). Conclusions: Among individuals eligible for the UK flu immunisation, posterior deltoid volume was greater than middle deltoid volume. These findings support further anatomical assessment of the posterior deltoid as a potentially safer injection target.

items.abstract: Machine learning and deep learning models for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based brain tumor classification now report accuracies above 98% on public benchmarks, yet clinical use has not followed. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is presented as the bridge, but whether the explanations are correct is seldom tested. This scoping review, following PRISMA-ScR-compatible reporting conventions, searched PubMed, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, ScienceDirect and Google Scholar on 13 July 2026 for studies published from 2020 to 2026. Of 105 screened records, 50 primary studies and 12 reviews were included. The 22 primary studies extracted at full text were audited with a five-level explanation-validation hierarchy and a nine-item reporting-integrity instrument, organised around five research questions. Twelve of the 22 studies applied no explanation; seven assessed explanations by visual narration, one against a segmentation mask and two with internal faithfulness metrics. None validated explanations against radiologist annotation (0/22; 95% CI 0–15.4%). Median best accuracies were similar for handcrafted (98.5%), hybrid (98.7%) and end-to-end deep pipelines (98.1%). Only two studies reported a verifiable patient-level split, three validated externally, two released code, two reported calibration, and four reported headline figures inconsistent with their own data. Interpretability is better described by where it sits in the pipeline, and whether it has been checked, than by the modelling paradigm. We summarise tumor types, imaging modalities, classification and segmentation methods and public datasets, and propose a 12-item checklist that makes agreement with expert annotation, patient-level partitioning and deployment cost routine reporting items.

items.abstract: Nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease (NTM-LD) is highly heterogeneous, geographically and etiologically, hindering effective timely identification. Prior CT radiomics studies require manual segmentation of pathology. We developed a whole-lung CT radiomics-based machine learning approach and identified common features across two geographically distinct NTM-LD cohorts. We included 1,300 chest CT scans from China (871 TB; 429 NTM, Dataset 1) and 173 independent NTM cohort from the University of Alabama at Birmingham (UAB), US. Whole-lung regions were automatically segmented on each scan, and 85 quantitative radiomic features were extracted using a standardized image-processing pipeline. We evaluated two frameworks to assess model performance and generalizability: (1) training on Dataset 1 with external validation on Dataset 2, and (2) training on the combined cohort. Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) was used as the primary classification method. Cross-cohort concordance analysis was performed to evaluate the reproducibility of radiomic features across datasets. In Scenario 1, the LDA classifier trained on Dataset 1 achieved an AUC of 0.79 (95% CI, 0.73-0.84) with high specificity (0.91). On the external UAB cohort, the model achieved an AUC of 0.94 (95% CI, 0.90-0.97). In Scenario 2, the combined cohort model achieved an AUC of 0.81 (95% CI, 0.76-0.85) with improved sensitivity (0.61) and precision (0.82). Feature importance analysis identified 16 features consistently ranked among the top 20 in both scenarios, predominantly texture-based descriptors reflecting distinct parenchymal patterns between mycobacterial species. In conclusion, whole-lung CT radiomics enables interpretable NTM-LD classification across geographically distinct populations without manual annotation. Suggesting population-independent parenchymal signatures of NTM-LD.

items.abstract: Objective This retrospective, multicenter study evaluated whether MRI-based radiomics can predict the histological response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in Ewing sarcoma patients and compared their performance to that of radiological findings. Definitive histological assessment is only possible during surgery, potentially delaying therapy changes and increasing metastatic risk; therefore, a positive outcome would enable early adaptations. Methods Radiomics features were extracted from pre- and post-neoadjuvant (after first chemotherapy cycle) chemotherapy scans of patients treated from 2004 to 2020. Four machine learning models were trained using nested cross-validation to predict histological response, and their performance was compared to models trained on semantic features derived from expert radiological readings. Diagnostic performance was measured by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Results 96 patients (mean age, 19.9 ± 11.7 years; 41 women) with Ewing sarcoma were evaluated. Radiomics features related to low gray level intensity changes in T1 fat-saturated contrast-enhanced sequences showed the highest responder identification performance (AUROC, 0.62; 95% CI: 0.59, 0.65), surpassing the best radiological model, which relied on the relative change in maximum diameter of extratumoral soft tissue components (AUROC, 0.58; 95% CI: 0.56, 0.60). Radiomics models relying on pre-treatment T2-weighted data performed similarly (AUROC, 0.61; 95% CI: 0.58, 0.64), outperforming the clinical baseline (AUROC, 0.53; 95% CI: 0.51, 0.55). Conclusion MRI-based radiomics moderately identified responders to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, suggesting a role for earlier, tailored therapeutic strategies in Ewing sarcoma. Larger studies to validate these findings within a multimodal framework are warranted. Clinical relevance statement Radiomics extracted from MRI scans may aid with non-size tissue signals in early prediction of neoadjuvant chemotherapy response in Ewing sarcoma patients, potentially guiding personalized treatment adaptations, reducing delays for non-responders, and improving patient outcomes. These exploratory findings are complementary to standard size-based assessment from clinical routine, and warrant larger, prospective trials to be established.

items.abstract: Learning whole-body mobile manipulation requires demonstrations that coordinate bimanual actions with locomotion across extended workspaces. However, existing interfaces trade off direct robot control, perception and action alignment, and natural operator mobility, making such demonstrations difficult to collect. We introduce HALO, a human-aligned data collection system for whole-body mobile manipulation. The system aligns the operator's perception and action space with the robot while preserving direct physical feedback and natural locomotion. Operators guide the robot end-effectors through kinesthetic teaching and move a low-resistance platform without the deployed mobile base while performing bimanual manipulation. This interface enables more natural whole-body demonstrations, but the close human-robot coupling introduces discrepancies between the demonstration and deployment settings. We address these discrepancies with deployment-aligned demonstration processing, which calibrates and temporally aligns platform motion with the deployed base response and masks and inpaints demonstrator hands in recorded observations. Compared with Mobile ALOHA and VR teleoperation, HALO enables up to 2.9x faster demonstration collection while maintaining comparable or higher success rates. Policies trained with HALO perform precise manipulation tasks, including zip-tie fastening, and achieve a 73.3% success rate on a six-stage long-horizon mobile manipulation task involving repeated coordinated base and arm motion. Project page: https://robbyant-research.github.io/Lingbot-ALOHA/

items.abstract: Efficient batch execution of agent tasks is critical to LLM training and development workflows, including benchmark evaluation, synthetic-data generation, and RL rollouts. Since these tasks alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction, we present coordinated optimizations to reduce batch makespan, the time required to complete all tasks in a batch. For hybrid LLMs, a workload-based resource model guides GPU-memory allocation between key-value (KV) cache and recurrent state and provides a reference sample concurrency to exploit parallelism while limiting recomputation. Trajectory-aware routing and scheduling promote cache reuse while balancing worker load. Under constrained environment capacity, we decouple sample admission from environment execution and introduce Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling (CAAS), which prioritizes long chains using observed progress to shorten the batch tail. Controlled replay combines actual inference with recorded environment responses and durations for ablations of individual optimizations. Live evaluations with Ling-3.0-Flash and Ling-3.1-Flash on the BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch, and MCP-Atlas benchmarks demonstrate makespan reductions of 10.4% to 65.0%, while evaluation scores remain aligned. Furthermore, these methods have been successfully applied to training and evaluation workflows for the Ling-3.x model series, accelerating the model-development cycle.

items.abstract: Given a set of LEGO parts and an image of an assembled object, our task is to infer the pose of each part to assemble the object. In contrast with traditional 3D reconstruction, doing so requires satisfying discrete physical constraints, which provide structure but render the problem combinatorial and highly sensitive to small pose errors. To learn a prior over how parts fit together, we train a set-conditioned SE(3) flow model on procedurally generated assemblies. We then finetune this model to inject image conditioning, using 1% as much data. However, while the learned flow captures global structure, it does not enforce connectivity. To address this, we introduce an analytic connectivity-field guidance to pull predictions toward connected assemblies at test time. Through this, we demonstrate improved build quality with model size, pretraining, and guidance. We make our models and data available for research purposes at https://kulits.github.io/BrickFlow/

items.title: Dual Flow: Joint Image-Measurement Interpolation for Inverse Problems
items.summary: Generative model-based approaches to linear inverse problems typically use the acquired noisy measurement to condition or guide sampling in the image domain. In this work, we introduce Dual Flow, a novel joint-flow model for solving linear inverse problems by jointly estimating the clean image and corresponding noise-free measurement from the observation. Specifically, Dual Flow formulates image reconstruction and…
items.abstract: Generative model-based approaches to linear inverse problems typically use the acquired noisy measurement to condition or guide sampling in the image domain. In this work, we introduce Dual Flow, a novel joint-flow model for solving linear inverse problems by jointly estimating the clean image and corresponding noise-free measurement from the observation. Specifically, Dual Flow formulates image reconstruction and measurement denoising as a coupled estimation problem, using coupled flows in the image and measurement domains. The acquired noisy measurement is used only to initialize the measurement state; thereafter, image and measurement states are jointly updated based on their current values. By construction, the final image and measurement estimates are guaranteed to satisfy the underlying forward model. We derive the sampling updates for the joint-flow which involves the conditional mean of the clean image given the joint state. We further derive a closed-form expression for a sufficient statistic of the joint state and show that the required conditional mean can be obtained by solving an image-domain Gaussian denoising problem involving operator-dependent, correlated noise. We train a velocity-prediction network using this formulation to estimate the conditional mean from the derived sufficient statistic. Extensive experiments across various linear inverse problems and image datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both distortion metrics and perceptual quality. Dual Flow requires no hyperparameter tuning beyond the number of inference steps and achieves shorter reconstruction times than competing methods. Additional analyses assess robustness to model mismatch, as well as the ability to generate diverse plausible reconstructions and characterize reconstruction uncertainty.

items.title: EvenVLM: A Text and Multimodal Dataset for the Even Language with Vision-Language Fine-Tuning
items.summary: We present EvenVLM, the first text and multimodal (VQA) dataset for Even (Lamut), an endangered Northern Tungusic language spoken by approximately 6,800 people in Siberia. Our dataset comprises 50,521 structured Even-Russian entries extracted from dictionary and phrasebook sources via GPT-4o Mini-based parsing, from which we synthetically generate 107,543 training examples spanning translation, grammar, reading…
items.abstract: We present EvenVLM, the first text and multimodal (VQA) dataset for Even (Lamut), an endangered Northern Tungusic language spoken by approximately 6,800 people in Siberia. Our dataset comprises 50,521 structured Even-Russian entries extracted from dictionary and phrasebook sources via GPT-4o Mini-based parsing, from which we synthetically generate 107,543 training examples spanning translation, grammar, reading comprehension, and semantic classification. To address tokenization inefficiency on Even's agglutinative morphology, we propose a three-step tokenizer expansion algorithm that adds Even-specific graphemes (eng, oe, o-umlaut), whitelisted vocabulary, and BPE merges, reducing average tokens per word by 27% (4.99 to 3.64). Using LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen3-VL-4B, we adapt the model for text tasks (0.53% trainable parameters, rank 32) and separately for visual question answering (rank 64, frozen vision encoder). Our best configuration achieves 11.4% exact match and a 13.6 weighted score on text benchmarks, 0.1283 chrF for sentence translation, and 65% accuracy on VQA (up from 0% for the base model and text-only fine-tuning). We release our datasets, evaluation benchmarks, and training pipeline to support further research on Even and other low-resource languages.

items.title: Alloy: A Multi-Material Physics Engine for Robot Learning
items.summary: Robots handle much more than rigid objects: towels, cables, water, sand. The simulators used to train robots at scale are strongest on rigid bodies, and adding another material usually means a second engine and hand-written glue between the two. We present Alloy, an open-source physics engine for robot learning in which rigid robots, cloth, cables, liquids, granular material and soft bodies share one scene. Each…
items.abstract: Robots handle much more than rigid objects: towels, cables, water, sand. The simulators used to train robots at scale are strongest on rigid bodies, and adding another material usually means a second engine and hand-written glue between the two. We present Alloy, an open-source physics engine for robot learning in which rigid robots, cloth, cables, liquids, granular material and soft bodies share one scene. Each object is described once; Alloy assigns it to a solver suited to its material, couples the solvers inside every control step, and runs the scene in many parallel worlds on one GPU, or on a CPU. Every world carries a health grade, to help tell a failure of the physics from a failure of the policy. Alloy is built on Newton, MuJoCo Warp and Warp, and it is written to be driven by coding agents: its documentation ships inside the package, every error names its fix, and the engine is exposed as tools over the Model Context Protocol. In a cold test, agents that had never seen Alloy installed a pre-release from the package index and trained policies for walking, cable handling and pouring on a single GPU. We also report how throughput grows with the number of worlds, depth-camera throughput, agreement with closed-form references, and a reliability test over a thousand worlds.

items.title: Parsed, Plausible, Wrong: Output Format Controls Silent Errors in Small-Model Semantic Parsing
items.summary: A small fine-tuned parser that emits a well-formed but wrong tree fails silently: nothing downstream can tell. We ask whether the output format, a free design choice, controls how often this happens. On the PIZZA ordering benchmark we fine-tune two sub-billion models (Qwen3.5-0.8B and LFM2.5-350M) with LoRA on six lossless encodings of the same target tree, from 44.3 down to 10.9 tokens per order, including two…
items.abstract: A small fine-tuned parser that emits a well-formed but wrong tree fails silently: nothing downstream can tell. We ask whether the output format, a free design choice, controls how often this happens. On the PIZZA ordering benchmark we fine-tune two sub-billion models (Qwen3.5-0.8B and LFM2.5-350M) with LoRA on six lossless encodings of the same target tree, from 44.3 down to 10.9 tokens per order, including two matched-length pairs that vary surface form at fixed length. Across 300 runs (5 training pool sizes, 5 seeds) with a hierarchical bootstrap and Holm correction fixed before the results were read, shortening alone never helps, but writing the target in ordinary words does. The word encoding is the most accurate format on both models (87.5% vs. 85.8% exact match for the native s-expression on Qwen) while emitting 4.1x fewer tokens, and it cuts the silent error rate by 2.3x on Qwen and 1.8x on LFM2, separating at every pool size. Error analysis locates much of the gain in negation. All runs also learn to refuse off-menu input (held out: 95.9-99.0% handled) and to apply in-utterance self-corrections. Strict refusal has a measured price: 2.1-10.1% of real, mostly polite, orders are refused.

items.title: Interpreting Coding Agents Through Their Behavioral Trajectories
items.summary: Standard coding-agent benchmarks primarily evaluate binary task success, treating execution as a black box and obscuring the behaviors that produce those outcomes. We analyze a large corpus of 143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 unique models. To enable comparisons across heterogeneous agent interfaces, we develop a rule-based parser that maps raw execution traces to high-level…
items.abstract: Standard coding-agent benchmarks primarily evaluate binary task success, treating execution as a black box and obscuring the behaviors that produce those outcomes. We analyze a large corpus of 143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 unique models. To enable comparisons across heterogeneous agent interfaces, we develop a rule-based parser that maps raw execution traces to high-level actions such as repository search, file editing, and test execution, and audit its predictions against a six-model consensus reference on 500 events. We find that agents with similar solve rates can nevertheless differ substantially in how they explore, modify and verify code. Moreover, without using task outcomes, token counts, or tool names as features, aggregate behavioral profiles retrieve the corresponding agent stack across disjoint repository sets and programming languages, although task composition is not fully controlled in the cross-repository setting. Through analyses of frontier models and agent scaffolds, we further show that scaffold choice and reasoning effort systematically shift agents' search, editing, and testing behavior. We release the deterministic parser together with the full annotation and analysis pipeline alongside an annotated trajectory subset.

items.title: eDMD: Endpoint Distribution Matching for Few-Step Diffusion Distillation
items.summary: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) has emerged as a leading paradigm for distilling diffusion models into few-step students, where an auxiliary fake score model tracks the student's distribution and the discrepancy between the teacher and fake predictions drives the student toward the teacher. In multi-step distillation, although only the student's final output is delivered, existing methods train the fake…
items.abstract: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) has emerged as a leading paradigm for distilling diffusion models into few-step students, where an auxiliary fake score model tracks the student's distribution and the discrepancy between the teacher and fake predictions drives the student toward the teacher. In multi-step distillation, although only the student's final output is delivered, existing methods train the fake model on intermediate states or across all denoising steps. Consequently, the student's update signal becomes entangled with intermediate distributions, which can distort the matching direction and remain nonzero even after the student's final outputs already match the teacher distribution. To resolve this mismatch, we propose Endpoint Distribution Matching Distillation (eDMD), which trains a single shared fake model exclusively on the student's final outputs and uses it to correct every denoising step. Our theoretical analysis proves that this endpoint reference guarantees that the distribution matching term vanishes if and only if the student's final output distribution matches the teacher's, regardless of intermediate distributions. Beyond the fake reference, we further strengthen teacher supervision through a precise teacher (PT) that replaces single-step guided predictions with short multi-step trajectories on the final noise interval, paired with a calibrated query density for intermediate steps. Experiments on SD3-Medium, FLUX.2-klein (4B and 9B), and Qwen-Image-2.1 demonstrate that eDMD consistently outperforms existing distribution matching methods for 4-step generation.

items.title: Evidence-Governed Adoption of Self-Generated Updates in Autonomous AI Agents
items.summary: Autonomous agents modify prompts, memories, tools, workflows, and policies using interaction histories. Yet a plausible modification is not necessarily suitable for persistent adoption: candidate selection is adaptive, evaluators may be imperfect, and local gains can hide degradation against an earlier baseline. We introduce Evidence-Governed Evolution (EGE), a framework for governing adoption of self-generated…
items.abstract: Autonomous agents modify prompts, memories, tools, workflows, and policies using interaction histories. Yet a plausible modification is not necessarily suitable for persistent adoption: candidate selection is adaptive, evaluators may be imperfect, and local gains can hide degradation against an earlier baseline. We introduce Evidence-Governed Evolution (EGE), a framework for governing adoption of self-generated agent modifications. EGE separates candidate generation from confirmatory adoption, evaluates frozen candidates on fresh paired audits, requires meaningful improvement on a prespecified primary objective, protects declared capabilities through reference-relative non-inferiority tests, and applies governance constraints before bounded canary deployment. We establish an evaluator-calibrated simultaneous lower-bound construction for a countable sequence of adaptively generated candidates. It combines candidate-wise Hoeffding bounds with independent calibration samples comparing the operational evaluator with a prespecified reference procedure. We also formalise reference replacement through bridge tests, derive a cumulative degradation bound along a versioned reference lineage, and provide an audit-planning condition relating effect-size margin, sample sizes, and acceptance probability. A Monte Carlo stress test illustrates calibration under candidate-dependent evaluator optimism; it is a stylised statistical experiment, not an evaluation of a deployed agent. The guarantees are conditional on bounded paired scores, fresh sampling, a valid reference-evaluation construct, and declared evaluation distributions; they do not establish universal agent safety or robustness to arbitrary distribution shift.

items.title: When Expert Disagreement Hurts: Prestige and Selectivity in LLM Decision Revision
items.summary: When language models revise a decision after another agent disagrees, neither reversal counts nor final accuracy shows whether they are fixing mistakes or abandoning correct answers. We introduce a controlled two-pass audit that holds the question, the evidence, and the model's initial answer fixed and varies only the revision context: neutral reflection, anonymous disagreement, or disagreement attributed to a…
items.abstract: When language models revise a decision after another agent disagrees, neither reversal counts nor final accuracy shows whether they are fixing mistakes or abandoning correct answers. We introduce a controlled two-pass audit that holds the question, the evidence, and the model's initial answer fixed and varies only the revision context: neutral reflection, anonymous disagreement, or disagreement attributed to a domain expert. For binary decisions the accounting is exact: revision raises accuracy only if it is selective enough, reversing wrong answers more than a/(1-a) times as often as correct ones, where a is initial accuracy (nine times at 90%). Across five models and 1,989 evidence-grounded decisions in medicine, science, and law, no model clears this bar under expert disagreement, and accuracy falls by up to 16.1 points. The expert label, a prestige cue, adds reversals for four of the five models, yet its effect on accuracy ranges from a 5.2-point loss to a 2.4-point gain, so reversal counts are a poor proxy for harm. With identical arguments from both sources, the label still raises reversal for three proprietary models and in a pooled analysis of four newer models. Models also respond to stated source reliability. Revision pipelines should therefore be evaluated with paired, conditional metrics, per model and protocol.

items.title: Dataset Distillation via Drifting
items.summary: The task of dataset distillation concerns the learning of a small set of synthetic samples that can serve as an effective replacement for a large real dataset when used for downstream tasks. While many solutions have been proposed since the problem's inception, most of them primarily seek to optimize the distilled data with respect to a classifier. In this work, we propose a new distillation method that learns a set…
items.abstract: The task of dataset distillation concerns the learning of a small set of synthetic samples that can serve as an effective replacement for a large real dataset when used for downstream tasks. While many solutions have been proposed since the problem's inception, most of them primarily seek to optimize the distilled data with respect to a classifier. In this work, we propose a new distillation method that learns a set of samples such that they directly approximate the per-class data distribution. Specifically, we "drift" our distilled data in the latent space of a feature extractor such that they move both toward the real data and away from each other without using a classification objective. We find that our drifted data cover the real distribution significantly better than existing methods while still serving as powerful training samples for classification. Furthermore, we showcase our method's use as a visualization tool for better interpreting models and extend it beyond images to other modalities. Our work advances the frontier of dataset distillation, offering a novel synthesis method and proposing distribution-based metrics as a complementary evaluation. More broadly, our findings help address the growing need to understand both data and models by uncovering more about how they interact.

items.title: Unfinished-Bench: Measuring Rule Violations by Persistent Agents in Realistic Work Environments
items.summary: AI agents are increasingly equipped with persistence toward task completion to run delegated work autonomously for long periods, under many unstated constraints from internal documents and other people's authority. When completion requires violating a rule, the agent must decide alone, yet benchmarks of instruction-rule conflicts state the rule in the prompt or keep it hidden and do not evaluate persistence. We…
items.abstract: AI agents are increasingly equipped with persistence toward task completion to run delegated work autonomously for long periods, under many unstated constraints from internal documents and other people's authority. When completion requires violating a rule, the agent must decide alone, yet benchmarks of instruction-rule conflicts state the rule in the prompt or keep it hidden and do not evaluate persistence. We present Unfinished-Bench, a benchmark that gives models persistence in autonomous runs without a user, in realistic work environments with embedded rules. In each of its 97 scenarios across 7 organizations and 7 risk categories, the goal and the rule cannot both hold. We find that persistence raised violations of a rule in an internal document from 32.2% to 43.6%, five times the 8.5% for the same rule stated by the user. Of the document-rule violations, 98.3% occurred after the rule was displayed, and in 89% of a judged sample the agent first wrote down the rule. Violations of rules placed in the environment without user oversight can lead to serious incidents, so persistence-driven risks need to be evaluated. Benchmark documentation: https://francis21c.github.io/unfinished-bench/

items.title: Kezek: Splitting Mono Two-Person Conversations into Per-Speaker Tracks for Full-Duplex Dialogue Data
items.summary: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models learn turn-taking, overlaps and backchannels from conversations recorded with one channel per speaker, but most available conversational audio is a single mono mix. We present Kezek, a model that turns a mono recording of exactly two people into one track per person with the original length and timing; overlaps and short replies ("yeah", "mm-hm") stay on the track of the person who…
items.abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models learn turn-taking, overlaps and backchannels from conversations recorded with one channel per speaker, but most available conversational audio is a single mono mix. We present Kezek, a model that turns a mono recording of exactly two people into one track per person with the original length and timing; overlaps and short replies ("yeah", "mm-hm") stay on the track of the person who said them. Kezek decides who speaks when and who is who once for the whole recording (stage 1: a two-voice activity model guided by a speaker fingerprint trained to be insensitive to phase), and a conditioned time-domain separator only carries out that decision (stage 2), with outputs that always sum to the input. Standard separation metrics miss the failures that matter for dialogue data, so we report short-reply retention, leakage onto the other person's solo, channel swaps and coverage. Against the open pipeline pyannote -> DialogueSidon on the same recordings, Kezek keeps more short replies (0.83 vs. 0.69 on Open Yap test; 0.80 vs. 0.71 over the other's speech on unseen telephone speech from CallHome English), mostly because it returns the whole recording while the external pipeline drops part of it (on the audio both return, reply retention is about the same: 0.859 vs. 0.865 on Open Yap); it also leaks less, swaps channels less often, and runs 4-5 times faster (about 230 hours of audio per GPU-hour). We also report negative results and an ideal-mask ceiling that locate the remaining gap: quiet replies under a louder voice. Code and weights are released under permissive licences.

items.title: LightTAR: Light and Fast Target-Aware Representations for Multimodal Tabular Learning
items.summary: Multimodal tabular learning involves classification and regression on tables combining structured numerical and categorical features with unstructured text and images. These unstructured fields are commonly represented by pretrained encoder embeddings reduced with principal component analysis (PCA). This reduction prioritizes input variance but may overlook information relevant to predicting the target. We introduce…
items.abstract: Multimodal tabular learning involves classification and regression on tables combining structured numerical and categorical features with unstructured text and images. These unstructured fields are commonly represented by pretrained encoder embeddings reduced with principal component analysis (PCA). This reduction prioritizes input variance but may overlook information relevant to predicting the target. We introduce LightTAR, a simple, inexpensive method that adapts dimensionality reduction to the prediction task. LightTAR augments the standard PCA representation with a few target-aware features extracted jointly from the final and an intermediate encoder layer using regularized partial least squares (PLS). We evaluate LightTAR with 21 tabular models, including tree ensembles, neural networks, and tabular foundation models. LightTAR improves average predictive performance for all models and, averaged across models, improves prediction on almost every MulTaBench dataset. These gains come with a small increase in total runtime relative to PCA representations. LightTAR integrates directly into existing encoding pipelines, improving tabular learners' predictive performance without modifying the encoder or the learner.

items.title: Duo: A Reciprocal World Model for Full-Duplex Interaction

items.abstract: In this report, we introduce the Reciprocal World Model (RWM) and present Duo v1, a full-duplex world model that continuously perceives audiovisual inputs while responding to users in real time. The RWM treats intelligence and physical reality as equally fundamental to what constitutes a world. Existing world models largely focus on simulating the latter, leaving reasoning and decision-making as external controls rather than intrinsic parts of the world itself. In RWM, we identify two equally fundamental capabilities: Intent, which provides the cognition underlying world interactions, and Realization, which generates coherent audio-visual behavior. To realize this formulation, Duo v1 introduces three key technical designs: (1) Leveraging autoregressive modeling for continuous interaction reasoning and participation decisions, rather than restricting it to instruction understanding for diffusion models. (2) Constructing chunk-specific conditions and synchronize tokens across Intent and Realization on a unified timeline. Module-specific attention masks enforce causal dependencies both within and across chunks, preventing access to future inputs. (3) Mitigating distribution shift in both modules through dual rollout distillation, training on autoregressively generated Intent tokens and synthesized audiovisual histories from Realization. Both modules continuously perceive real-time audio, video, and text, enabling full-duplex interaction with spontaneous conversations and interruptions. Beyond conversation, users can share real objects, reshape virtual scenes, guide assistants, or play audiovisual games without mouse or keyboard controls. The release of Duo v1 makes our first step, with the next version coming soon. We look forward to broader exploration of this emerging field.

items.abstract: Alveolar echinococcosis, caused by the parasite Echinococcus multilocularis, is a potentially lethal disease that requires the development of new medical treatments. Current drug screening methods depend on manual microscopy to count stained and unstained protoscoleces to determine viability, a process that is often slow and subject to human error. This study developed machine learning models to automate the classification of protoscolex survival to accelerate drug discovery. A total of 111 images containing 1,302 protoscoleces stained with eosin or methylene blue were analyzed. Histogram-based image features were extracted and subjected to preprocessing, dimensionality reduction, and feature selection. Six classification algorithms were trained using five-fold cross-validation and evaluated on internal test sets and an external validation set via receiver operating characteristic curve analysis. Results indicated that several models were highly effective, with internal test scores ranging from 0.8905 to 0.9467 and external validation scores between 0.7772 and 0.8214. Models based on support vector machine, logistic regression, and linear discriminant analysis demonstrated promising discriminatory performance across both internal and external datasets. The study concludes that machine learning can accurately and objectively classify the viability of protoscoleces based on stained images. This automated approach offers significant potential for standardizing high-throughput drug screening and facilitating the discovery of new therapeutics against this neglected zoonotic disease.

items.abstract: The scarcity of large, diverse, and unbiased protein–ligand binding datasets limits the performance of machine learning approaches in drug discovery, particularly for understudied proteins. The Target 2035 initiative aims to address this gap by generating open-access binding data for more than 2,000 human proteins, a goal whose value depends on maximizing the diversity of the selected targets. Because proteins with different folds can share chemically analogous binding sites, we reasoned that pocket similarity, rather than sequence or fold similarity, is the appropriate criterion for selecting representative targets that maximize coverage of the human pocketome. Here, we use PocketVec, an alignment-free descriptor of binding sites, to map the human globular pocketome, identifying 51,535 predicted druggable pockets across 15,559 proteins. A two-level hierarchical clustering, first within protein families and then across the whole proteome, grouped these pockets into 1,865 clusters of chemically similar binding sites. After discarding 533 clusters containing pockets with known ligands, we selected the 100 most populated of the remaining 1,332 ligand-free clusters and chose two high-quality representative pockets per cluster, ranked by their resemblance to known ligand-binding sites. Finally, we implemented two complementary prioritization strategies, one favoring structurally unexplored proteins and the other proteins amenable to experimental follow-up, and selected 200 pockets from 100 different clusters from each strategy, with 89 clusters in common. Both selections cover over 10,000 pockets in ∼5,600 proteins, approximately 36% of the human proteins with annotated druggable pockets, which represents a 2.8-to 4.4-fold increase in the number of covered pockets, domains, and proteins than random selection baselines. This pocket-based framework offers a principled strategy to select diverse targets for Target 2035 and other large-scale protein–ligand data generation efforts in chemical biology.
